HANKOW, China, Aug. 26.-Vice
Consul John Davies, jr., returned
tonight from an investigation in
Kiangsi Province, where the status
Of Americans had been in doubt, and
reported none had been harmed.


Before Davies left here August 9,
mystery had surrounded the situa-
ton of the Rev. L. w. Holland,
Methodist missionary from Pasa-
dena, Calf, who had been arrested
two months before on charges of
carrying on anti-Japanese propa-
ganda.


The vice consul, who visited Kiu-
kiang, Kuling and Nanchang, said
that although Mr.. Holland and the
other Americans were well, their
movements were restricted by Japa-
nese soldiers.


Foreigners at Kiukiang have not
been permitted to re-enter their con-
cession areas since the japanese took
the city, Mr.. Davies found, and they
are continuing to live in foreign oil
company quarters outside Kiukiang

Representative James H. Fay,
Democrat, of New York was in
Walter Reed Hospital today await

few inches above the place where
the limb was amputated during the
World War.

been bothering the Representative

JERUSALEM, May Is @.-
Jewish leaders were reported yes
terday to be drafting the most
drastic plans they ever have pro-
posed in an effort to defeat Britains
expected new policy for Palestine.


Reliable sources here expressed
belief that Britain might put the
white paper, scheduled for issuance
Wednesday, into effect Immediately
after its publication and said Jews
would make every effort to pre-
vent what they generally believe
will mean the end of Palestine as
their national home.


David Ben Gurion, chairman of
the Palestine Jewish Agency EXecu-
tive, met with Jewish leaders from
all over the Holy Land to consider
anti-White paper plans and consid
cradle activity was noted also
among other Jewish political
leaders.


There was no immediate indica-
ton. however, Of what form their
plans might take.


Palestine authorities, meanwhile,
apparently made plans to put the
new policy into force


All illegal Jewish immigrants in
concentration camps at Haifa and
Sarafand have been released and
their numbers are being deducted
from forthcoming Jewish immigra-
ton schedules.


The government also began re-
leasing Arabs detained in military
camps during British Army maneu-
vers, although control was being
kept over them through daily police
checkups.

HAIFA, Palestine, April "a
Police fired into the air today to
disperse crowds watching the sailing
of 270 refugees who were refused
entry to the Holy Land because
they had no passports.

here as protest against deporting
the refugees to an unknown des-

captain had been released from

refugees into the country.


Another party of 218 Jewish i'm
migrants, including SO women and
10 children, who allegedly had en-
tered Palestine illegally, was found
wandering along the coast yester-
day between Jaffa and GAIA. All
were arrested.

Instructions went out today to
locals of the International Union
OF Operating Engineers to carry
out the decision of a special adjust
ment committee settling a Nation
wide jurisdictional dispute between
the engineers union and the in
ternational Brotherhood of Team
sters, Chauffeurs, Stablemen and
Helpers of America.


John Possehl, president of the
operating engineers, directed local
unions to accept into full member
ship, without initiation fee, former
members of the teamsters' union
placed under the jurisdiction of the
engineers union. He also author
lied local unions to transfer men,
bers who are now under the juris-
diction of the teamsters' union.
The transfers were made contingent
upon the members being in good
standing.


The Special Adjustment Commit
tee of the Building and Construc-
ton Trades Department., American
Federation of Labor, handed down
its decision on October 27. The
ruling provided that all power
driven equipment used exclusively
to transport materials and other
matter for building or other con-
struction comes within the juris-
diction of the teamsters' union.
All power-driven equipment used
on any and all types of building
and construction work and all
power-driven equipment that has
been in dispute between the two
unions were placed under the juris-
diction of the operating engineers
union.
headline:

To Accept Teamsters

VALETTA. Malta, April 24.-This
key center of Great Britain's naval
power seethed with excitement to-
day as authorities rushed prepara-
tions for suddenly announced
cruise in the Eastern Mediterranean
Of more than 80 Warships of the


Mediterranean fleet.


Among the vessels ordered to
steam eastward Wednesday-the
destination and purpose undisclosed
are the battleships Warspite, Bar
ham and Malaga, the cruisers
Shropshire, London and Devonshire,
% destroyers and the hospital ship
Maine, with one guardian cruiser
and one destroyer.


Several British Warships have ar
rived at Alexandria, near the north
ern end of the strategic Suez Canal,
from Malta within the past few
days. The bulk of the Mediter-
ranean fleet has been concentrated
! at Malta since the Italian invasion
of Albania.


An undisclosed number of REIN
forcements arrived at Alexandria
yesterday. Britain and Egypt now
have at least $4,000 troops for
Egyptian border defenses.

second undefeated boxing season in
three years under the coaching of
Coach Heinie Miller was realized be-
fore $500 spectators here tonight.
Aided by the opposition's fouling,
the Terps preserved their clean slate
and smeared Armys hitherto un-
blemished record, 4l2-3l2, in an up
set.


The Southern Conference cham
pions, laboring under an extremely
heavy burden after yielding a 80
lead to the West Point punchers,
rallied to snatch four successive de-
cisions and draw for its third vic
tory of a season that also included
a trio of ties.


Army virtually fouled itself out of
a triumph, forcing Referee Elder
Craft to issue repeated warnings,
and in both the 145-pound and 175-
pound engagements the Cadets
might have grasped victories had
they not been guilty of costly tactics.


Army Off to Flying Start. 4.


Maryland elected to forfeit the
heavyweight bout and its chances of
winning appeared slim when Army
captured the first two tiffs. Walter
Lavendusky, 1888 Eastern intercol-
legiate bantamweight champion, ex-
ploded right hands off angular
George DORIS anatomy, survived
some solid lefts. and continued to
bounce short rights off DORIS chin
and midsection to take the 100
pound class decision.


The battery for the 127-pound
argument was Walter Clement of
Army pitching and Bob Bradley of
Maryland catching. at least in the
first round. In the second session
Bradley found the range, but after
he twice had staggered Clement he
met with a minor disaster in the
form of butt. The resulting cash
over his right eye and flow of blood
stopped the scrap after l minute 25
seconds of the second round, with
Clement credited with a technical
knockout.


Maryland Gets Busy.


Then Maryland went to work.
Flinging his last leather for the
Terps, semi-bald Benny Alperstein
floored a game, but outclassed Harry
Rising, local lad, once in the first
round and twice in the third to win
the 135-pound division decision.


Rising made the mistake of rush.
Ing Benny and was greeted enthusi-
astically with authoritative pokes to
the head


Personifed perpetual motion,
Army's Tom Stanley. Eastern in
tercollegiate champion last year,
patterned his punching after pro-
fessional standards and for that
reason was dealt a defeat by Nathan
Askin in the 145-pound class. Shan
ley insisted on infighting. taboo in
collegiate circles, and that was in
strumental in his losing.


The awkward Askin, his left eye
sliced in the second round, suddenly
developed vicious streak in the
third canto and poured steady
stream of leather to Shanleys face,
but the Army fighters fouling was
the factor that swung the bout to
Maryland.


Cronin Scores Easily.


Frank Cronin, Maryland 155-
FOUNDER, terminated his college feud-
ing with nine successive victories
by easily outpointing classic-fea-
tured Dick Negley. Cronin, senior,
who pulled On boxing gloves for the
first time this year, ended per-
sonally undefeated season impress
sively, but Negley took his severe
shellacking standing all the way.


Don Hull of Army and Newton
Cox of Maryland danced merrily
through two rounds, but Cox syn
chronized the only persuasive punch
of the bout with the bell ending
the third round to drop Hull heavily
and earn the verdict.


Assured at least a draw but zeal
Gus to climax its record with a win,
Maryland entered the decisive light
heavyweight bout an underdog. and
although the Terps' Morton Stein
bach was dropped with a stiff left
to the midsection and sizzling right



nevertheless was given a draw with

Fouls Costly to Taylor.


Taylor's left hooks were more dis
tressing than Steinbachs jabs in
the first round, but the Maryland
lad found an easy target in the
second round, repeatedly swapping
the Army fighters head back with
left hooks and jabs. Taylor PROB
ably would nave won the fight on
his third-round display, but he
landed below the equator several
times and was penalized severely.

insisted on strict adherence to the
concordat.

Rust closed the theological school
yesterday after differences with the
cardinal over appointment to the
Munich faculty of Prof. Barton of
the Braunsberg, East Prussia, Ro-
man Catholic academy. About 1900
students were affected by the closing.


Catholics said Barton was given
his chair without consultation with
Cardinal Won Faulhaber and that
consent of the Archbishop was nee
essary under the concordat. The
cardinal forbade students to attend
Barions classes. and the boycott
lasted through the winter term,
now closed.

After underdog Yale, playing in
spring football, had outfought heav.

ment.

the strangest and greatest human

Hitler's swastika-emblemed bombers had

all school children, all nursing and expectant
mothers all hospital patients and all the blind

More than two million of them moved out

her mind this scene of moving millions and
had blueprinted it for smooth action when the
hour should strike.

chairman of the Women's Voluntary Services
for Civil Defense.

mainly from her headquarters in sandbagged
Office block in Westminster. but her hand

BY the Associated Press.


ALLENSVILLE, Pa, Aug. 21.-
This tiny hamlet, not even a dot on
most maps, became the center Of
the world today for hundreds of
somberly-garbed. quiet plain peo-
ple"-delegates to the general con-
ference of the Mennonite Church.
Frugal, averse to a display Of
worldly things, they have come from
the United States, Canada, South
America, Africa and India for a
week of sober discussions in circus
like tents. Two thousand are ex-
pected before the conference ends.


Members of the far-fung sect,
whose forefathers migrated from
Germany more than q century ago,
placed peace and industrial strife
near the top of discussion topics.


Their sober mien, their dark-hued
and plainly-cut garments distinguish
them from the towns inhabitants.
Their women folk wear little hood
like caps, resembling abbreviated
-bonnets. Silk stockings are
taboo.

WINDSOR. England, April 22.-All

beth are sure to have the roast beef
and Yorkshire pudding of old Eng
land on their trip next month to

don, Rene Roussin. the court chef,

battle cruiser Repulse how to pre-

and Queen like.


Roussin gave the naval cooks and
stewards a workout in Windsor

likes an early breakfast-at 7:30-
and a three-course luncheon. He
prefers plain food such as hot joints
with cabbage and potatoes.


The most difficult task for the
packers was the boxing of the deli
cate crinoline style gowns ordered
by the Queen for the tour, which
will begin with the sailing of the
Repulse from Portsmouth May 6.


These are among her majesty's
favorites. They are tulles and satins,
mostly white. Some are richly en-
broidered in gold and others in sill
yer. All skirts for evening just

whats this about ghosts?"

asthmatic Australian tennis team

NEW YORK, Oct. 7.-Americar
travellers this winter will, have q
wide variety of destinations in spite
of the European war, and travel
within and between the Americas
promises to reach banner proper
tions, according to the monthly
survey and forecast of travel ten
dencies released yesterday by the
American Express Travel Service.


The survey is, gathered through
the company's domestic and foreign
Offices and Is checked with all lead
ing railroads, steamships and air
lines.


Americans are already adjusting
themselves to the world situation
and preparing to spend their win
ter vacations in our Southern resort
States, in Latin America, the West
Indies and Hawaii" states Douglas
Malcolm of the Travel Service.


Domestic escorted tours and the
Independent travel plan bid fair
to come into much wider popularity
The use of domestic railroads and
airlines for pure pleasure travel is
bound to increase, and all winter
resorts will be given q decided
impetus"


Local Travel Expected.


october, the survey finds, will be
a month of local rather than of
long-distance travel. Excellent hunt
ing is promised in most States. The
football season will get under way,
with resultant heavy travel over
week ends. The New York Worlds
Fair, which now has 50-cent gate,
will continue through the month,
and the Golden Gate International
Exposition in San Francisco will be
open until October 20. The theater
season will get under way In New
York, and starting october 13 San
Francisco will have its fall opera
series. Northern States will be in
fall dress and Vermont will cele-
brate on October 16 with a State
wide Autumn Foliage Festival.


In the immediate rail picture, the
Northern Pacific reports the best
September in its history for its east
ern territory. The Missouri Pacific
finds that travel to Mexico has
shown very noticeable increases in
the last two or three weeks, and the
Union Pacific expects October to
show gains over the same month a
year ago. The Santa Fe reports
traffic for September ahead of last
year.


New Train Makes Debut.


In the equipment field. the Chi
cago & North Western has just put
into service two new streamlined
and Diesel-powered "40O's." During
the month the Lehigh Valley will
put in service the first of 10 new
coaches. The Exposition Flyer, op-
Grated jointly this summer by the
Burlington, Denver & Rio Grande
Western and Western Pacific, will
be kept in service the year around.


During October all railroads will
lay plans for winter traffic, the sur
vey says. The Santa Fe reports
that every one expects exceptionally
good traffic to California and Ari-
zona. The Florida season looks very
promising to the Atlantic Coast Line,
and both that road and the Seaboard
Air Line will provide faster and
better service this winter to the
West Coast resorts of Florida. The
Great Northern looks for a very
definite boom in domestic travel.


The Rock Island expects very good
and California business this
winter and the Southern Pacific
finds the outlook very promising.
Mexico should have a wonderful
winter, according to the Missouri
Pacific, and the American Express
and other travel companies are now
planning tours there, Both Cana
dian Pacific and the Canadian Ma
tional are now laying plans for the
ski season in Canada. Americans.
these railroads report, can enter
Canada with the same ease and
facility that they always have. The
Northern Pacific finds growing in
terest in Grand Coulee Dam and
this winter will open new ski runs
at Martin, Wash, at the top of the
Cascade Mountains.


Airlines See Upturn.


Airlines, like railroads. expect
banner traffic, with Southern resorts
enjoying greatest favor. Pan-Amer-
lcan looks for heavy travel to the
West Indies and South America,
and Eastern is buying three new
sleeper transports for its New York
Brownsville service. American,
which has just ordered 20 new 81
planes for next spring,
expects a good October, and Eastern
estimates So per cent increase in
revenue passengers for September.
Other news is that Trans Canada
Alrlines is putting in a two-city
service between Montreal and To-
ronto, to supplement its other flights,
and that T. w. A. expects excellent
Southern winter travel.


In the steamship field the travel
picture is rapidly clarifying. Some
September cruises showed a passen-
ger decline, but every indication is
that West Indies voyages will be Of
fered as usual this winter by Amer.
lean and other neutral ships. Cuba
Mail reports that it is optimistic
about the coming season, and that
both Cuban and Mexican traffic are
ahead of last year. United Fruit
and other lines are running their
cruises as usual, and Clyde Mallory
reports that bookings on comparable
sailings have been better than last
year.

Faced with one of the toughest
schedules in recent years, but backed
by IS players including IL lettermen,
Coach Herman Littman today ex-
pressed belief that his Roosevelt
High School basket ball team would
enjoy a highly successful season.


Busy getting the large squad into
shape for its opening game against
Baltimore City College in Baltimore
Friday, Littman sees great chance
for the team and hints that it might
move up notch or two over its
third place ranking in last winters S
interhigh series.

petition.

isingly and such junior varsity play
ers as William Penn, John Sholl,
Dan Hankin and Bernie Kolker, the
200-pound fullback on the grid
team, are expected to aid the team S

Those who know a good deal about
camels claim that they are the
most useful animals in the world.
The camel has been called the
train of the desert, and it can travel
30 miles day for weeks on end. No
other creature seems to possess
anything like the same stamina un-
der similar conditions, states a writ
er in London Tit-Bits Magazine.
Abstinence from food and water
for days does not seem to impair
its efficiency. The hair is woven
into mats, carpets and clothes, the
hide into tents, shoes and thongs.
The beast provides meat and milk,
and its dung is used for fuel. The
camel has another asset which can
be relied upon. 1t has an excellent
homing instinct, and animals have
found their way $50 miles across the
Australian desert when those who
have ridden them had no means of
finding out their direction.

NEW YORK, Sept. 23-San Jose
State, the little California college
where Glenn Pop) Warner is an
advisory" coach this year after a
long career Of developing great foot
ball teams, plays its third game Of
the season tonight against the Uni
versity of San Francisco.


That's sign the 1899 football sea-
son really Is under way, although
another week or two will pass before
all the major" teams get into ac-
ton. San Jose already has knocked
of Montana State and Texas A. e. l.,
while the burly San Francisco Dons
fell before st. Mary's of Texas last
week.


Only Big Games in South.


Big-time competition. however, is
limited to the South. Three South
ern Conference games, involving
couple of, possible contenders for
Dukes title, start the season, and
nearly every team in the circuit Is
due for action of some sort.


North Carolina, Dukes perennial
rival, takes on The Citadel for its
opener; North Carolina State plays
Davidson, possible dark horse" In
a night game at Greensboro; and
South Carolina, another team that
may make trouble for the leaders,
plays Wake Forest on the latters'
field at night.


Other games involving Southern
Conference members are Clemson
VS.. Presbyterian, Virginia Tech VS..
Randolph Macon, William and
Mary VS.. Guilford and Virginia Mill
tary VS.. Roanoke. Florida and Mis-
sissippl State are the only Southeast
ern Conference schools to open, play
ing Stetson and Howard, respectively.


Swinging to the West, two South
west Conference colleges, Texas A.
g. M. and Arkansas. will get the Jump
on their rivals. The Texas Aggies
aren't fooling about getting started,
either. They will play Oklahoma
Aggies, one of the strong teams of
the Missouri Valley Conference, at
Oklahoma City.


Similarly, Iowa State of the Big
Six. Brigham Young of the Noun
tain States Big Seven and Wash
ington State Of the Pacific Coast
Conference get away ahead of their
circuits. Their respective rivals are
Coe, Arizona State of Flagstaff and
Gonzaga, none of which should cause
them any difficulty.


OF the big independents" those
with games on tap today or tonight
are Virginia against Hampden-Syd-
ney; Centenary, surprise loser of its
first game, against Hardin Simmons
Of Texas, and Texas Tech against
Texas Mines.


Southern Conference teams also
took the lead last night when Fur
man routed its neighbor, Erskine, 3D.
7, and Richmond whipped the New
port News Naval Apprentice School,
$40. The University of Detroit
gave the Midwest curtain raiser by
beating Central Michigan Teachers,
20-7, while the East also got its first
taste of football with Providence
College downing Rhode Island State,
60, in the leading game.

BROOKLINE, Mass, Aug. l6.-
Heartened somewhat by yesterdays
results, United States Davis Cup
BOSSES watched eagerly today as their
1889 hopefuls went into action in
the third round of the national
tennis tourney.


Longwood officials have given the
foreign survivors in the mems divi-
sion an extra day of rest while
calling upon such favored domestic
pairs as Frank Parker of Beverly
Hills. Calf, and Don McNeill of
Oklahoma City. and Bobby Riggs of
Chicago, and Elwood Cooke of Port
land. Greg, the Wimbledon titlists.
to take to the courts and strive for
quarter-f1nalist berths.


Australian Pair Pressed.


The top-seeded Parker and Nc
Neill engaged Robert Peacock and
Douglas Imhoff of San Francisco,
the national intercollegiate cham
plons, in one of today's third
FOUNDERS and Riggs and Cooke op-
posed such sturdy Southern rivals
as Russell Bobbitt of Atlanta, and
Frank Guernsey of Orlando, Fla,
in the other mems match.


The Parker-McNeill and Riggs
Cooke combines came through with
comparative ease yesterday, while
Adrian Quist and Jack Bromwich,
the Australian Davis Cup pair, had
plenty of trouble disposing of a
pair of Los Angeles youngsters, Jack
Kramer and Welby Van Horn. 1t
was that trouble which heartened
the Davis Cup chieftains.


Quist and Bromwich tomorrow
will be called upon to face Gene
Mako, reputed to be the worlds
greatest amateur doubles player, and
his new partner and Los Angeles
townsman, Jack Tidball.

uled for Thursday, will bring the
remainder of the Australian forces,
Jack Crawford and Harry Hopman,
against such capable rivals as
Charles Hare of England. and
Ladislav Hecht, former Czecho-
Slovakian Davis Cup star.


Play in the women's division,
which has stuck strictly to form to
date, appeared even skimpier, as far
as today's program was concerned.
The only feminine matches on the
docket were the last two second

BY BETSY HAYFORD, IA,

Do you ever see;

Children just like me?

With their moccasined feet;
Run along here swiftly,

Did you ever see oxen
Go by with creaking cart,

By the Associated Press.


The three ships of the United
States European Squadron have left
Villefranche, France, and are en-
route to Lisbon, Portugal, and Mar
seille, France, the Navy Depart
ment announced yesterday.


The department stated that, con-
trary to reports from Europe, the
transfer did not involve any change
in the policy not to convoy Amer
lean merchant ships.


Otherwise, plans of the squadron,
stationed in European waters since
the outbreak of the Spanish civil
war, were not known here. Its
commander, Rear Admiral Charles
E. Courtney, has authority to op-
crate as he sees fit without specific
instructions from Washington.


The flagship cruiser Trenton and
the destroyer Jacob Jones left Vile
franche yesterday for Lisbon, while
the destroyer Badger departed for
Marseille.

To the Editor Of The Star:


What a contrast between what our
country is today and what it was 20 to
40 years ago! Then we were great
people and Nation, striving for our own
welfare and cooperating with other
nations for the good of mankind. For
eign possessions were acquired; the op-
pressed inhabitants were liberated; the
allies were helped to defeat the ruth
less German invasion of Belgium and
France; treaties for international peace
were signed; we pledged ourselves, along
with other great powers, to guarantee
the nationality and territory of China.


Recently, compelled by the cold
blooded, selfish isolation sentiment, our
Nation has repudiated every obligation
and responsibility. We are now like
the individual who thinks he or she will
never need assistance or friend, and
will do absolutely nothing for the well
fare of others.


Even victorious Germany would
probably not attack our own shores.
But against an alliance of ruthless Eu-
ropean and Asiatic powers we could
not, unaided, defend the whole Western
Hemisphere and could not defend our
own coasts and island possessions. We
must sympathize with the countries that
are striving for world peace and civii-
zation and against banditry, terrorism,
devastation and massacre. Neutrality
must not mean indifference toward the
ruin of civilization and the enslavement

Jefferses had been framed.

M over whom neighbors shake their
AV6 heads. He had knack for getting ex-

Twenty years later, this amazing boy is still

And Hollywood blinks as it looks toward

Bren's family were Tennesseans who were

father was captain of Confederate infantry.)
They migrated to St. Louis, where Milton was
born; then to Los Angeles.


Milton at nine became necessary factor

kitchen or behind an ancient sewing machine.
Good ground round" could then be bought

neat; they lived in decent neighborhoods;

killed by woman, Detective Capt.

township, Montgomery County, was
emphatic in dismissing this posi-
bility.

Grebes, like the looms and other
diving birds, are expert in making
their escape by swimming under
water, coming up some distance
from where you saw them go under
Flying to evade trouble does not
appeal to the grebes. though they
are strong, swift flyers.


During the counting days the head
has handsome crest or ruff. The
plumage is smooth, compact and
halrlike, and after careful groom
ing, the well-dressed bird is very
handsome, indeed, in its waterproof
coat.


The American cared grebe is about
IA inches long and a dusky color
above, white below. During the
summer the parents have long, fan
shaped ear tufts of very fine feath-
ers and these are a lovely golden
brown. The crown, chin, throat and
neck are soft, deep black and the
upper parts dusky. The eyes are red
and the lids orange.


During the winter the ear tufts
disappear and the crown and narrow
band on the back of the neck and
upper parts are a gray-dusky with
white sides and f1anks tinged with
gray. This is an ideal color camou-
flage for the winter months.


These birds prefer floating nest.
A platform made of reeds and the
close growing vegetation about them,
to which the nursery is anchored, is
usually af1oat upon shallow water of
the ponds, lakes or lagoons favored
by the grebes. There are from four
to six rather soiled-looking eggs laid
upon the platform.


Western North America is the
range of these birds. They breed
from Central British Columbia,
Great Slave Lake, Saskatchewan and
Manitoba south to Southern Cali
fornia, Northern Arizona, Northern
Nebrask and Northern Iowa

weeping together while the men
stood silent and grim.

appeared down the tracks did they
leave, for empty homes.

United States Ambassador Norman
Armour called at the foreign office
today to ask how the United States
could help relieve suffering in the
earthquake stricken region of South
Central Chile.


He was informed medical supplies
and condensed milk were urgent
needs Of the region, where it was
feared the death toll from a Tues
day night earthquake would reach
$4,000.


1.-TWO United States Army
planes were ordered to leave the
Panama Canal Zone this after
noon with serum for earthquake
victims)


Evacuation of the quake zone was
begun. Planes brought children
needing urgent surgical attention to
Santiago. Trains, automobiles and
trucks were pressed into service to
bring others northward from Chillan
and the surrounding heavily dam
aged territory.


From Conception, Talcahuano
and other coastal cities injured sur
vivors were rushed by boat to points
where they could receive better
medical attention.


The minister of the interior or

offices to remain under military con-

disease in the stricken earthquake
area today. Militia directed the
work.


The death estimates at their high

BERLIN, Sept. 16.-Legal experts
tonight studied Germany's tenta.
tive list of war contraband articles
to determine where to draw the line
between outright war materials ard
those which might prove Of indirect
aid to the enemy.


Their decision, informed sources
said, would be factor in determin-
Ing the Reich's policy at sea.


Present lists are divided into the
classifications of unconditional"
and conditional" contraband.


Unconditional" contraband, which
would be destroyed or seized with
out formality whenever possible, was
defined by German sources as every.
thing hitherto recognized as such In
international law.


That would include munitions,
chemicals, guns, fuel, war vessels,
Warplanes, spare parts for war
equipment and all other equipment
and material for use directly or in
directly in battle.


Under conditional" contraband
the list includes articles which Ger
man sources said were placed on
contraband lists by Britain in con-
travention Of accepted international
law.


This classification covers material
that would affect the civilian popu-
lation in wartime-foodstuffs, live
animals, clothing and machinery.

Meath the skies serene.

Smiles which February


Strove for all in vain.

Is there praise or censure
Due them? Who shall say,

The leaves of the trees turned yell
low and red and brown. They began
to drop, few at first, and more and
more every day until all but the
spruce trees and the pine trees and
the hemlock trees and the fir trees
and the cedar trees were bare. The
fur of Peters coat was growing
thicker. The grass of the Green
Meadows had turned brown. All these
things were signs which Peter knew
well. They meant that rough Brother
North Wind and Jack Frost were on
their way down from the Far North
to stay.


Peter spent a great deal of time in
the dear Old Briar Patch, just sit
ting still and listening. He didn't
know what he was listening for. 1t
just seemed to him that there was
something he ought to hear at this
time of year, and so he sat listening
and listening and wondering what he
was listening for.


Then, late one afternoon, there
came floating down to him from
high up~in the sky, family at first,
but growing louder, a sound unlike
any Peter had heard all the long
summer through. The sound was of
many voices mingled. "Honk! Honk!
Honk! Ka-honk. honk, honk, ka-
honk!" they cried. Peter gave lit
tie jump.


That's what I've been listening
for" he thought. "Honker the Goose
and his friends are coming! Oh,
do hope they will stop where I can
pay them call.


He hoped out to the edge of the
dear Old Briar Patch that he might
see better, and looked up in the sky.

text:
Associated Press Financial Writer.


An unusual summer squirt in steel
production frightened the business
horizon this week.


The American Iron and Steel In.
stitute estimated that industry's op-
erations jumped to 60.6 per cent Of
capacity, new peak for the year
and the highest since the week Of
November, 1888, when the rate
was 607.


Normally the steel industry runs
along at sluggish pace at mid
summer. The weeks sharp runup
was fueled mostly, experts said, by
heavier demand from miscellaneous
sources and some forward buying
from the motor industry.
The boost in steel output con-
trasted with lower figures posted for
carloadings, electric power and mo-
tor production.


Meanwhile, trade reports from
steel centers said steel would prob
ably get further boost from the
motor industry. Iron Age said the
motor division was expected to lift
the rate well above that for this
week. Previews of some leading mo-
tor manufacturers, 1t was stated,
confirmed expectations of an early
start for the new production season.


Hopes for brisk output of motors
were not without foundation. The
Commerce Department in its report
of business conditions in 36 cities,
cited figures which showed sales Of
new cars were holding higher than
a year ago. Wayne County, Mich,
reported sales of new passenger
cars totaled lat, compared with
1,514 the week before and 428 in
the like week last year.


Auto Trend Repeated.


Although automobile production
dipped this week, Wards Automotive
Reports said the trend was follow
ing an almost exact parallel with
last years. A year ago the industry
hit bottom in the second week Of
August.


Scrap steel prices chalked up an
other gain, the third successive
weekly rise. Farm equipment makers
did their part in keeping the steel
industry's backbone stiff. Rejecting
the sharp advance in building opera
tions over a year ago, structural
steel orders were reported at two
year top. The rising tide of orders
for steel from the motor field, build
| ing and miscellaneous sources only
served to make more conspicuous
the absence of the railroad industry
as big steel buyer.


| Normally about one-third of the
railroad industry's entire purchases
fall to iron and steel. But buying
power has fallen to an abnormally
low level because of shrinkage in
earning power and-for some sys.
tems-a wobbly credit situation.
Railroad experts summing up the
current situation said this week that
the industry as whole had its
head barely above water.
Although figures issued this week
showed carloadings running 13 per
cent ahead of the like week of 1898,

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 25.-Illiana
Laurel, Russian singer and dancer,
who wants her divorce from Film
Comedian Stan Laurel set aside,
was up against prospective inves-
tigation today.


Superior Judge Joseph w. Vickers,
denying Mrs. Laureps petition to
set aside an interlocutory decree
granted the actor last May, said
sharply:


"The court believes this witness
has committed perjury and recon-
mends that the matter be investi-
gated by the district attorney and
that prosecution be carried out"


Mrs. Laurel charged that she
failed to contest the default divorce
because of fear of her husband, and
said she was not legally represented.
Attorneys testified, however, they
had served as good legal counsel.


Deputy District Attorney Bonner
Richardson said court records would
be studied before his office took any
action.

NEW YORK, April 3.-Songs of

hummed in the copper trade last
week without attracting consumers.

mouth basis that has distinguished
business in the red metal for weeks.


The secondary market. however,
came in for good deal of attention

siderable metal had changed hands
at a price of around 1924 cents a
pound

cause of the disparity between the
current export level of 1926 cents
and the domestic basis, some units
without fabricating subsidiaries had
no incentive to sell their metal
abroad and are instead selling In
the outside market.


The export price was firmly main
tanned through the week despite
continued tenseness abroad. Over
seas consumption and production
were reported fairly we'll balanced

demand would Immediately be re-
flected in price improvement.

no one left a vessel.

Marie, Ont, Canadian guards have
been on duty at the locks and
bridge since last Monday.

Bey that France could not grant

NEW YORK, Dec. 9.-Among those
taking life a bit easier since the out
break of the war are the customs
inspectors, and yet they are by no
means idle. Hundreds OF travellers
are coming into New York from
cruises to the scores OF neutral
foreign ports in this half OF the
world-and they seem to find quite
as much to buy as travellers return
ing from the ports across the globe.


On the piers are suitcases and
trunks, boxes and native baskets
overHowing with bargains picked up
In the Caribbean countries and in
ports on the west coast of South
America. From Curacao they bring
perfumes, delftware from Holland
mems white linen suits and boxes
of liquor. The latter usually contain
at least one of those unique four
necked bottles containing four dif-
ferent kinds and colors of liqueur
each in its own compartment in the
bottle. Venezuelas best buys seem
to be riding crops and native sandals
called alpargatas.


Colombia Offers


Variety of Souvenirs.


Colombia contributes to incoming
suitcases articles cut from bone,
colorful bowls made from half
gourds, native groups nodded from
rubber and tinted, tortoise shell
articles of all kinds-cigarette cases,
earrings, necklaces, bracelets, belts.
One returning passenger even
brought in the head of tortoise
to be made into lamp.


Panama presents for inspection
Just about everything a globetrotter
would assemble on trip around
the world-carved chests, articles
carved from ivory, oriental kimonas,
mandarin suits, pajamas, lingerie
and jewelry, beautiful laces and
linens, perfumes and Panama hats.


In Haiti, the favorite buys seem
to be end tables, smoking sets and
trays made from mahogany and
articles woven from straw, such as
fans and highball-glass guards, and
sturdy handled double-lid baskets.
The latter come in amazingly large
sizes-and usually are used to catch
the overflow from trunks and bags.
Ecuador Provides


Many Novelties.


The west coast republics seem
quite as successful as the Caribbean
in tempting travellers to part with
their money. Ecuador bats them
with articles of all kinds fashioned
from alligator skins. tiny little
dishes. dolls and vases cleverly cut
from tagua nuts, the vegetable ivory
of commerce; gorgeous fabrics woven
by the Otavalo Indians, beautifully
woven baskets and Panama hats.
Ecuador is the original source OF
Panamas and the worlds best are
found there. some of them so fine
they can be passed through finger
ring.


Suitcases bearing Peru stickers in
variably disclose Spanish colonial
silver vases and cocktail sets, bowls
and pitchers bearing designs found
on the clay huacos and portrait
vases taken from the ancient tombs
of the Incas. If the passenger has
been fortunate enough to find them.
there'll be beautiful old wooden
stirrups, heavily embossed with
silver, and lavishly engraved silver
spurs worn by the Spanish con-
querors.


Visitors to Chile generally bring
back articles made from reptile skins,
beautiful woolens and heavy bar
baric coin jewelry and bright-color I'd
shawl and blankets made by the
Araucanian Indians.


Thus the traveller returning from
Southern cruises does his bit to keep
the customs inspector in training.

BASEL, Switzerland, Oct. 4.-Ru-
mors of an impending German
thrust at France through Alsace
and historic Burgundy Gate were
heard today with reports of the
strengthening of Nazi upper Rhine
garrisons and unusual activity along
the river.


For centuries the gateway between
the Vosges and Jura mountains
has been a route for armies in
vading France from the east.


The Germans were said to be
concentrating thousands of soldiers,
many of them veterans of the Po-
ish war, at Black Forest and upper
Rhine forts.


At Istein, Germany's "Rhineland
Gibraltar" shielded lights were re-
ported at night over the Rhine
shadows on the German side. Pom
toons have been shipped into the
Rhine valley by the Nazis.


A German strike from the Istein
area probably would be routed
&C, oss Alsace territory between Null
house and the Swiss frontier which
forms the entrance to Burgundy
Gate.


The French, however, have built
strong Notifications along 40-mile
strip between Istein and Belfort
Guns placed along the mountain
slopes command the sides of the
gate and it's path ends under the
cannon of great Fort Belfort.


This section has been the locale
recently of much air activity, with
French observation planes drawing
heavy anti aircraft fire as soon a.
they appear. German planes dart
out of Black Forest bases to aiC
in driving back the invaders. Dur.
ing early war days only few Naz
aircraft were seen in the area.


Swiss observers expressed little
concern about the concentration ol
troops near their borders, believing
that any action would be directed al
Alsace, not Switzerland.

Special Dispatch to The Star.


AUBURNDALE. Mass, March 25.
The index of commodity prices
compiled by the McGill Commodity
Service strengthened moderately
during the third full week ended in
March.


The latest index number of 68.5
compares with 68.4 for the previous
week and 72.l on this date year
earlier. Strength in the index was
due primarily to higher prices for
agricultural products, as the two
other major groups-industrial prod
ucts and livestock-declined slightly


OF the IA individual group classifi-
cations making up this index, were
unchanged from the previous week,
4 were higher and S lower.


The index for industrial commodi-
ties fell off slightly, as lower prices
for hides and leather and fine and
coarse textiles Offset advances in
building materials, paint materials
and vegetable oils.


Strength in the agricultural in
dex was attrloutaDle TO hlgher prices
for oats, rye, potatoes, sugar. flax
seed and butter. These advances
offset weakness in wheat, corn, bar
ley, cotton. eggs and wool.


The livestock index declined frac-
tionally, as lower prices were noted
for cattle and hogs. In this group
sheep and lambs advanced.


Strength in the building materials
index was noted for the first time
this month The advance was at
tributable to an increase in glass
prices.


The fine textiles index declined on
weakness in the three major items
cotton, wool and silk.


Coarse textiles were lower, solely
because of decline in burlap prices.

Tradition has been shattered-a
tradition which insisted a child
movie star could not attain success
as an adult.


Brunette and radiant Helen Par
rish is the living, walking proof that
the above mentioned tradition no
longer holds water. Helen broke
into the movies when she was 3
years old, her. first picture being
with Babe Ruth in Babe Comes
Home"


Today Helen has attained young
womanhood. And a very lovely
young lady she is. But that's beside
the point. The thing that counts is
that she is attaining even greater
success than she ever enjoyed as a
child.


True, she went through the "awk-
ward age" and was away from the
movie cameras for three years. Two
years ago she came back, playing
the role of the little "meanie" in
Deanna Durbin's Mad About Mu-
sic" Since then she has been cast
in increasingly important roles, top
ping them all with her present role
Of Miss Durbin's wealthy society
cousin in the singing stars new
Universal picture, FIRST Love-" This
is Helen's most important part to
date and it will probably do much to
advance her toward eventual star
dom.


Helen's achievement means more
than merely success for herself. 1t
has broken down a barrier which for
years has blocked the progress of
other child actors who wanted to
continue acting after they grew up
For some reason or other that rarely
happened. Hollywood had a buga-
boo about youngsters and put them
on shelf as soon as they showed
signs of becoming adults. There was
only one conspicuous exception
Madge Evans. But there have beer
a hundred other children who died
professionally soon after they were
born.


| Helen hopes she has helped t.
change al that.

BASEL, Switzerland, Sept. 20 (P).
Swiss observers, expecting a big
push" momentarily to break the
western front lull, saw indications
today the Observation-Disclosures Ger
man line would take the offensive
from the French.


So far, they said, French and
British division thrusting across the
frontier toward the Siegfried Line
were numerically stronger than the
Germans. That was reported chang
ing rapidly. however, as seasoned
troops and vast amounts of fighting
equipment were rushed from battle
broken Poland.


There were increasing indications
that when the drive comes it. may
be in the northern sector, where
French have penetrated the rich
Saar Valley that went to Germany
by a plebiscite. Big guns continued
to thunder there.


A movement of German troops
into the Baden section, north OF
Basel, had been observed earlier,
but this was said to have developed
only into a transit movement-not
a concentration.


With Bohemia in German hands
since the conquest of Czecho-
Slovakia, dozen railway lines from
Poland pass through the Baden Sec
ton to the western front. These
routes as well as central German
lines apparently are being used to
shift fighting strength to the West
Wall.


Swiss sources said the veterans
from Poland were replacing the
lower Rhine fort troops which, in
turn, were moved north where most
Of the fighting has taken place.

TOXIC, Aug. 10-The United
States and France were reported to-
day to have declared to Japan their
interest in economic problems arlS-
ing from the war in China, adding a
complication to the already stale
mated British-JapaneSe conference,


1t was believed by observers that
the question of including other pow
ers in consideration of issues be-
tween Great Britain and Japan had
become a new barrier to resumption
of the talks.


Sir Robert Leslie Graigie, the
British Ambassador, has insisted
that Britain could not withdraw
support from the Central Chinese
governments currency because other
powers were concerned.


Authoritative scources, however,
said that Sotomatsu Kato, Japanese
Minister-at-large in China, had
pressed Japan's desire for speedy
resumption of the negotiations with
Britain at his third meeting with
Sir Robert in three days.


Officers Threaten to Leave.


Japan's military negotiators who
came from Tientsin, Kato was said
to have warned, are determined to
return to China unless there are
clear signs of resumption within
the near future"


The press declared they would
return Monday and said Kato had
presented a Japanese demand for
resumption 1t was reported reliably,
however, that no time limit had been
mentioned.


The British Ambassador was said
to have replied to Kato that final
instructions from London still were
pending and that he had no knowl-
edge when they would come. He
was said to have argued that the
japanese army officers delayed the
conference considerably longer at
the beginning and that, therefore, 1t
was inconsistent for the japanese
government to expect Britain to
make such vital decision in short
time.


Denies Third Powers Involved.


A japanese foreign spokesman
declared Japan will not yield her
position that economic questions are
solely between Britain and Japan.
We cannot support any opinion that
third powers are involved


The American and French repre-
sertations were understood to have
been made by Eugene H Dooman,
United States Charge d'Afaires, and
Baron Guy Fain. French Charge
dAffaires.


Mr.. Dooman conferred Tuesday
with Seijiro Yoshizawa, head OF the
American affairs section Of the
japanese foreign Office, and while
1t was understood the American did
not express support for Britain in
her talks he did point out that eco
nonic questions affected American
business in China.


Conference on Alliance.


The japanese press hinted that
Britain. before resuming her own
talks. was awaiting the outcome of
conference of the i've key minis
ters of the japanese cabinet on a
proposed japanese military alliance
with the Rome-Berlin axis.


This was to follow return of War
Minister 1t. Gen. Seishiro Itagaki
from an audience with Emperor
Hirohito on European developments.


Newspapers predicted the five key
ministers-Premier Baron Kiichiro
Hiranuma and the ministers of war,
navy. finance and foreign affairs
would meet tomorrow after the reg
ular cabinet session and possibly
reach a decision on the alliance pro-
posal.

AUBURNDALE, Mass, June 49,
Industrial commodities continued
their advance during the second
week ending in June, the McGill
Commodity Service announced to-
day. This advance constituted the
eighth consecutive week of higher
prices in this index. The index of
all commodity prices declined quite
sharply during the week because of
lower prices for livestock. OF the
IA individual groups which comprise
this index, 7 advanced, 4 declined
and 3 remain unchanged from the
previous week.


The advance in the industrial
group was featured by higher prices
for fuels, hides, paint materials, fine
textiles and vegetable oils. Slight
declines we're noted in building ma
terials, nonferrous metals and
coarse textiles.


The index for agricultural prod
ucts also advanced, as stronger prices
were noted for wheat, barley, cot
ton, eggs, wool, f1axseed and but
ter. Declines in this group were
confined to corn, rye and potatoes.


A slight decline in the index for
building materials was attributable
solely to a lower average price for
Southern pine lumber.


Fuels advanced, as higher prices
were posted for anthracite coal. The
advance was tempered by weakness
in kerosene prices.

The announcer had carried on far

Temporarily, at least, the only

The rest of Europe, which had

ports said German-Soviet Russian

These advices envisioned the crea-
ton of buffer state between Ger
many and Russia.


Except for isolated instances of
Polish resistance, such as in War
saw, they said, the only unoccupied
territory appeared to be a thin line

rectly south to the Bug River, thence

Russian and German motorized

One Of these places was Turka, in

ish-Russian border.


Between the two fast-moving

Hungary.


Early today it was estimated some
10000 Poles had crossed into Hun
gary ana the stream of refugees
still was coming.

wall of AFRAID sirens could be heard

nouncer and four times the drone

air.


The broadcaster said the raids

siege included another appeal to

tered city.


Before silence again sealed War

LITTLE ROCK, Ark, May 23.-
Two Negro convicts, who escaped
with or 10 others when wind de-
nolished their stockade, were shot
to death by trusty guards in a hand
to-hand fight near the Cummins
State Prison Farm today.

Of spring storm which killed four
persons, injured scores and caused
property damage of more than

yesterday.

with intent to kill, burglary and
grand larceny, and James Patterson,
serving 7 years for burglary and
larceny.


Prison officers said they were
killed by two Negro TRUSTEES when
they sprang upon one who was beat
ing through the dense woods be-
tween Cummins and Gould, Ark.


Willie Rayford, life termer, was
recaptured without resistance. An
other fugitive returned to camp
voluntarily, explaining he just took
to the woods" for safety.


Several prisoners were injured in
the collapse of the stockade.

Japanese columns pushed north

important Yangtze River cities Of
1chang and Shasi


In North China guerrillas con-
tinued widespread daily raids. In
one such raid Chinese guerrillas
entered Taierhchwang, the Shan
tung province village where the
Chinese had won their only out
standing victory of the war.


Dollar Wins First Skirmish.


Financial sources reported mean
while that the Chinese dollar, out
lawed yesterday by the japanese,
won the opening skirmishes in a
currency war when the Japanese
sponsored Peiping governments re-
serve bank attempted the huge task
Of forcibly replacing the Chinese
currency throughout North China
with Yuan notes.


The Peiping government forecast
the circulation of the new notes
with the backing of Japanese bayo-
nets In a decree that divided North
China into Japanese occupied and
bandit zones and instituting the
actual circulation of the new notes
only In II Japanese occupied areas.
Among these districts were Peiping,

The decree added that the new
notes would be used in the bandit"
zones as the japanese army sue
ceeds in wiping out resistance. For
eign observers considered that the
decree emphasized the fact that the
Japanese actually controlled only
areas contiguous to the largest
cities and along communication
lines.

Japanese deaths.

began and had operated them.

son. Usually they are not in de-
mand until around THANKSGIVING.

lected for your first blouse of the

ing rapidly-and we're not surprised.

shades for dress. Golden beige sat-
ins, lovely rose crepes, vivid blues
and all the other shades that lend
interest to suits are yours this sea-
son, so it's no wonder that more
and more colorful blouses are being
used.


One thing that's particularly i'm
pressive is the fine workmanship
to be found on most styles. Copies
of terribly expensive imports are
really made just as well, and contain
the same fine detailing at perhaps
one-tenth of the original price!

pleated fronts and buttons all the

Eye beauty can be most cOmpell-
ing with a woman of so or more
years. Life has given her eyes a
history and that history is portrayed
through them. Deep, intelligent
eyes-knowing eyes twinkling with
humor-clear eyes shining with
warmth and sympathy-gay eyes
concealing the age of their owner!
Through them you judge woman's
charm, her experience, her person.
ality. How wfong if she does not
make them her outstanding beauty
asset!


Even though she may disapprove
of lip and cheek coloring for women
of her age (Which shouldn't be the
case) she need not hesitate to keep
her eyes attractively groomed and
their loveliness artfully enhanced!
Her friends will praise her-her enc
mics Gf they exist) will envy her!


The meticulous woman keeps her
brows trim by plucking what we call
the stragglers. She never attempts
to alter their shape or character,
knowing that would detract from
beauty. To dress her brows and
lashes she dips into colorless cream
and brushes them until they are
sleek and pliable. Or If they have
faded as her hair, she chooses a
darker cream to give them more
definiteness. With a clever little
curler she trains her lashes upward
making her eyes appear smiling!


Those are the basic steps for daily
eye grooming for the woman of good
taste. But gala times will come
when she will want to bring out all
the latent beauty in her sweet face.
It is then she will shade her lids
with lustrous cream of soft blue
or gray and use mascara on the tips
of her upper lashes-never on the
lower lashes.


For truly dramatic evenings she
may wear shadow of blue or mauve,
glinted with gold with pastel or
white gowns, or a glistening bronze
with darker formal attire. If she is
modern beauty for her years, she
will carry blush rouge high on her
cheeks to give her iris deeper hue.


White vaseline applied to brows
before you pluck them will soften
the hairs. And if they are still stub
horn etoopo vo,,r I,roxuc xpitI, a oloAl,
wrung from hot water placed over
the vaseline. Pull in the direction
the hair grows-pull toward the
right on the right brow, toward the
left from the left brow. Tweezers
with a scissor like handle greatly
help you to groom without pain.


If your lashes are very dry keep
them fabricated each night with a
bit of odorless castor oil. Use mas
cara sparingly for most brands are
drying.


Experiment with the softer shades
of eyeshadow, for frequently even
during the daylight hours you may
wear an inconspicuous shade, and If
it is discreetly applied even your
most discerning friend will not de-
tect it!


Never, never shade beneath your

rouge does wonders in blending dark
circles into your skin tone If you will

text:
LONDON, Jan. 2 GN.S).-A
Daily Express dispatch today
from Warsaw reported theft of
the secret plans Of Russia's latest
fighting planes and the murder
of a prominent Soviet aircraft
engineer.


The plans were stolen when
Stefan Jakowski, 42-year-old So
Wet airplane designer and chief
engineer of the Moscow airplane
works, was murdered in his apart
ment last Thursday, the dispatch
said. Jakowski's safe had been
robbed.


SEARCH NATION


Charging foreign spies COM
mitted the murder, the Soviet
secret police (OGPU) are making
a nationwide search to prevent
the plans from being smuggled
abroad, the Express continued.


All frontier guards have been
ordered 10 scrutinize minutely the
clothing and other effects of trav-
elerS entering or leaving the coun-
try.


SAFE OPEN


The shots which killed Jakow-
ski were not heard by his neigh
bors. According to the Warsaw
article, a servant, returning from
a shopping tour, found Jakowski
lying on the floor of his study
with six bullet wounds in his
chest.


A heavy safe built into the wall
of the engineers study had been
blown open. Unimportant papers
were scattered on the floor but
the plans were missing.

BY the Associated Press


SHANGHAI. July 19.-The Ameri-
can liner President Coolidge and the
japanese freighter Nissan Maru
collided today in the Whangpoo
River. Numerous plates of the
liners sides were bent. No one was
injured.


The President Coolidge was turn
ing in the river, preparatory to tie
ing up at buoy, when the japanese
ship. coming down river, apparently
mlsjudged the current and struck
the liner on the port side amid
ships. The bow Of the japanese
craft was damaged.


Aboard the President Coolidge
was Rear Admiral Thomas Charles
Hart, arriving from the United
States to take over command of the
United States Asiatic Fleet from
Admiral Harry E. Yarnell next
Tuesday.

BY the Associated Press.


MANILA, May 20.-Gov, Vicente
Caedo of Batangas Province tonight
denied reports tiny Verde Island,
some 100 miles south of Manila, was
sinking into the sea.


The Governor said he visited the
island today, found it's inhabitants
panic stricken and abandoning their
homes. The Governor found no evil
dence the island was sinking and
urged residents not to leave.


Earthquakes have terrorized the
islands 1000 inhabitants for two
weeks, but the Governor reported
there were no new tremors today.
The only evidence of past earth
quakes was several landslides.


Several hundred of Verde's in
habitants already have crossed the
10-mile channel to the Batangas
Province coast. They reported more
of the islands population was pre-
pairing to evacuate.
headline:
Sinking of Tiny Island


Is Denied by Governor

The wholesale commodity price

compared with 76.7 in the preced-
ing week, 1853 month ago and
72.7 year ago, based on the 1926
1928 average as 100.


Food prices were slightly lower
last week on the average, making
the fourth consecutive weekly de-
cline. The farm product index turned
upward, with cotton, grains and
live stock showing increases. The
trend of prices of industrial COM
modities continued upward, with the
index for all commodities except
farm prices and foods rising for the
ninth consecutive week. This aver
age is now higher than at any time
since October 1887.


Higher prices for anthracite coal
and petroleum took the fuel index
to a new high for the year. The
textile index rose sharply, due in
large part to higher quotations for
woolen goods and yarns. Burlap,
silk and cotton were also higher
for the week.


In the metal group rising prices
for brass and copper products more
than offset declines for steel scrap
and tin, resulting in a slight rise
in the group average. An upturn in
the building material index to the

urgent request for American made
warplanes, Col. Per Zilliacus, the

today


Col. Zilliacus said the request
was received yesterday. 1t COIN

the Russian invaders, hurled back

planes.


Col. zilliacus was accompanied
on his visit to the War Depart
ment by 1t. Gen. Vilho Peter
Nenonen, head of the Finnish Pur-
chasing Mission, and two technical
advisers.


They surveyed with War Depart
ment officials the possibilities of
getting additional planes and other
war materials with which to fight
the Soviet invaders. The Firms
recently obtained A of the Nays
latest type of fighting ships from

signated number of the latest type

gas masks.

purchasing mission is facing serious
difficulties in obtaining the much
needed war supplies. He explained
that the problem is one of imme-
diate delivery. Few, if any, chan
nels are open for that.


At present the best hope to obtain
war planes appears to be to get the
British and French to waive their
prior orders. Both England and
France placed large orders with
American manufacturers soon after
repeal of the embargo provision OF
the Neutrality Act and these planes
are being delivered now.


Gas Mask Contract Open.


The military attache said the
Firms have not yet closed a con-
tract for the $4,000 gas masks, on
which bids were received last week
from four American manufacturers.
He said final authority is being
awaited.


He also disclosed that his govern
ment is interested in purchasing
marine engines for small and speedy
torpedo boats, which could be used
in combating Russian naval vessels.


He added that negotiations for
these engines had been held with
Swedish, British and American
manufacturers since October, but
no contracts have been concluded.

lin the morning., and for the fol-

BY the Associated Press.


BANFF, Alberta, May 27.-King
George and Queen Elizabeth rested
today in the roof garden of Canada,
away from the crowds attending
their arduous tour across the Do
minion.


About them were the majestic
Rockies. Nearby was a plunging
mountain stream, the Bow River,
along which they walked alone
last night soon after their arrival
from Calgary.


Every one in the town of Banff
seat of a national park, was out
to welcome their Brittanic majesties.
They went to their hotel--opened
especially for the royal visit-but
reappeared in a few minutes.


The King and Queen exchanged
whispers, thanked the officers for
their attention and then asked to
be permitted to walk alone through
the woods along the river.


They will rest here until Sunday
morning, when the tour resumes
toward the Pacific Coast.

L. Leibell said was similar to the

cal, and that she had complained
constantly against dietary and dis
ciplinary conditions, about illnesses
and about her surroundings.


Offered her choice of being re-

NEWCASTLE, England. Feb. 81.
king George VI, guarded by more
than 1000 police, today launched
Britain's great new battleship which
bears the name of his father, King
George V.


May God bless her and those
who serve in her." the King cried
as the 35,000-ton ship shot down
the ways into the River Tyne, the
first battleship Britain has launched
in more than 13 years and the
first of new group of monster
vessels that will total at least nine


AS the King and Queen Elizabeth
came to Newcastle for the ceremony
they were under the strictest guard
ever given a modern British mon
arch In his own country.


Because of the wave of bomb
terrorism in recent weeks which
was attributed to Irish Republican
sympathizers, nearly 500 special
constables were called to augment
local police. Every place the King
and Queen were to visit was in
spected for bombs.


To Have Ten 14-inch Guns.


Pulling silver lever which re-
leased magnum of Australian wine
to smash against the great craft,
King George watched eagerly as the
vessel slid into the stream.


The ship will mount ten l4-inch
guns and have secondary armament
of sixteen 54 inch guns in eight
turrets, as well as numerous smaller
pieces. The Admiralty said she
would be "appreciably faster than
the % knots of the last battleships
built by Britain.


Three battleships will be launched
later this year, and another early
in 1910. Two other battleships have
been authorized and the govern
ment has announced plans for two
more.


The royal train arrived early in
the morning and halted on a track
which had been especially re-laid
against the possibility of bombing.


Thousands Jam Tyneside.


The train, with cordonS of detec-
tives surrounding it, will be the
home of the King and Queen during
their three-day visit to the northeast
coast-a semi-state tour since it is
the last of 10 visits to the provinces
following the coronation.


Scores of thousands jammed the
Tyneside. traditional center of Brit
ish shipbuilding. for a glimpse of
their majesties and the launching.


Tomorrow the King and Queen
will visit housing sites around the
Tyneside-one of Britain's hardest
hit areas during the depression.


Some of Britain's closely guarded
ornaments secrets were shown the
King and Queen during the morning
when they walked 2 miles through
the gigantic Armstrong -Vickers
plant.


Frequently they came to screened
off areas. While most of the party
was forced to halt, the King and
Queen got privileged peek behind
the screens while officials of the
company explained what was there.

BOSTON, Nov. 4.-Expressing in
dignation at the British admiralty
for ordering them into Weymouth,
England, harbor and neglecting to
provide pilot through its mine field,
crew members of the American
freighter Black Heron said today q
Dutch vessel was blown up by the
same mines.


Although Capt. Leonard Frisco
would not discuss the episode, the
crew Of the vessel, which arrived
from Antwerp today, declared that
British naval officers who boarded
the Black Heron after 1t had an
chored In the harbor expressed sur
prise that the freighter had thread
ed the field safely.


The American ships crew said
that shortly after the Black Heron
anchored the Dutch freighter Bin
nendyk struck a mine and was blown
up while entering the harbor. They
did not know whether she carried
an English pilot.


The Black Heron was held 10 DAYS
at Weymouth while authorities re-
moved all mail consigned to Ger
many and the Netherlands for in
spection, the crew said.

OF Cornell from the East, Bob Ney-
land of Tennessee from the South,
and Edward (Slip) Madigan of St.
Mary's from the Far West.

staff by getting the most points for

SEATTLE, Aug. 21.-British Co.
lumbia and Washington forests were
closed today as Pacific Northwest
firef1ghters continued a desperate
battle against multiple blazes that
taxed available man power.


The British Columbia order closed
the forests to everyone-loggers,
miners, trappers and vacationists-
but in Washington, the order af-
fected only logging in the western
part of the State.


These measures were taken as
California controlled its dangerous
blazes, and Oregon, the heaviest
loser of the four commonwealth so
far, found new hope in rising hu-
midity. A plan to close Oregon
forests was held in allegiance due to
the improved weather. Idaho fires
no longer threaten inhabited COM
munities, although at least one still
burned out of control.

near the newly created Olympic
National Park, where a revived
blaze at Deep Greek resisted efforts
OF 500 men and ate into park timber
after sweeping over old slashings,

OF Sappho in the extreme northwest
corner Of the United States.


Another 100 men fought a small

Hood National Forest. Choking
smoke drifted into Portland. Refu-

LONDON, Oct. 31.-Heavy naval
and warplane concentra tions along
Great Britain's East Coast, military
observers said today. indicate the
British are prepared for a gigantic
North Sea battle.


Its such ruddy queer war" one
tactical expert declared. that pre-
dictions aren't much good, but you
can be sure of one thing. and that is
that Great Britain wouldn't be
caught out if Adolf Hitler sent along
his planes and submarines in
bunch for one terrific North Sea
battle"


Much of the British feeling that
the North Sea will be one of the big
backgrounds of the war comes from
such German announcements as
that which appeared in Hitler's
newspaper Voelkischer Beobachter
over the week end.


England Principal Target.


The paper asserted if England
persists in throwing overheard one
after the other all conceptions of
international rules, then it must
reckon with inevitable intenSifcation
OF war against its commerce"


The British foresee England as
the principal target of German air
and sea attacks, just as she has been
so far the principal target of German
verbal attacks.


British tactical authorities regard
the periodic raids and reconnaissance
flights thus far over the Scapa Flow
and Firth of Forth naval areas and
the attack on one British convoy as
experimental" actions to feel out
resistance and test the ground for
bigger things.


British tacticians expect the "se-
rious" bombing raids to be conducted
in waves of probably six planes each.


Aerial experts hinted Britain is
prepared for such attacks as follows:


First, the raiders would be met
over the North Sea by fast fighting
planes.


Second, they would encounter
Britains balloon barrage and anti
aircraft batteries.


Third, heavy fighters, strongly
armed, would meet the raiders near
their objective.


Air Ministry Report.


The air ministry last reported:


"Extentive reconnoisSances Of
aerodromes in Northern Germany
today. In spite of the opposition,
much valuable information was
gained and many photographs were
taken"

return.

IOWA CITY, Iowa. Nov. H.
Iowa's fighting iron men toppled
proud Notre Dame from the ranks
Of the country's indicated foot
ball teams today. The durable
Hawks. eight of whom played the
full go minutes, snapped Notre
Danes six-game winning streak by
a 7-to-6 score in an exciting. pulse
tingling game that had 5000 fans
standing for the last four minutes
Of the battle.


Durable Nile Kinnick, who COM
pleted his fifth straight game with
out relief. sent the Hawkeyes into
q 7-to-O lead with q 4-yard touch
down plunge and a successful drop
kick for the extra point with only
40 seconds remaining In the second
period.


Iowa had recovered a tumble to
get the scoring chance.
The Hawks fought off Notre Dame
until late in the third period. The
fighting Irish" climaxed the surge
with Milt Piepuls cut-back through
center from the 4-yard line for a
touchdown on the second play in
the fourth period.


Zontini's Kick Is Wide.


Lou Zontini dropped back to try
for that big extra point that would
have meant q tie. He took careful
aim. but the big halfback, whose
points after touchdown beat South
ern Methodist and Carnegie Tech,
booted the ball to the left Of the
goal posts.


That was all for the Irish" The
game they had scheduled for .
breather backflred to end Notre
Dame dreams of its first undefeated
season since Knute Rockne's last
Irish" team won the national
championship in 1890.

The Iowa victory also duplicated
the performance of the 1921 Hawk
eye eleven which whipped the
IRISH" 10 to 7, to crack q 20-game
winning streak.


It was q terrific break that set
the stage for Iowa's touchdown, but
the fighting Hawkeyes. who had
only one scoring opportunity, beat
back every Irish" drive except for
the fourth-quarter thrust.


tumble Helps Iowa.


Just when 1t appeared that the
first half would result in a scoreless
tie, Kinnick tossed long pass into
the end zone. Steve Sitko. the
Irish" safety, intercepted the ball,
raced back into the playing field
and then apparently tried to lateral
when he saw that he was cornered
by the onrushing Iowans. He was
cracked hard by Bruno Andruska
and the ball went aflying. Alert
Dick Evans and Floyd Dean bounced
on the oval and 1t was Iowa's ball
on the Irish" 4-yard line.


Kinnick and Dean tried the
stout Notre Dame line, but were
piled up without gain. Then Kim
nick, shifting over to right half
back from his customary left half
slot, hit over Notre Danes right
tackle for the touchdown.


The Iowa backfield star DROP
kicked the extra point to give Iowa
4 lead 1t never lost.


Piepul Scores for 'Trish."


Getting the ball in mid-field the
Irish" opened their touchdown
drive. Stevenson hurled a pass to
Bill Kerr who was downed on the
Iowa %. Piepul, the hard driving
fullback, and Stevenson pounded to
the Hawkeye 10 as the third period
ended.


On the first play in the fourth
quarter Stevenson cracked OIL
Iowa's left tackle for 6 yards and
Ptepul followed through with his
touchdown smash. Then Zontini's
kick missed.


The victory gave Iowa q record
OF f1ve triumphs In six starts. The
Hawks have beaten South Dakota,
Indiana, Wisconsin, Purdue and
Notre Dame, They lost to Michi-
gan.


Notre Dame had knocked off Pur-
Que, Georgia Tech, Southern Metho-
dist, Navy, Carnegie Tech and Army
before today's battle.

three hard coal miners, protesting
they had not been paid, remained
deep in a Wolfe Collieries mine at
nearby Oneida for the second day
today while company officials ar
ranged to distribute current wages
they said were five days overdue.


Bunched around steam pipes for
warmth on levels $50 and 500 feet
below the surface, the miners sent
up word, however. that they in
tended to stay underground until
they also received back pay they
contended was due them for more
than year from a previous COM
pany regime.


The present operating concern
was organized a year ago through
bankruptcy proceedings.


The miners, comprising the day
force, announced their demands at
the end of the afternoon shift yes

BY DILLON GRAHAM,


Sports Editor, A. P. Feature Service.


NEW YORK, Dec. 9.-There's a
gridiron adage which says college
players hit their competitive peak
in their junior year. They no
longer make the errors Of sopho-
mores and they have more spirit
and drive than seniors.


This football axiom was borne out
fully during the past thrill-packed
season for six players on the 18th
annual Associated Press All America
team, announced today on a basis
of nationwide survey Of expert
opinion, are juniors. The other five
are seniors.


In no other year, since the As
sociated Press began its all-star
selections in 1925, have juniors
ousted the more experienced seniors
for plurality of All-America berths.


Harmon Outstanding Junior.


Perhaps the most spectacular Of
the juniors who emerged to chal-
lenge and overtake their upper
class rivals was Michigan's Thom-
as Dudley Harmon, who put on
the most eye-fllling one-man show
the Middle West had seen since
Harold (Re6 Grange ran wild back
in the 2Os.


Another was the 210-pound full
back. John Alex Kimbrough, who
cracked opposing forward walls
wide open to lead the Texas Aggies
to their most fruitful season in
many years. Four stalwart linemen
complete the junior group: North
Carolina's Paul Vincent SEVERN at
end: Tulane's Harley Ray McCollum
and Cornells Nicholas Drahos at
the tackles, and Tennessee's Edward
Michael Molinski at guard.


Five Seniors Sparkle.


The five seniors who closed out
their intercollegiate careers by
gaining the accolade were 1owa's
sturdy iron man" back, Nile
Clarke Kinnick; Clemson's triple
threat, James Banks McFadden;
Southern CALIFORNIA; Harry Bur-
dette Smith at guard; Santa Clara's
John George Schiechl at center and
Notre Danes William Howard
(Bud) Kerr at end


The Old South, with probably
the greatest collection of football
talent it ever has produced, gar
nered more first team posts than
any other sector, four.


Three spots went to the Middle
West. two to the Far West, and one
each to the East and Southwest.


Great Backfield Combine.


The quartet of backs chosen pos
sessed every requisite. They were
tops for running, passing, kicking,
blocking and defensive play. Fur
thermore, they had speed and power,
and, even more important, brains.


Because Of his long downf1eld
runs, which caused many gridiron
followers to compare him favor
ably with Illinois famous "Gallop-
ing Ghost" Of a decade and q half
ago, Tom Harmon probably was the
most spectacular back of the year.


Not only did the 1o5-pound Gary,
Indiana. youngster run and pass
his rivals dizzy but he booted IS
extra points during the year and
kicked one field goal for good
measure.


Kinnick Is "Solid" Back.


The solid" man of the campaign
and likely the most inspirational
leader was Nile Kinnick, who keyed
his Iowa iron men" to such q
fighting pitch that they played their
hearts out every Saturday as the
Hawkeyes became the Big Tens big
gest sensation in many semesters.


Perhaps the best combination
punter-passer in college ranks,
Kinnick was scoring threat every
time he handled the pigskin.


McFadden, 6-foot-3 Clemson half
back, an exceptionally talented
passer and runner, stood out even
more as long distance, accurate
punter. Particularly adept at quick
kicking, McFadden repeatedly drove
rival teams to the ropes with sur
prise boots.


Kimbrough Fast, Strong.


,Kimbrough was so fast that he
was used on sweeps in addition to
the traditional plunging duties of
fullback. He apparently had no
weaknesses. A terrific blocker and
a Standout defensive ace on the
strong Texas Aggies team, KIM
brough was possibly the most pow
erful back in the country.


SEVERN and Kerr drew their end
nominations only by the slightest
of margins. They have all the re-
quisites.


The guards come from two of
the Nations best power teams,
Tennessee and Southern California.
Molinski of Tennessee, 1877
FOUNDER of Polish extraction, caught
the eye of Southern observers with
his alert and effective play. The
Trojans' Harry (Blackjack) Smith
was a standout on the coast.


McCollum South's Best.


Some observers ranked McCollum
as the best tackle in Southern his
tory, an effective giant on the
offense and defense.


Drahos, the only carryover vet
eran in Cornells strong young line,
was an aggressive worker all the
way.

center in 220-pound Schiechl Of
Santa Clara, whose defensive ability
and strong downt1eld blocking may
be traced to his high school expert
ence as fullback. Schiechl played
in every game during his three-year
varsity career and finished with q
record Of never having made a bad

las Marchitello, the Italian chef.

NEW YORK, Aug. 31.-The $20,-
100000 NaZi liner Bremen plowed
the Atlantic today, homeward bound
after rigid inspection by American
authorities that kept her at New
York pier two days past her sailing
date.


The 898-foot vessel, examined
from top to bottom to make certain
she carried no armaments for pos
sible offensive use In the event OF a
European war, had no passengers
aboard as she steamed down the bay
last night.


The ships band blared the Horst
Vessel" and Deutschland Uber
Allies" as the Bremen slipped out
into the Hudson, but the usual
gaiety of leave-taking was absent.


A few of the crew shouted Hell
Hitler" and the ship dipped her
colors IN an exchange with the
French liner Normandie, but that
was all. Only the navigation lights
shone in the twilight. Port holes
and saloon windows were dark.


Normandie Free to Sail.


The Normandie, at an adjoining
pier, was free to sail at the same
time, but remained in New York on
orders from Paris.


Also sailing eastward about the
same time as the Bremen, but after
somewhat briefer inspections by
customs of11cials, were the Cunard-
White Stars Aquitania and the An
chor Lines Pennsylvania, both
British.


There were reports, lacking con-
flrmation, that two British navy
ships were standing out to sea to
convoy the Aquitania home. Among
her 434 passengers was Sir Ronald
Lindsay, recently retired as British
Ambassador to the United States.


Radio messages to the liner went
unanswered. Her ports and win
dows were painted black.


The Pennsylvania, with nearly 300
passengers, carried a supply of sand
bags for possible defensive place.

Persons unfamiliar with Washing
ton and vicinity cannot conceive that
foxes, reds and grays, flourish within
few miles of the Capitol. They do
not believe, until shown, that real
wild ones actually abound in nearby
Virginia and Maryland. But for
more than 100 years the fleet-footed,
tenacious red has roamed the hills
and valleys along the Potomac River
and its tributaries, and the cunning,
lodging gray was here before Colum-
bus came.


"Just why has the willy fox chosen
this particular territory in which to
reside?" is a question many people
ask.


Any one who hunts regularly in
this section can easily explain the
great abundance of foxes.


To thrive, reds, running aristocrats
of the fox family, must have safe
dens or holes in the ground, and
ample food. They do not climb trees
to escape from dogs that would de-
stroy them. Grays, a commoner
species, must have thickets in which
to feed and hide. Hard pressed, they
can and will climb trees. Reds have
their young in the ground, while
grays use hollow logs or old stumps
for theirs.


In the hills and valleys here where
red foxes range there are ample
dens to which they can go when in
danger, or for their families. In the
lowlands and level country grays
find plenty to eat and cover for pro-
lection.


Not Newcomer Here.


The fox is not a newcomer to this
area. George Washington, before he
became President, hunted grays, but
reds were not seen here until about
$50 years ago.
