ANNAPOLIS, Oct. 24-Telegrams
and letters from all parts of the
State today flooded Gov. O'Conor's
Office commencing his advocacy of
legislative program to preserve
and protect roadside beauty in
Maryland.


Mrs. Harry P. Slack, president of
the Garden Clubs of Maryland, was
among the first to telegraph the
Governor approving his stand.


Gov. O'Conor said there was wide
spread sentiment for statutes regu-
lating signboards and the CONNER
cial use of land along State roads.


The question recently came to a
head in Anne Arundel County when
county commissioners found exist
ing laws impotent to prevent COM
mercial exploitation of property
along the new Gov. Ritchie high
way.


So long as prospective builders
comply with laws respecting public
health and safety, the county COM
missioners must issue building per-
mits. Permits have already been
issued for an open-air theater. a
truck depot-garage and two filling
stations along the new Ritchie road
and more are in prospect.


Circuit Judge Ridgely P. Melvin
this month charged the October
grand jury with the duty of inquir-
ing into the trend toward COM
liberalization" of land along high
ways, to determine if existing laws
are adequate and to suggest law
changes for legislative action if
present laws were held insufficient
to prevent DETACHMENT and CONNER
cialization of highways.

the present stalemate."

SHANGHAI, March 25-More
than 10000 Chinese and japanese
troops engaged today in bitter fight
ing on three widely separated fronts
along Chinese rivers and in four
other sectors, with a steadily mount
ing toll of casualties adding to the
more than 100000 rolled up since
the hostilities began more than
twenty months ago.


The bloodiest battles were being
fought in Northern Kiangsi Prov
ince. along the 100-mile Sui River
front, where the japanese were
making a general offensive south
ward toward Nanchang-the pro-
vincial capital ITO air miles SOUTH
east of Hankow-as possible
prelude to resumption Of cam
paign down the Hankow-Canton
Railway.


After bitter fighting the invaders,
attempting to encircle Nanchang,
captured Fengsin. 80 miles to the
west. and Wucheng. 40 miles north
ward, while major force estab-
lished positions on the Nanchang-
Kiukiang Railroad some distance
north of Nanchang.


Fight Southwest of Nanchang.


A sanguinary conflict along the
Loki Wuning Pinkiang highway
southwest of Nanchang and inces-
SAINT air bombings were said to have
caused 5000 Chinese deaths, the
wounding of 10000 and the capture
Of 1000


After many months of skirmishes
and artillery duels, the Japanese
succeeded in crossing the Yellow
River north of Chengchow, about
300 miles north of Hankow and at
the junction of the vital Peiping-
Hankow and Lunghai Railroads. A
Japanese column from Kaifeng
reached point within 80 miles of
Chengchow.


The Japanese have been unable
to cross the Han River west of
Hankow. Chinese counter attacks
held up a Japanese advance near
Shayang, Southern Hupeh Province.


Thousands were fleeing Hangchow
as an estimated 100000 Chinese
troops were moving into that east
ern coastal city in an attempt to
block a threatened Japanese march
southwark along the Tsientang
River.


Severe Clashes Reported.


Severe clashes have been reported
daily from Shansi Province, with the
Japanese unable to pacify the prov
ince and the Chinese unable to drive
out the invaders.


Chinese guerrillas continued their
hit-and-run fighting behind the
Japanese lines nearly everywhere.


Chinese military leaders reported
their men had driven back the jap
anese near Chengchow and admitted
other Chinese units had Withdrawn
from Wucheng after shelling from
Japanese warships and planes.


The Chinese said their lines had
been reformed to the south and were
barring the way to Nanchang.

SHANGHAI June % (P.-The
japanese blockaded Foochow and
Wenchow today and thereby took
control of the last major Chinese
ports along more than 1000 miles of
coastline between the Great Wall
and Canton.


A japanese warning to all foreign
vessels to leave the ports because
they would be closed by dangerous
objects" (mines) and "other OBJ
stacles" went into effect at noon I'll
pm. Wednesday, E. S. T). The
warning had been rejected by the
United States through Clarence E.
Gauss, Consul who notified
Japanese officials that Japan would
be held responsible for any damage
to American interests in the closing
operations. The British and French
took similar stands.


British Ship Reported Trapped.


All foreign merchant vessels were
said to have left Foochow and
Wenchow, respectively about 500
and 300 miles south of Shanghai,
and foreign warships were believed
to have moved outside the harbors
to escape the possibility of being
bottled up.


Domei Japanese news agency re-
ported that British destroyer was
trapped inside the Min River en-
trance at FoochoW, but British naval
officers here said that was extremely
unlikely.


Most of the resident foreigners de-
clined to leave Foochow. Twenty
seven foreigners, including six
Americans, were said to be remain
ing in Wenchow, and 18 missionaries,
including Americans, were reported
to have left Wenchow for Hong
Kong aboard the British steamer
Joan Moller.


Nearby Villages Bombed.


The Chinese were said to have a
considerable military force in or
near Foochow. Nearby villages were
bombed from the air. Nine Japanese
transports were reported in the
vicinity.


Chinese ports occupied or block
AIDED by the Japanese include Che
foo, Tsingtao, Shanghai, Ningpo.
Wenchow, Foochow, Annoy, Canton
and Swatow. The British crown
colony, Hong Kong, and the Portu-
guese colony, Macao, remain open
but have been reduced to trans
shipment centers, their trade with
interior and coastal points having
been cut of entirely. Foreign ships
still are allowed to enter Tientsin,
North China, but have been subject
ed to searches and delays.

cannot get away from this funda-
mental, paramount issue.

COLUMBUS, Ohio, Jan. THE
State of Ohio granted a non-profit
charter today to the United States
Trotting Association, marking the
final step in the merger Of three of
the country's largest harness racing
parent bodies.


The United Trotting Association,
the National Trotting Association
and the American Trotting Register
Association consolidated under the
new name. Incorporation papers
bear the names of 80 directors, rep
resenting various sections of the
United States and Canada. Twenty
six attended today's meeting.


Only the American Trotting Asso-
citation, with headquarters in Chi
cago, did not participate. The new
group plans to invade the Ameri-
cans territory, however, directors to
supervise racing in every State hav-
ing been selected.


E. r. Hartman of New York, pres
ident of the former American Trot-
ting Register Association and one
of the Grand Circuits leading reins-
men, described the merger as the
most forward step ever taken to
help the harness sport"


Under the new setup only one
registration card for owners and
drivers will be required. For two
years the groups had operated un-
der the same rules and classifica-
tons. but Hartman said the merger
would permit closer supervision of
racing and make rule changes easier
to approve and enforce.

BY EDGAR ANSEL MOWRER,

PARIS, Nov. 15-The Netherlands
was saved from German week
end attack at the 18th hour only by
a Belgian declaration conveyed to
Germany that a NaZ invasion of
Holland would automatically bring
Belgium. France, and, naturally,
Great Britain, to the Netherlands
defense.


Faced last Friday by what was
considered virtually certain evidence
that Germany intended to launch
its armies against the Dutch over
the week end, the Belgian cabinet
acted with a magnificent burst of
courage. Having received assurances
from both France and Britain that
Belgium could absolutely count on
their military support to the limit,
the Ministers simply told the Ger
mans that Belgium and Belgium S
big friends would not stand for an
attack on Holland and would not
treat it as a localized affair, but
would enter into action in the de-
fense Of the Dutch Immediately.


This information, conveyed to
Adolf Hitler at the last available
moment, forced the Fuehrer to halt
his planned attack.


Strong Forces Ready.
1t has been known for a long time
that the German forces opposite
Holland, particularly in the hollow
Of the frontier near Cleves, were
being increased to size out of all
proportion with any but offensive
intentions. The last news insisted
that no less than Is German divi-
sions were identified along the
Dutch border and could be speedily
reinforced by others stationed near
Belgium and still others within easy
distance in the German interior.


Not only this. These divisions
we're pyramided one behind the
other, like a football team for a
smash through tackle, with armored
divisions we'll out in front. Holland,
it was commonly figured, might be
smashed and the seacoast reached
in a narrow strip, within 48 hours,
whatever measures the Dutch took,
for the Dutch Army is inexperienced
and none too we'll equipped and the
Dutch water, though the most for
midable of all barriers, is slow to rise,
while most of the highroads on which
armored divisions would travel fol-
low dikeS high above the general
plain.


No Limited War"
Then the Germans were suddenly
informed that they would not be
allowed to eat another artichoke
!eaf"-meaning the Netherlands-in
peace and that the moment the
! first German crossed the Dutch bor-
der Belgium's 20 divisions would
swing into action. 1t was known
that British air support to the
Dutch was certain, furthermore, and
that once Belgium opened its gates
British and French divisions, ar
mored and otherwise believed quail
tatively superior to German similar
units, would swing into action with
a speed which might open the eyes
even of Col Gen. Johannes Blasko-
witz and Col. Gen. Walter Won
Reichenau, who with their army
group commanders were prepared to
do to the Dutch what they had done
to the Poles.


In other words, the general limit
less war the Germans so far have
done everything to avoid would have
started, and the allies and Germans
would have met along the almost
completely open Dutch frontier
British air attacks on advancing
German columns would almost GER
talnly have started the air war which
both sides SO far have done every
thing to avoid


This correspondent can now state
that last Saturday the French staff
feverishly took all necessary meas
ures in expectancy Of an imminent
attack on Holland and the real
beginning OF the war"


Holland has been saved, at least
for short time. Obviously those
who know Hitler do not expect him
supinely to accept this terrific de-
feat.

BERLIN, Nov. 21.-French artil-
lery abruptly ended 35-hour silence
on the western front today with
heavy shelling in the Perl sector. at
the junction of the German, French
and Luxembourg borders, the official
German news agency reported.


The agency, DNB, said the rest of
the l00-mile western front sector
between the Moselle and the Rhine
Rivers was quiet.


On the Upper Rhine front, French
searchlight batteries were active
during the night at several points.
DNB interpreted this as due to "the
enemy's nervousness.


The agency said that there was
heavier rifle and anti-tank fire here,
and that floods had forced the
French to clear out of some bunkers.


Reconnaissance flights of the Ger
man air force over France and
England during the past few days
have yielded important results -
DNB said. The agency reported
"ineffectiveness" of French anti
aircraft fire and said that British
chasers southeast of London did not
hamper German reconnaissance.


DNB said the enemy did little
accommodating yesterday, as Ger
man pursuit planes met no enemy
planes over German territory.


German submarines, cooperating
with the Nazi airforce in the Baltic
and North Seas, have compelled l27
merchant ships to enter German
harbors for search since the begin
ming of the war, DNB reported.


Tonnage of the vessels searched,
1t was said, totaled 245 Ass. Because
the ships or their cargoes were not
subject to seizure under prize laws,
they were discharged, DNB stated.


In addition, the report said, several
hundred other merchantmen were
halted on the high seas for search,
but released Immediately.

NEW YORK, Nov. 1.-THE Ma
tional Professional League Place.
ment Kickers-the fellows who,
week after week, are putting the
foot back in football-have become
the best argument for return of the
goal posts to the goal line on the
college gridiron.


That extra point, which decides
so many of the collegiate tea par
ties, rarely is the all-important win
or-lose difference in the pay-for-
play get-togethers-all because the
hooters assigned to kick that oval
piece of pig leather do just that.


Only twice this year, in some IS
ball games, has the extra point
been the deciding factor in a pro
game. And down through the years,
the National League "figger fill
berts" have found, some 81 per cent
OF the extra points are converted.
The loops statisticians also tell
you that only three times in four
years has team lost because of
failure to kick the extra point.


It's not because the games haven't
been close, but rather that the
kickers Are specialists, like the
butchers who whack those lamb
chops off a quarter of meat all day
without getting their thumbs in
the way. They aren't paid to miss.


Manders Kicks " Straight.


Take Automatic Jack Manders,
the Chicago Bears needle-thread-
ing kicker, for instance. Jack &C
quired his nickname because he
once booted u extra points in a
row in league competition, which
is about par for the course. Now
Jack has been ailing much of this
year, but his aches and pains
haven't prevented him from con-
verting on II out of IL chances.
And Tiny Engebretsen, Green Bay
Little" 240-pounder, hasn't missed
in II shots at the uprights this
year.


Altogether, 1l9 extra points have
been converted out of 146 touch
downs scored in the loop this fall,
with the best club averages turned
in by the New York Giants, who
have a 10-for-1O mark, and the
Pittsburgh Pirates, whose Armand
Niccolai has turned the trick after
each OF the BUGS nine touchdowns.


All of which adds up to a pretty
fair argument in favor of those who
want the college uprights on the
goal line instead of 10 yards back.
Some one has figured up that only
63 per cent of the conversions have
been made after collegiate touch
downs. The reason may not be
the extra 10 yards to the goal posts.


Extra Points Tie Eastern Race.


The pro coaches tell you, how
ever, that fellows like Manders, En-
gebretsen, Niccolai, Bo Russell, who
has converted 10 out of II this year
for Washington, and Chef Adams,
with five for five for Cleveland, do
it simply because the posts are
nearer and the kickers spend hours
rehearsing the play.


The two extra points which de-
cided pro league games this year
have left the Giants and the Wash
lngton Redskins all tied up, like
your new four-in-hand, for the lead
in the loops Eastern Division
championship race, and the chances
are they'll stay that way until their
au-important game December 3 in
New York. Tomorrow the Giants
are hot favorites over the Chicago
Cardinals and the Redskins should
come out on top of Ace Parker and
his Brooklyn Dodger company.


The western title race, however,
is still awhirl, with tomorrows top
league game a strong factor in the
stretch drive. The leading Detroit
Lions, who snapped the Giants 49,
game unbeaten run last week with
superb passing and field-goal kick
ing display, entertain the high
scoring Chicago Bear machine in
what is strictly a toss-up.


Bears Lead in Gaining.


The Bears were in slump there
for a while and have three defeats
against five victories for the season
to date, but they showed plenty OF
what it takes in their 1927 decision
over Green Bay last week. They
still remain the top yard and point
getting machine in the league, hav-
ing advanced the ball 1850 yards
passing and rushing and piled uu
the impressive total of 200 points
In eight games.


Green Bays Packers, whose two
defeats and five victories place
them second to Detroit's once-beat-
en- combination in the Western
race, figure to have breeze against
the Philadelphia Eagles tomorrow
and if they win can go into a first
place divisional tie should the
Lions lose.

BY the Associated Press.


BUENOS AIRES, Sept. 1.-South
America, anxious to maintain neu-
trality in the European conflict and
keep its raw materials moving to
the Old World, looked to the United
States today for signal which may
indicate the course of the southern
continent.


The outbreak of hostilities between
Germany and Poland found Latin
American nations and the United
States more nearly in complete &C
cord than in 1914.


The three most powerful South
American countries - Argentina,
Brazil and Chile-have frequently
demonstrated that their interests are
| linked closely with those of the
United States, Britain and France.
There have been indications recently
that the crisis in Europe has been
swinging Argentina's policy closer
toward a strong Western Hemisphere
defense alliance which Secretary
Hull sought and which Argentina
rejected at the Pan-American Con-
| ference in Lima, Peru, last December.
Argentina Swings Away.
Experienced observers said that
whatever lead might be taken by
the United States, Argentina, Brazil
and Chile would be followed by the
other Latin American nations.
A strong bloc of Argentine deputies
and citizens has been pressing for
an open avowal of support for the
British-French alliance.
President Roberto Ortiz of Argen-
! tina started to swing away from the
Rome Berlin axis last May when he
, told Congress that unilateral trade
agreements with Germany and other
nations were objects of necessity
rather than desire Indicating
Argentina's greater dependence on
the Western Hemisphere. the Buenos
Aires government on the same day
announced its decision to negotiate
commercial treaty with the United
States and new agreement with
Brazil.


Strong Financial Reasons.


Argentina has strong financial
reasons for leaning toward the
United States, France and Britain.
Britain is her best customer and
Argentina knows that in wartime
England and France will be the only
old world countries able to buy her
wheat and meat. Argentina re-
manned neutral in the World War,
but the recent publication of pur-
ported private papers of wartime
President Hipolito Yrigoyen dis
closed that he had signed decla-
ration OF war against Germany
which was withdrawn after Berlin
agreed to pay indemnities for SUBJ
marine attacks against Argentine
shippings.


Well-informed sources in Santiago
expressed the opinion that Chile
would be unable to follow its 1914
policy ofindependent neutrality but
WOULD favor common inter-
American stand in accordance with
Pan-American consultative agree
ments.

Cut the turkey carcass into pieces
and put it in a kettle with six cups
of water. Simmer, covered, for one
hour. Add to the soup one cup cut
carrots, one or two stalks of celery
with the leaves attached, one-half
cup diced turnips, one-half cup
sliced onions, one cup tomatoes, one
quarter cup parsley, three table
spoons rice or barley, one-half tea
spoon salt and little black pepper.
Cover again and simmer for one
hour longer. Strain, chill and re-
move fat. Reheat the soup, adding
more seasoning if necessary. If the
carcass is small, or has been too
well picked" little beef extract
may be added to give the soup color
and flavor.

BY the Associated Press.


VERA CRUZ, Mexico, Dec. 15.-
Speculation arose today that Ger
many's third largest merchant ship
the 32,581-ton liner Columbus, was
being used to lure British warships
into a battle trap.


Foreign sources said the big pas
senger ship, painted battleship gray
and carrying provisions and fuel for
a 50-day voyage, sailed from Vera
Cruz yesterday as bait for British
war vessels, as supply ship for
Nazi men O. war or to make a bold
dash for home.


No word had been received from
her since she sailed, ostensibly for
Oslo, Norway, but unconfirmed re-
ports said she already was being
trailed by a British destroyer.


Believed Conveyed by Subs.


Foreign sources said that the Co.
lumbus representatives seemed, with
carefully contrived appearance of
secrecy, to have taken pains that
any interested party-such as Brit
ish and French agents in Mexico
know the exact hour of her de-
parture and her early course.


With persistent reports that Ger
man, as we'll as British, warships
have been operating in the Gulf of
Mexico and the Caribbean Sea, they
expressed belief that the liner, a
tempting prize of war, was being
used as a decoy.


They suggested that the Colum-
bus, sailing apparently unarmed and
defenseless on open seas, actually
would be conveyed by German SUBJ
marines waiting to torpedo any Brit
lsh or French sea raiders that might
attack the passenger ship.


These sources expressed belief
that the British and French, aware
Of the possibility of a trap, prob
ably would gamble their chances OF
seizmg or destroying the Columbus


May Refuel Submarines.


Another answer suggested for the
mystery of the liners departure
after having found haven in Mexico
since early in the war was that she
might have rendezvous at sea with
Nazi submarines or destroyers to re-
fuel and reprovision them.


Both this explanation and the
possibility that she might attempt
to run the allied blockade into Ger
many despite clearance papers for
Oslo, it was said, were indicated by
her concealing gray paint and huge
stores of food and fuel.


There were rumors that the 4,147-
ton Hamelin, the only Nazi vessel
remaining here, also would sail soon.


The German freighter Arauca,
which left just before the Columbus,
was reported sighted of shore q
short distance north of Vera Cruz
with destroyer, unidentified, but
believed part of the United States
neutrality patrol, following her.

By the Associated Press.


BERLIN, Aug. 23-All avenues
Of travel out of Germany were
jammed today with French and
British citizens and other foreigners
fleeing for fear of war. No seats
in airplanes could be obtained after
early morning. Trains ran through
out the day with corridors filled.


British and French citizens were
advised by their local diplomatic
officials to leave Germany. The
French step followed upon a direct
order transmitted from Paris to the
French Ambassador, Ribert Cou-
londre.


American residents beSieged con-
sular and diplomatic officials asking
for advice. Invariably they were told
that United States officials have no
information on which to give coun-
sci.


Many tourists in Berlin, however,
took to their heels without waiting
for specific word.
Only one French newspaper cor
respondent was left behind to hold
the French journalistic fort. All
British newsmen departed excepting
five chief correspondents.

KIRKENES, Norway, Dec. L.
Russian troops dropped by para
chutes from huge bombing planes
were reported to have occupied Pet
samo, Finland's chief port on the
Arctic Ocean, today following bomb
ing raids which left the port and
another town in flames.


Violent fighting between the Fin
nish and Russian forces was re-
ported.


Refugees said the Russians took
the ancient monastery Of Petchenga,
10 miles south Of Petsamo, cutting
off Finnish troops north Of that
point.


The whole town of Liinahamari,
in Finland's corridor to the Arctic
near the Norwegian border, was in
flames from repeated raids by Soviet
bombing planes.
Warplanes also bombed Salmijervi,
which is just across the Pasik pa
cific) River from Kirkenes, appar-
emily trying to stop refugees from
crossing the frozen river into Nor
way.


Despite machine-gunning from
low-f1ying airplanes, 600 refugees
crossed the frontier.


Crowds of women and children
were seen on roads leading to the
border as Soviet planes roared over
head.


The air raids, during the brief
hours of daylight inside the Arctic
circle, continued where they left of
yesterday.


Liinihamari is the Arctic Ocean
terminus of Finland's Baltic-to-Arc-
tic rad. known as the worlds
northernmost highway"

1916, joined the band of young
Americans flying with the allies. He
downed six enemy planes and was
shot down once and rescued.

man patrols operated on reconnals-

their activity was concentrated in
the region east of the Moselle River
and that the Germans were par
ticularly active in the Med River

able pitching.

this jagged line running between
France and Switzerland.


One country modified to get into
the war, the other mobilized to
keep out. And both have gone

other.


From the southern tip Of Switzer-

at Basel, both nations have manned

French Seek to Reassure Swiss.

Yet just to show there are no

BY the Associated Press.


PARIS, Oct. French ard
British sources indicated today that
the allies were playing delaying
game to prevent the start of major
German operations on the western
front in order to let winter weather
give full effect to the blockade Of
Germany.


These sources indicated that allied
leaders were convinced that If Ger
many had to face a winter siege
without sensational land battles to
bolster the morale, the Nazis would
be much weaker when weather
cleared again for military opera
tions in the spring.


French military observers set the
end of October as the outside Limit
for the German offensive to start.
While there often is Indian sum-
mer" weather in Alsace-Lorraine
through October, the weather turns
bad with the beginning of Novem-
Der and stays bad through February.


Experienced French military men
recalled that during the last war
the weather was such that there
never were more than two weeks in
December and January when it was
possible for airplanes to take of,
even for reconnaissance fights.


Hope to Prolong "Lull."


The French and British appeared
to be taking full advantage of Adolf
Hitler's peace lull," doing every
thing possible to prolong it until
the end of October. After that the
war probably would settle down to
. winter siege with the western
front stalemated and the British
And French fleets drawing a sea
Gordon about Germany.


In that connection the French
general staff's communique tonight
SAID the French Navy in the last
week had intercepted 10000 tons of
merchandise destined for Germany.
The communique also reported ar
tillery action on both sides between
the Moselle and Saar Rivers and
patrol action. also by both sides,
south of ZWeibruecken.


The French high command, far
from pressing an offensive against
German lines, seemed to be care
fully strengthening its own advance
positions against occasional attacks,
which were reported repulsed.


Attacks Try Out French.


During the last week the Germans
made perhaps 10 or IL of these small
attacks against French lines estat1-
Gshed on German territory.


Most German attacks were made
during the night, the French in
dicated. In the largest there was
scarcely platoon involved and in
the majority the Germans used
only combat group or section
8 to Is men.


These German night attacks of
the last week seemed designed to
test out French strength in the
areas where they advanced farthest
into the German no-man's land
separating the Maginot and Sieg-
fried Lines.


French advance posts were kept
IN a constant state of alert, watch
ing for shadows sliding over ground
soaked by days of rain. AT first
sight of suspicious shapes crawling
over the mud the French sent up
flares, throwing norman 's-land into
bold relief. In the light of the flares
the machine-guns picked out targets
while the artillery began shelling.


French reports said the Germans
froze to the earth at the first shots,
then slowly inched their way back
ward


Aerial Activity Curtailed.


Bad weather already has curtailed
aerial activity The French said
German planes were noted OCCASION
ally flying behind the German lines,
apparently trying distance spotting
for the artillery, but rarely did the
Nazis venture over French territory.


French planes likewise were
pinned down by the weather. Al
though the weather in the strictest
sense was not too bad for flying,
heavy fogs which lay over river val
leys between the Rhine and the
Moselle made flights almost useless,
as it was impossible to see through
the heavy curtain drawn over posi-
tions of both armies.

NORFOLK, Va, June "A tanker
crashed into two spans of a toll
bridge across the Elizabeth River
today, partially wrecking the struc-
ture and halting temporarily all
harbor traffic.


Two of five spans of the bridge.
connecting Norfolk and Portsmouth,
were demolished, but the crumbling
mass Of steel and iron fell clear of
the tanker Rhode Island, owned by
the Texas Oil Co.


Bridge-Tenders c. L. Cunningham
and Lee Zimmerman leaped from
their watchman towers, 100 feet
above the water. They were rescued
from the river and taken to a Nor
folk hospital, where their condition
was regarded as serious.


Two unidentified women, waiting
in their automobile on the span, saw
the impending danger and ran from
the car off the bridge safely.


Since the wreckage from the
bridge spans fell away from the
tanker, witnesses said they believed
no one was injured on the ship and
that the vessel was not damaged


The highway bridge is several
miles from Norfolk proper.

SHANGHAI, July 29.-British and
japanese troops faced each other
across newly erected japanese
barbed-wire barricades on Shang-
hal boundary tonight as result OF
an incident which caused Japanese
British friction here to flare anew.


Japanese naval forces ran up the
barrier along mile and half of
the British defense sector after an
encounter in which japanese seized
and held four British soldiers for
two hours and a half.


British military commanders pro-
tested the barricade, asserting it was
on territory inside the British zone
There were strong indications that
the encounter held further possibil-
tiles of trouble.


Four Britons Seized.


The friction began when four men
Of the Seaforth Highlander Regi-
ment in a truck entered the jap
anese defense zone to repair barbed-
wire. British officers said the men
mistakenly believed they were in the
British zone.


Quickly men of the japanese naval
landing force - the permanent
Shanghai garrison-blocked off the
alleyway in which the Britons were
working, cutting off their escape.


Then 200 Japanese, working at
high speed. strung three strands of
wire along a mile and half stretch
from Soochow Creek to the northern
limit of the British defense sector.


Panic Among Chinese.


Reports of British-Japanese trou-
BILE running through the nearby
Japanese occupied part of the city
caused panic among Chinese resi-
dents, thousands of whom left that
area.


After two and a half hours nego-
tiation British officers obtained the
release of the men and truck.


The northern and western bound
aries of the International Settle
ment, adjacent to Japanese-held
sections of Shanghai, lie within de-
fense zones held by United States
marines and British Army troops.
The British boundary especially has
been the scene of continual friction
ever since the Japanese Army and
Navy completed occupation of the
Greater Shanghai area In Novem-
ber, 1887.

ROME, April 8-Some of the
1000 or more Italian refugees from
Albania said today they fled that
country because of insurrectional
movements which broke out the past
week.


They said that for week they
had noticed an anti-Italian move
ment which reached alarming pro-
portions" last Wednesday when Al
bapians celebrated the birth of an
heir to King Zog and Queen Ger
aldine. Their accounts conflicted
with that of an American woman
refugee who refused to divulge her
name, fearing reprisals on Albanian
friends in Tirana.


The American maintained that
groups of students sang patriotic
songs in Tirana streets last Satur-
day and Sunday following popular
concerts. She insisted nothing was
said about Italy but that the reason
for the songs, which had indie
pendence as their theme, was OBJ
vious since there were rumors of
impending italian invasion.


King Zog, fearful of incidents,
forbade further demonstrations.
Nothing further happened, she
added, until the birth of the Crown
Prince when the people again were
allowed to celebrate in the streets,
and again gave vent to their feel
ings in patriotic songs.

BURGOS, April P).-National-

had sent a message to Generalissimo
Francisco Franco expressing thanks
"for the desired victory of Catholic
Spain


Nationalists said the Pope sent the
following telegram to Gen. Franco:


Raising our hearts to God we
thank him and your excellency for
the desired victory of Catholic Spain
and pray that this beloved country,
having found peace, may renew
with vigor her ancient Christian
traditions which made her SO great.


with these sentiments we send
your excellency and the whole
Spanish people our apostolic bless
ing"


Gen. Franco replied:


Intense emotion has been pro-
duced by the telegram of your
holiness, inspired by the total VIC
tor of our arms, which fought an
heroic crusade against the enimies
of the religion of the fatherland
and Christian civilization.


1.-The Spanish people, who have
suffered. raise also with your holi-
ness their hearts to God, who gave
His grace, and beg Him to protect
our great work in the future. The
Spanish people with me express to
your holiness immense gratitude
for your loving words and for your
apostolic blessing. which has been
received with religious fervor and
with greatest devotion to your
holiness"

Secretary of State Hull, asked for
comment on the British German
naval battle off the Uruguayan coast
yesterday, said that any violation
of the American neutrality zone
naturally would be Of concern to
the American nations.


He said, however, that he had not
yet ascertained all of the details
concerning the naval engagement.
The department had heard nothing
to confirm reports that the German
pocket battleship Graf Spec had
sunk two merchant vessels immedi-

battle with three British cruisers.


Awaits Additional Details.


Mr.. Hull said any further develop

ton of Panama which set out
neutrality zone around the Amer
ican nations which they considered
should be free of any belligerent
actions by any other of the nations
involved in the European war, would
be determined later as fuller infor-
matlOn came TO light.


The declaration of Panama pro-
vides that any other of the Amer
ican republics may call upon the
other nations of this hemisphere for
consultation whenever Pan-Amer-
lean security might be considered
threatened


The Secretary pointed out that
there never was any contemplation
that the so-called safety zone" dec
laration would be enforced by the
use of force.


The declaration provided for Joint
representations by the American
governments to secure agreements
from the belligerent governments to
comply with the principles of the
neutrality zone. Mr. Hull said that
so far as he knew there had been
no replies to notices sent the bel
ligerent nations Of the Panama
declaration.


First reports from South Amer
lea brought the reaction here
that a pitched battle between war
ships within the zone might not
raise any issues with the American
republics unless some interests Of
the republics were involved.


Such interests, however might be
involved if the naval battle inter-
fered with Western Hemisphere
shipping lanes.


Observers were of the opinion that
the Graf Specs sinking Of the two
merchant ships, which were prob
ably carrying Latin American car
goes to Britain, definitely involved
Western Hemisphere interests If the
sinking occurred inside the neu-
trality zone.

The drastic innovations in gov
ernment financing announced by
Germany after the annexation of
Bohemia, Moravia and Memel reveal
the depths to which Chancellor Hit
ler's imperial expansion has plunged
the Third Reich and gives the world
some hope that the Nazis' money
troubles will curb any immediate
resumption of their aggressive for
eign campaigns.


Preparations for war-both rearm-
ament and the mobilizing and move
ment OF German military forces
during the past year-have placed
heavy drain upon the Reichs fiscal
resources. Even with prices and
wages rigidly controlled by the gov
ernment against excessive increase,
Nazi economists have been severely
taxed to provide the money for re-
armament and the costs of mobil-
ization and invasion, as we'll as for
the vast public works program which
Is virtually building a new Germany.


To solve the problem Germany
now announces that government
obligations to industry will be paid
sixty per cent in cash and forty per
cent in non-interest-bear tax
certificates, thus easing the drain
upon the Nazi Golfers, but at the
same time bringing in its train the
prospect of even greater troubles
which may include outright infla-
tion-for the tax certificates will be
legal for the payment Of future taxes
at a premium over their face value.
Collaterally, the certificates will be
legal tender and in effect increase
the amount Of paper money in cir
culation, although, at least for the
present, imitation through new note
issues is avoided.


The German people have horror
OF currency imitation, remembering
1922-24, when they carried away
their wages in suit cases full of
worthless paper bills nominally val
ued to the extent of thousands of mil
lions Of marks. The Nazi masters
know, too, that any bold attempt to
relive those wild times would inev-
itably undermine and very probably
topple their government.


Yet by the present device currency
imitation becomes a fact under an
other name, and the German people,
through what amounts to forced
loan begin paying for the extremities
to which their leaders have gone to
build not new Reich, identical with
the old, but an empire over subject
peoples who were never a part of
modern Germany.


What will the final cost of con-
quest and empire be for the German
nation, and will the profits of empire
repay the expense of creating it?

PARIS, July 29-The Paris shops
: world-renowned for their chic and
= glitter, are bustling with shoppers
: French and foreign, and shop win
dows are more colorful than ever.
: Advance fall models are already
/. being shown in the ateliers Of the
haute couture; furriers are featur-
|. ing their new winter fashions, and
buyers from all over the world are
congregating here. For Paris is
ever the capital of elegance, and to
. shop here is the dream of every
woman.


Notwithstanding the early show
: ings of fall models, Paris shops are
summery. Windows display the
most amazing headgear for Ship
. board, and also sports clothes of all
: kinds. There are more beautiful
. evening frocks, and yards and
yards of rich and colorful fabrics.
There are gloves and shoes such as
only Paris can produce, and all that
wondrous array of lovely and often
useless things that down through
the centuries have been known as
articles de Paris"


Shops of All Kinds.


There are famous jewelry marts-
shops where porcelains are sold,
shops for laces, shops for silks, shops
for works of art. And there are
little shops tucked away in unpre-
tentious streets that have been
known for their excellence since the
days Of the French Revolution and
before 1t. The rue de la Paix is
conceded to be the most distin-
guished shopping center in the
world, but not all the charm of
Paris shops is compressed within
this magic street All over Paris
there are stores that sell enchant-
ing things. Some of them have been
known to connoisseurs for gener-
ations.


There are perfumers that sold
scents and pomades to ladies and
gentlemen Of the Emperor Napol-
cons court, and haberdashers who
sold shirts and ties to Talleyrand,
but these shops with their back
grounds of elegance and tradition
are not more interesting to the Wis
itor from overseas than are the
many little open-air markets that
are such an agreeable feature of
Paris life.


Art While You Wait.


There are bird markets and flower
markets, and vegetable markets.
There are days when artists exhibit
their paintings under the spreading
branches of the trees that border
the "Boul Mich" or, better still, set
up their easels within the shadow
Of the Madeleine. There are the
book stalls on the quays, where one
may buy old books. and new books
too, and there is a fabric mart in
old Montmartre where more than
one successful American designer
got her start!


Not every French woman knows
about the fabric market in the rue
Charles Nodier, but young dress de-
signers, without fame or capital, are
quick to discover it. Here are sold
remnants Of 10 dollar yard fabrics
at so cents to dollar yard. There
are tweeds and woolen cloths in the
very newest weaves and hand paint
ed cire satins, lovely stuf1s for eve
ming jackets, black silk organdies
with shining threads running
through them, cloudy pastel satins,
reversible chiffon velvets, and
glinting heaps of brocades. The
gorgeous stuffs are piled on low
tables spread across the pavement
the length of the street. 1t is just
another of the surprises that await
the shopper in Paris!

WARSAW, Sept. THE defenders
of this Polish capital were reported

River, where they rallied and were
fighting like lions" against German

The defense line ran between
Plonsk and Pultusk. northwest and
northeast of Warsaw, respectively
About 80 miles of open country and
the protecting Vistula River lay be-
tween Warsaw and the invaders
from the north.


The right wing of the Poles had
been hammered back from Ciecha
now. about Is miles northwest OF
Pultusk, pivoting on Plonsk.


Pultusk Recovered.


At one stage of the struggle the
Poles were driven from Pultusk and
the Germans threatened to turn
the Polish flank and thrust on to
the Vistula and Warsaw. Pultusk
however, was regained in the face
of whitening German fire.


A staff officer slightly wounded

holding the Plonsk-Pultusk line
beating off repeated German at.
tempts to break through.


The Poles are fighting like lions,
he said.


The officer related that Germans
with tank vanguards succeeded in

umns, destroying and capturing q

The officer assured members OF

and some Poles took heart from
memories of Marshal Pilsudski's
great counter offensive in August
1920, when Bolshevist troops were
halted just outside Warsaw and

Speaking on "Germanys Growing
Pains" before the District branch of
the National League of American
Pen Women last night, Mrs. Lydia
van Hogen van Zandt, lecturer and
traveller, who recently visited in
Germany, declared that she found
that country an armed camp, with
capital, labor, industry and agri-
culture all modified to support the
army.


Mrs. van Zandt illustrated her
talk with propaganda maps which,
she explained, are used in German
schools. One of these illustrated
Hitler's plan for the return of Ger
man colonies and other outlined
his plan for uniting all Germany.


The speaker, whose talk followed
the Pen Women's weekly family
night dinner at the Grafton Hotel
said she found it very easy to obtain
information about the program in
Germany, as the Germans are very
proud of what they are doing.


She declared, however, that the
visitor feels sorry for the real Ger
man people because they are domi-
mated by minority group.


Mrs. van Zandt spent six months
IN Central Europe with her husband
Maj. j. Parker van Zandt. who made
an airline survey of that section, and
made three visits to Germany. She
was introduced last night by Mrs.
Gilbert Grosvenor.

Peacocks always have been glamor
birds. Even Solomon imported them
from the jungles of India to add
gorgeousness to his magnificent
palace grounds.

the fate of lesser barnyard fowls,
only people of great prominence
have been considered worthy of eat

them at their most sumptuous
feasts, Romans considered peacock
tongues and brains the quintessence
of royal dishes.


In Merrie England, ceremonies OBJ

a modern Hollywood preview. To
prepare the fowl for cooking Britalns

stuffed with rare spices, then
roasted. When slightly cooled, 1t

| feathers, which was sewed on to
keep it in place. The peacock was
then arranged gracefully on a huge
silver charger, ready for serving.

highly priced privilege fell to the
most beautiful guest present. AS
she entered the dining room carry
ing her handsome burden, the host
ignited a wad of cotton which had
been saturated with brandy and
stuffed in the gilded beak. All lights
were dimmed. With appropriate
dignity the fowl was placed before
the guest OF honor for carving, job
that called for considerable talent.

Her death, in way, was a bless

NEW YORK, Oct. 19.-After
weathering "lost" hurricane, the
United States liner President Hard
ing ploughed through subsiding seas
today with 73 persons under treat
ment for injuries.


Twenty-three had broken bones.
Paul johnson, a cabin waiter, was
lost overheard.


Engine Room Storekeeper Henry
Heinsoth underwent an emergency
appendicitis operation at the height
of the storm, while a 75-mile-an-
hour gale bowled passengers and
crew about and knocked them
against furniture.


Among those less seriously injured
was Paul van Iceland, former
Belgian premier, who suffered
bruises.


$50 Americans Aboard.


The storm toll was the highest
aboard a modern liner in North
Atlantic waters in several years.


The sturdy l3,869-ton vessel, carry
ing 800 Americans among the SGT
passengers it was bringing to New
York from the war zones, was tossed
in heavy seas by a wandering hur-
ricane that had swept northward
from Bermuda.


Weather officials had been un-
able to chart the storms path and
issue warnings because of lack of
reports from vessels along its course,
a result of wartime measures ban
ming radio messages that might be-
tray merchant shipping to belliger-
ent WarShlpS


Cutter Brings Medical Supplies.


A wireless appeal by Capt. James
E. Roberts brought the Coast Guard
cutter Hamilton speeding to the
liners side with medical supplies.


Although waves ripped away a
starboard rail, a lifeboat and davit,
Capt. Roberts abandoned a plan to
put in at Halifax after an inspection
disclosed mo structural damage"
The liner was expected to dock here
Saturday.

fury. the 3.509-ton British freighter
Blairbeg, sent out distress signal
after its rudder chains were carried
away but later proceeded on its way
unassisted.

The first of a series of informal
indoor horse shows staged yesterday
by the Student Riding Club of Ar
lington Hall Junior College in nearby
Virginia gave a small group of in
terested spectators an insight into
what patient teaching can accom-
plish with absolute novice riders in
q short time.


Under the direction of Fritz Klee-
man, the schools instructor, the
show was divided into sections for
those who have ridden only few
months and graded on up to those
who have had anywhere from year
to five years of experience. Even
the rankest beginners made COM
mendable showings and others dis
played enough ability to compete
with almost any feminine rider here
about. Several will be selected to
represent the school at the first Fort
Myer show December 13.


Jean Holden Winner.


The feature of the program was
the open jumping class in which 20

horses, and despite inadequate space

formances. The class was won by
Jean Holden, who has been riding

Ia faults over the 12-jump course.

last year and one of the best riders
in the school, took second place with
King Rock after a jump-off with
Phoebe Tolhelm, who rode the
famous Kismet, now 80 years old.


The advance horsemanship class,
for girls who have been riding from
one to two years, found Miss Tolhelm
moving up to take the blue ribbon,

bred she trained herself for his show
ring debut yesterday, the president
of the Student Riding Club made
favorable impression on Capt. James
3. Quill of Fort Myer, the judge, to
get the nod over Maryl Ritter, run
ner-up.


Make Rapid Progress.


According to Kleeman, who has
built up the riding club from l8 men,
bers to almost 100 in five years, sew
eral of the girls who competed in
the four beginners classes already
are showing ability expected only
of more advanced students. The
four winners, Anne Williams, Martha
Brooks, Dorise Bell and Mildred
Walner, all are strangers to the diff
cult art of correct riding, but all
proved they have learned much since
starting year or so ago.


The classes we're not merely the
usual walk, trot and canter events
that require only average ability, but
intricate tests of making horse re-
spond to various and eXacting de-
mands of the rider. Many of the
girls competing yesterday never be-
fore had been in show ring and
one of the main purposes was to
build their confidence. Each came
through in fine style and none suf-
fered fall.


An added attraction was the musi-
cal drill in which 20 uniformed rid

BY the Associated Press.


BUDAPEST, Sept. 13.-To more
than 100000 Jews in Poland war
has come as a new fear that goes
beyond the danger of loss of homes
and property and the normal risks
of war.


They flee not only the German
Army but the anti-Semitic policies
they believe will come with any Ger
man occupation. Today they were
crowding into the entire area of
Southeastern Poland-but their way
was difficult If not impossible.


The Rumanian border was blocked
to them and the Soviet frontiers also
apparently were closed.


Among the refugees Jews were
prominent, from well-dressed busi-
nesmen to black-gowned orthodox
Jews with skull caps and side curls.


The German drive has struck into
areas which long were regarded as
the stronghold of Eastern European
Jewry-villages and schools where
customs have not changed for GEN.
turies. Among the buildings aban-
doned were schools for rabbis, where
life and instruction had no modern
note.


| Among the Jews who fled such
cities as Krakow and Katowice were
thousands who escaped from Ger
many during the last year. Home
less to begin with, the new flight
was only a continuation.
Meanwhile, Jews were fighting in
Polish uniforms in an effort to stem
the German drive. Thousands of
Jews were among the reserve officers
called up.


Everywhere the Polish Jews, con-
stituting Poland's second largest
minority, were directly involved in
the war.

KAIFENG, China GA year after
japanese occupation, 1000 Chinese refu-
gees in this Honan Province capital still
receive their daily bread from American
and other foreign missionaries.


The missionaries say their charges are
mostly Kaifeng natives who have no
means of supporting themselves. There
were 10000 others to be cared for when
the japanese took the city, but they
have found work or gone away.


Kaifeng remains frontier city. A
few miles to the southwest at the Vel
low Rivers new course are the front
lines. Japanese thus far have shown no
disposition to cross the stream and con-
tinue to the west. Chinese troops fire.
quently cross to the east and raid Kai-
fengs environs.


When the native raiding forces are ac-
tive the Japanese here close the city
gates, sit tight until reinforcements
come.


The city's population virtually has re-
turned to normal. The employed for the
most part are laborers engaged by the
Japanese In building new dyke on the
Yellow River and on a new railway con-
Meeting Kaifeng with the Peiping-
Hangkow line northeast Of here.


Approximately one-haf of Kaifeng's
shops have reopened, but their stocks are
small.

Because his entry lay overlooked
in the Columbia Country Club office
while the draw was being made,
Harry Brinkerhoff, jr., Central
Highs No 2 player and one of the
leading junior netmen in the city,
had the unique distinction this
morning of starting in a tennis
tournament as one of the foremost
favorites-yet unSeeded.


Brinkerhoff, son of the public
parks professional, sent in his entry
for The Star tourney this week,
but it became waylaid with several
routine papers and was not delivered
to Columbia's tennis shop until late
yesterday. Had it been among the
others, Brinkerhoff would have
been seeded no lower than fourth,
as he holds that District rating
among the juniors who were seeded
in the regular draw


Fast Early Match Looms.


Officials, following customary pro-
cedure in such matters, paired him
against the top man in the lower
half who had drawn a first-round
bye. If both win their first-round
matches, Brinkerhoff and Ham
Bonham Of Western, seeded No. 4
in the draw, must meet in the second
round-an exceptionally early match
for two such high-ranked entrants,
but the only possible solution under
the circumstances.


The winner of that match faces an
almost unobstructed path to the
semi-finals unless Bobbie Bensinger.
boys champion last year who is
attempting the herculean task of
playing in both the boys and juniors
tourney, upsets him in the quarter
finals.

The first champion of The Stars
three-Week tourney was crowned
yesterday when Mary Cootes Belin.
as expected, defeated Willie O'Steen
for her second City of Washington
title in three years. Margaret
Robinson is the only other woman
in the Journeys 10-year history to
win twice.

stubborn fight than the 6-3. 6-l
scores indicate, but, like all of Mrs.
Belln's previous victims, never really
threatened. Once she got the feel
OF her powerful drives. the repeating
champ drove the public parks queen
from Sldeline to sideline and the
plucky little loser had all she could
90 merely to return the ball.


At that, Miss O'Steen forced three
games of the first set and five of
the second to deuce and fought off
match point in the sixth game of
the second set before finally sue
cumblng. Mrs. Belin out-pointed
her opponent, 1926, in the first set

francs.

Twin sisters hold the highest
Offices in the Junior Republic of
Richard Montgomery High School.
They are Jean and Eleanor Leighton
Of Montrose, Md, and they are presi-
dent and vice president. respectively.


In appearance, the twins are near
ly identical. Both are blonds with
blue eyes and fair compilations, and
they accentuate their resemblance
by dressing alike. Their scholastic
standing has been about the same,
with scarcely tenth of a point diff
ference. Both skipped the fourth
grade.


They sing duets, one of them be-
ing soprano and the other a con-
tralto; they hold important posi-
tions on the schools track team,
and they also work together in All
Club activities, having won many
prizes.


The only important difference be-
tween the twins involves their plans
for the future. Jean wants to
teach, while Eleanor is set on doing
secretarial work.

Mrs. Helen Hudson Jones, So, for
mer Baden (MdD school teacher.
who plunged to her death late yes
terday from the center span of the
Calvert Street Bridge, was declared
suicide last night by Coroner A.
Magruder Macdonald.

take her own life a month ago by
slashing her wrists and had been a
patient in Cedarcroft Sanitarium
since November l, after her release
from Garfield Hospital.


Investigators learned that Mrs.
Jones left the sanitarium with three
friends yesterday and disappeared
while attending downtown theater.


Her 140-foot leap from the bridge
railing was witnessed by Arthur Slu-
man, 1014 Eighth street NV, who
said the woman suddenly stopped
walking, placed her purse on the
rail and climbed over. Her body
struck the macadam roadway in
Rock Creek Park below.


Police learned that Mrs. Jones had
been separated from her husband
for some time and that a 6-year-old
daughter, Anne, had been taken to
California by Mrs. Jones' sister fol-
lowing her first suicide attempt.


She had been an instructor in the
Baden School for three years, friends
said, and had been under a physic-
ianS' care for several months.

QUITO, Ecuador, March 24.-Gov-
ernment officials asserted today that
a "Marxist" revolutionary attempt
had been quelled by Federal police,
who yesterday used tear gas and
fixed bayonets to rout striking stu
dents and textile workers.


One student and several workers
were injured. The students, who
had conducted their strike by hold
ing out in the National University,
and the workers, who had occupied
plants in sympathetic sit-in strikes
supporting the students, were elected
from their positions.


Beyond branding it as "Marxist"
officials would not discuss motives of
the student strike but said police
measures were invoked after dis
covery" of a plan of action which
was to be followed had the "Marxist"
movement succeeded.


Serious trouble at the university
was averted when the students with
drew after receiving promises of lib
erty.


Quito was nervous throughout last
evening, however, as mounted federal
police rode through the capitals
streets and prevented all lettering.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 21-After
long deadlock marked only by spo-
radio fighting. both Chinese and
japanese reports indicated today
that renewal of warfare on a ma jor
scale was near.


From Chungking, Chinese military
authorities frankly admitted they
expected increasing activities in the
West River sector, near Canton, to
develop into an offensive against
Shiuhing, important military base
40 miles west of the South China
metropolis.


From there the japanese would
be in position to carry out their
long ng-threatened invasion of KWangsi
Province.


Thirty miles northeast of Canton,
fighting Vas becoming more intense
near Tsungfa where the japanese
were trying to advance northward
along the Canton-Hankow railway.


Reinforcements Near Pakhoi.


The Chinese were reported moving
heavy reinforcements to the vicinity
of Pakhoi, on the southwestern coast
of Kwangtung Province near French
Indo-China anticipating a Japanese
attempt to land troops.


While continuing their widespread
mopping-up campaign in Shansi
Province, North China, the japanese
indicated an offensive against
Shensi, the Communist stronghold
to the west, would be begun soon.


The Chinese expressed belief the
Japanese would attempt to skirt the
strongly fortified town of Tungkwan,
at the extreme southeastern corner
of Shensi, and cross the Yellow River
near Pingmin, to the north.


From Sian, capital of Shensi, the
Chinese reported they had sur
rounded the town of Hotsing, in
Southwestern Shansi, cutting off
Japanese reinforcements with heavy
casualties. They also reported con-
tinued attacks against other Jap
anese-held stations on the Shansi
railway.


Japanese Drive on YOchow.


Reports from Chungking said
strong Japanese reinforcements were
moving toward Yochow, Yangtze
River town 122 miles upstream from
Hankow, preparatory to resuming a
drive southwark along the Canton
Hankow railway.


The Chinese again were active in
the HangchoW sector, 100 miles
southwest of Shanghai. They re-
ported they had recaptured Fuyang
20 miles southwest of Hangchow
and Yuhang, IS miles west of Hang
chow. Fuyang and Yuhang were
the deepest points of Japanese pene-
tration into the interior after the
invaders dramatic capture of Hang
chow more than year ago.
The Chinese also said they had
recaptured Changching. in North
Chekiang Province, controlling the
south shore of Lake Tai.


Meanwhile, nearly one-fourth oi
Chungking's population was said tt
have left the city since Sundays
air raid and subsequent japanese
warnings that more raids were com.
ing. Chungking, Chinas provisional
capital, is in hitherto untouched
territory on the upper Yangtze.

STORY She had dreamed so


long of having a
home of her own. Sometimes the
tears would come when she thought
of it but with stern New England
will she had repressed tears. 1t
had been hard at first, not to think
of what she had almost had. Her
eyes would persist in straying
across the hedge to the house where
Elijah Benton had once lived.


Elijah, tall and fair, with the ten
derness that she remembered so
well on the day that he had asked
her to wait for him. She remem-
bered to the day, how she had stolen
down to the garden to meet him.
She had not dared to meet him
openly. For years the two fam
lilies had not spoken. All because
of trouble over the boundary line
between the two houses.


But love knew no boundary line,
and Emma and Elijah had sworn
that nothing could keep them apart.
That was before he had come home
from the sea to die. Fever from
the tropics had followed his ship.
While he lay i'll he had begged for
her, and she had not been allowed
to go. Pride and the family quar-
rel had prevented. Then when she
could endure it no longer, she had
gone secretly, only to find she was
too late.


Across the hedgeway the Benton
house had long been closed, for
there were no Bentons to care for
it.


Because only a memory and an
empty house are lonely company,
Miss Emma asked Mary Ellen Lew
is to come and live with her. Mary
Ellen was Prescott by blood. She
was young and blue eyed, with a
sunny laugh and a way with her
that made the village smile back
at her. But what worried Miss En-
ma was that she never had any
beaux.


Spring came and the Benton gar
den needed attention. Miss Emma
and Mary Ellen worked together,
! with Mary Ellen doing the work
and Miss Emma giving the orders.
! Quite often Mary Ellen worked in
( the garden alone. Her dreams could
live among the flowers.


4 When John Parker first saw the
garden, its rare beauty stopped
him. 1t was so primly old-fashioned
in the way it was hidden behind the
hedge. He was glad that he had
remembered the old place belonged
to him. His painting would 60 well
there.


So quietly had John Parker come
into the garden that even his foot
| steps had not sounded. The slender
little figure in blue went on reach
ing for roses and talking to the
thrush that sat on the bough of the
apple tree.


"You think it's a shame, too,
that any man should own this gar
den, don't your" the figure was
saying. He's an artist, and he's
coming next week to live here, so
that I can't come over any more. I"


"But I'd rather like it if you would
come over, even if l am here"
| protested John Parker.


The figure whirled around with a
suddenness that sent the thrush
winging over the hedge. John Par
ker smiled, and wondered what on
earth he should say next. The girl
laughed in disconcerting manner,
and dropped a rose from the arm
full she held.


At Mary Ellen's description of the
Benton descendant, Miss Emma's
heart beat little faster; he seemed
so much like Elijah.


The final effort to have her ro-
man have happy ending took
Miss emma herself to the garden.
John Parker must paint a picture
of the garden with Mary Ellen sit
ting beside the lily pool.


On the last day of August the
picture was finished. The day after,
John Parker went away. Mary FL
len did the housework with a forced
cheerfulness that did not deceive
Miss Emma, nor did Mary Ellen s
explanation deceive her. John
Parker had gone-with only good
by. Miss Emma nodded wisely.
Mary Ellen had found she did pos
sess a heart after all.


Then she saw the Boston paper,
and on the front page was the rea-
son why John Parker had hurried
away. Very carefully Miss Emma
hid the paper behind the wood box,
in the kitchen.


Mary Ellen went each evening to
the garden, to sit beside the lily
pool and dream. So when John
Parker appeared, Miss Emma knew
where to send him, and she smiled
as she watched him run down the
path. She even spied a little; saw
him show Mary Ellen a newspaper
clipping, then take her in his arms.


Miss Emma sighed, content at
last. II knew he'd come back, )"
she said to the rose bush by the
door. "And with all the prize
money that picture got at the ex-
hibit, they can fix up the garden and

COPENHAGEN, Dec. 2 R.-The
streets of neutral Denmark's capital,

sounded tonight to an outburst of
sympathy for Finland.


Two thousand students marched
through the business district shout
ing Long live Finland"


Then the demonstrators marched
to the office of a Communist news
paper and shouted their disap-
proval.

brief furry of excitement spread
through this Cape Cod town today
when it was learned that two life
buoys marked "Bremen"-apparently
belonging to the huge German liner
unreported since she left New York
last Wednesday-had been washed
up on Orleans beach.


Coast guardsmen said, however, the
first buoy was found at midnight
Wednesday. Since this was only
approximately four hours after the
Bremen left New York, officers as
serted it would have been physically
impossible" for the ship herself to
have reached Cape Cod in that time.


1t would have been even more
impossible for the lifebuoys to have
floated any distance to the shore
at this spot-near the "elbow" of
the cape-in the brief time after the
Bremen sailed.


Boatswain's Mate Louis Silva ex-
pressed the belief the buoys might
have been lost overheard on the
Bremen's westward crossing.
headline:
Bremen Lifebuoys Found
Before Liner Sailed

OSLO, Norway. Sept. 26.-Dis-
patches from Farsund. Southwest
ern Norway, reported that naval
skirmish occurred today just west
OF Norway's southern extremity, be-
ginning about noon and ending at
1:40 pm.


Watchers from the shore said they
saw three large warships, two sub
marines and many small craft TAX
ing part In the action and air
planes maneuvetfng overhead. They
estimated that between 80 and 40
shots were fired.


First reports did not identify the
ships which shortly disappeared
below the horizon-.or estimate any
damage caused.


Three Norwegian airplanes
watched the encounter to see that
Norwegian territorial waters were
not violated.


Eight or ten merchant vessels has
tened toward shore during the en-
gagement. which started just "a
hours after another naval action
was believed to have begun of the
Norwegian coast little farther
north. Gunf1re today could be heard
plainly at Lister Fjord.


The British admiralty said last
night it had no reports of any naval
battle of Norway 'as would have
been the case had one taken place. -

Bergen said British and German
warships took part in yesterdays re-
ported encounter, during which

gunfire were heard for about II or

For the third time since the 1898
football season ended. the Washing
ton Redskins today were bemoaning
the loss of a valued player to the
coaching profession.


Bob Masterson, last years rookie
end from the University of Miami
whom both Owner George Mar
shall and Coach Ray Flaherty
had predicted a great professional
career, has accepted a contract to
coach the Ponce de Leon High School
eleven of Coral Gables, Fla, next fall


Masterson not only proved a bril-
liant pass-catching end and good
defensive man last year, but it was
his drop-kicking that enabled the
Redskins to tie Brooklyn, 1916, in
the last five seconds of Washington's S
first home game.


Riley Smith and Bill Hartman are
the others who have deserted the
Indians for coaching jobs.

BY DORIS SCHEITLIN, 18,


Eastern High School.
There dwelt a maid of beauty,
A caretree lass was she:
For pastimeS she had many,


But best she loved the sea.
A-sailing DER the billows,


Sails all blowing in the breeze;
She was known for her sailing
OF nearly all the seven seas.
She loved the smell of the salt air,
The sting of the spray in her face
And to hear the gulls a-crying
And the horizon she would trace
Many gale she had sailed in,
Many storm she had braved,
And out on the briny ocean


Many a life she had saved.
But now at the oceans bottom,
Down where it's mighty deep,
This brave and courageous beauty
Lies now forever asleep.
headline: The Sailor Girl

Republics and Nine. Oumansky en-
tertained at a reception last night in
honor of the two Soviet flyers, Brig.
Gen. Vladimir Kokkinaki and Maj.

gown of chiffon, which was made
over orchid-color taffeta, with full
skirt and short sleeves. A corsage OF
orchids blended with the gown.


Three buffets were used, one in the

salon and one upstairs. The ball
room was profusely decorated with
pastel-color spring flowers, snap
dragons, narcissus, roses and tulips
blending with the many lovely colors
worn by the feminine guests.


Diplomats, Army and Navy officials
and many from residential circles of
Washington were invited to meet the
two flyers. whose plane was forced
down when they attempted non-
stop flight from Moscow to the New
York Worlds Fair.

and Queen of England, regally calm
but flushed with pleasure at the
mighty ovation that delayed their
progress through the city, arrived
at the New York Worlds Fair
today for quick inspection of
British exhibits.


Their closely guarded limousine

Fair authorities estimated that

inent.

man, Mayor F. H. La Guardia and
others. Mrs. La Guardia presented
the smiling Queen with a corsage

The greatest concentration of DO

AT the end of the Court of Peace

Before the King and Queen had

BRUSSELS, Sept. 9-Belgian pur-
suit planes battled two British bomb
ers over Belgian territory last night
and brought them down in an Incl
dent expected here to have diplo-
matte consequences.


A Belgian plane fell in flames
during the battle. and its two occu-
pants. who took to their parachutes.
were injured.


The bombers were returning from
a reconnaissance and leaflet-drop
ping flight over Central Germany
when they were intercepted by the
Belgians near Mons.


One of the British craft came
down Immediately, and the two Off
GERS and three crew members were
arrested. The second plane refused
to land and was taken under fire
after being chased by the Belgians.


The British air ministry said the
two British planes crossed the Bel
gian border inadvertently" in "un-
favorable weather conditions" Lon
don said the British Ambassador in
Brussels had been instructed to pre-
sent an apology to the Belgian gov
ernment.

Strength of Positions Tested.


Throughout the first few days of the
week German patrols raided sector
after sector testing the strength OF
French positions established on Ger
man soil An ominous calm settled
down over the western front Friday
morning. 1t lasted until late after
noon, when the Germans attacked
simultaneously French outposts from
Saarbruecken to Lauterbourg after
preparatory artillery fire. Heavy
lighting lasted throughout the night.


French advices from the front said
the Poilus held their lines and
stopped the Germans with counter
attacks which gained what military
observers considered to be several
new strategic positions.


The heaviest German attack was
against the wooded highlands in the
Blies Valley, about II miles east OF
6aarbruecken. The Germans were
reported to have used full battle
formation, sending wave after wave
of assault troops against the French
positions as contraSted with previous
rading party operations.


The brunt of the German attack
was borne by three companies OF
assault guards, whose total strength
was reported to be just under 500.
= The French described the German
battahon's attacks as particularly
tenacious"


Troops Rushed From Poland.


Advices from the front said that
as fast as the Germans were driven
back by field guns firing point blank,
machine guns and automatic rifles,
they reformed their lines and
surged out to renew their assault.


Military information from the
front said the Germans had rushed
troops from Poland-released by
Russia's invasion-and sent them
into almost immediate action in the
west against the French.


Although Nazi Propaganda Minis
ter Paul Joseph Goebbels declared
two days ago that Germany had NO
intention of violating the neutrality
of Belgium, the Netherlands or
Luxembourg, the French general
staff has not accepted his statement
ut face value.


France was reported speeding
production of mechanical military
units for fear the Nazis might strike
through neutral nations in an effort
to turn the flanks of the Maginot
Line

Mrs. Roosevelt at her conference
today indicated that The Star knew
that Joseph Measell, 16, and Miss
Beatrice White, is, who crashed"
the White House New Year eve, were
going to do it before it occurred.


She intimated that was the only
way the story could have appeared
on page one of The Star when 1t did.


She advanced as proof the fact
that the Washington Post called the
White House to verify the story
while the boy and girl were still
being detained in the usher's Office.


The fact that The Star had the
story when it did. she declared, was
the most interesting part of the
situation.


Pictures on Page One.


She said the incident happened
after 11:30 pm, which. she under
stood, was after the time The Star
went to press.


The cards autographed by the
President and herself. she declared,
appeared on page one of The Sun
day Star although The Star had
gone to press before the incident
occurred.


Mrs. Roosevelt added these re-
marks after retelling the incident
at the request of a reporter, saying,
the two youngsters involved were
lucky to escape serious injury.


The Presidents wife expressed re-
gret that the incident had been re-
garded as joke in some quarters.
She said it was miracle that MOTH
ing happened to the pair.


She was afraid, she said, that
what Joseph and Beatrice did would
be repeated by some one else with
disastrous consequences.


Said They Were Expected.


Recounting the incident, she said
the young pair had been asked by
the guard and the doorman If they
were expected and had responded
that they were Mrs. Roosevelt de-
clared the two were put in the Red
Room to await word from the usher
and while there, the girl wandered
around the room to hold the atten-
ton of the doorman while the boy
came up the back stairs where no
one could have seen him.


Only some one who had been told
the layout of the house and knew
that the usher would be occupied
upstairs in turning on the lights at
the conclusion of motion pictures the
family had been watching could
have accomplished that feat, she
declared.


Had a Secret Service man been
on the back stairs at the time, she
added, and seen a stranger going up
to the family's quarters, he would
have shot or beaten up the youth
without hesitation.


The assurance of the boy when he
entered the room where the family
was gathered kept them from sus-
pecting he was an unlimited guest,
she said. It was not until the girl
was questioned later that any one
discovered the truth, she added.


The misunderstanding about the
boys identity, she said, came from
the fact that she thought he had
been invited there by the President,
while the President thought the boy
was a friend of one of his guests and
wanted the autograph to raise
money for infantile paralysis VIC
Tins. The boy, she said. had not
mentioned. such benefit to the
President, but Mr.. Roosevelt was
under that impression.


Commenting in vigorous terms on
what she termed the lack of rever-
ence of the couple and the bad man
ners shown in going any place un-
invited, she said the incident would
make necessary even closer super
vision Of the White House.


She said she had received a note
OF apology from the girls mother,
and added that she didn't blame
the parents, but only the children
Tor their lack of regard for the con-
sequences to themselves or others
from their adventure.

Civil War; the Olympia, Admiral
Dewey's famous flagship. the Span
American War, and a World
War destroyer. The Constellation
was chosen, Chairman Vinson said,
rather than the Constitution, since
the latter, now at Boston, is def
nitely identified with that city.


The berthings would carry out
project on which Chairman Cochran
OF the Expenditures Committee has
been working for nearly 10 years.


This building project for the Navy,
according to Chairman Vinson, will
provide adequate quarters for the
last of the executive departments
needing adequate quarters.

located between the present Naval
Hospital site and the Potomac River
and would include the site of the
Heurich Brewing Co. plant and other

and Potomac Parkway.

period of years, would include a de-
partmental building facing Consti-
tuition avenue between the Naval
Hospital site and the Potomac River;
the naval musetm building facing
the river; an underground garage;
ship berths for the permanent hous-
ing of historically important naval
vessels; connecting tunnels between
the buildings, and relocation of
Potomac drive.


The site proposed for the building
group already has been tentatively
approval for this purpose by the
National Capital Park and Planning

manent development plan for Con-

building group is "the next major

PARIS, Oct. 25.-Sporadic artil-
lery fire doomed along the western
front today as small infantry patrols
skirmished in the cold and mud west
of Forbach, where French troops
still occupy a narrow salient on Ger
man soil.


Through the sullen rumble of the
guns, loudspeakers in the German
front lines blared monotonous re-
frain:


"Frenchmen, lay down your arms
and shake hands. The Germans
don't want to fight"


The French soldiers shouted back:


Change the record!"


Military dispatches said French
machine gunners silenced one loud
speaker mounted on truck behind
the German lines.


The French general staff summed
up the situation in terse COM
munique this morning, saying that
ION the whole the night has been
quiet" The communique noted
patrol and artillery activity to the
west of the Saar."


Soldiers Want More Jazz.


The lack of action spurred those
at home to call for new steps to
bolster the morale of the soldiers.
The press insisted that radio sta
tions change their programs to suit
the taste of the troops. who have
been calling for more jazz music.


Authorized French circles de-
clared German Foreign Minister
Joachim Won Ribbentrop's speech
last night In Danzig was an admis-
sion of internal decay under the
allied blockade.


"Ribbentrop credits England. per-
sonified by Chamberlain. with all
the ambitions and perjuries which
the universe, doubtless misinformed.
usually attributed to Germany"
these circles added.


IL was disclosed To-Day that Alfred
Napoleon Beauvais, 46, an American
Legionnaire with two sons in the
French army, had set out for the
front with a volunteer ambulance,
minus orders or credentials. With
his wife, Beauvais managed to reach
a point four miles behind the lines,
where he remained for two days be-
fore being sent back.


In that time, he said, he trans
ported 68 wounded or i'll soldiers to
the rear.


Lebrun Visits War Zone.


President Albert Lebrun returned
from a trip to the war zone where
he visited Strasbourg, now almost
completely empty of civilians, and
inspected sandbag projections erect
ed around the Alsatian city's archi-
tectural treasures.


Military commentators said the
Germans yesterday renewed efforts
to push the remaining French out
posts from German soil near the
Warndt Forest.


Infantry in groups of not more
than 100 men each were repulsed by
French gunf1re, these sources said.

Every time you walk the street
What a lot of folks you meet
Whom you never saw before:
Whom you'll ne'er encounter more!
Every car that rolls along
Holds of strangers such a throng!
Every dot upon the map
Marks city. Not rap
Do these myriad beings care
For the ills that others bear,
Nor the pleasures others know
AS their various ways they 20.
All are strangers till a song
Or story comes along.
Or some little sentence fraught
With a new and forceful thought.
Then one mighty impulse thrills ,
And the song or laughter fills
All the world with echoes gay.
And each mortal seems to say:
What a pleasure tbs to strike
Men with taste to mine alike!
Though know them not by name,
All our moods are much the same.
I'm regretting more and more
That we hadn't met before!"
