VIIPURI, Finland, Dec. 26.-Long-
range artillery shells burst through
out the night on this seacoast city
previously abandoned by most OF
its citizens.


Numerous fires were started and
homes in the southeast section were
destroyed, but the damage was COM
paratively slight.


(Helsinki had a Commute air


raid alarm today when four


planes were sighted, but no bombs


were dropped inside the city. Dis


tant detonations indicated a


probable Russian attack on out


lying points. The clear signal


was sounded at LOS PM.


The Soviet Russian forces APP
peared to be concentrating in this
area by long-range hammering and
air raids as the Firms took the wal
into Soviet territory in another Sec
tor. driving toward the Murmansk
railroad, Russia's main supply line
to the far north.


Viipuri firemen kept a constant
vigil, fighting flames started by the
shells, apparently fired from bat
teries Is miles away.


This would place the Russian ar
tillery about 10 miles within Finnish
territory on the Karelian Isthmus


Firemen Battle Flames.


AS firemen battled flames in the
southwest section of Viipuri a shell
ripped big hole in nearby back
yard. The size of the crater, about
seven feet deep, led military experts
to believe the Russians had brought
up heavier batteries than previously
used.


Russian warplanes in four-hour
raid over the ancient city yesterday
bombed a workers section but the
only casualties known were, two
women and a girl injured. The few
remaining residents huddled into
bombproof shelters at intervals
throughout the day. Public gather
ings for Christmas celebrations were
quickly dispersed.


At least 80 warplanes flew over
the city and one was shot down by
anti-aircraft fire. Approximately
200 bombs shook the city, including
four or five 2O0-pound missiles and
incendiary bombs.


Shrapnel tore holes in many
homes in the workers district. Elec-
trical and telephone service was in
terrupted periodically, gas was cut
of completely and water pressure
reduced


Although the Russians apparently
were aiming at railway line
through the area, the tracks thus
far had not been damaged.


War Carried Into Russia.


Finnish troops pressed within IS
miles of the strategic Murmansk
Railway, as the war carried into
Russian territory in the Lieksa
area, approximately 100 miles
northeast of Viipuri


East of Lieksa, military opera
tons are taking place on the other
side of the frontier" said the Fin
nish communique which noted for
the first time that Finnish troops
had entered Russian territory.


Christmas Day Finnish successes
included an advance in the Kuhmo
district on the Vaara River, where
the Firms said our troops have
defeated two enemy companies and
the remainder of the enemy forces
are retreating."

NEW YORK, Dec. 29.-The usual
post Christmas decline in retail
buying was cushioned this week by
active and unexpected demand for
heavy apparel, Dun g. Bradstreet
said today in a weekly survey.


Despite the drop from the preced-
ing week, retail distribution out
stripped the similar 1888 week by
2 to 6 per cent for the country as
a whole, the agency estimated.


THE cold wave that swept out of
the West to the Atlantic seaboard
sent consumers scurrying for long
deferred heavy clothing needs.


Winter wearing apparel moved
out at the fastest rate this month
in most of the leading centers Of
distribution.


Demand was especially strong for
trimmed and untrimmed coats, fur
garments, overcoats, mems suits and
children's clothing.


Few store-wide clearances were
in progress. ''' On many offerings
mark-downs were small, as holdings
were light"


The survey said the drought
stricken agricultural districts and
some centers of the Southwest and
the Pacific Coast showed the largest
lags in buying.

Cantigny was the location of heavy
enemy reinforcements observed COM
ing by train and truck from Mont
didier. These were about to launch
a heavy counter attack from cover
OF woods. For two days and nights
the Twenty Eighth Infantry, which
had been assigned from General Bill
lard'S First Division to take Cantigny,
was the object Of a murderous Of
fensive. More than half of Colonel
Ely's officers were killed or wounded.
Enemy units were reported to have
penetrated into the American front
line trenches. The position was a
fortified village and, because of its
altitude, the Germans were able to
rake the American sector opposite
them with devastating artillery and
machine gun fire. The place changed
hands repeatedly during seventy-two
hours Of incessant battle. Finally,
thanks to the bulldog tenacity of our
troops in their baptismal major en-
counter with the German army, vic
tory rested irretrievably with the
doughboys.


Cantigny filled Hindenburg and
Ludendorff with abiding respect for
the fighting quality of the heretofore
despised raw recruits" who were so
soon to take the field in dimensions
that doomed Germany to definite
and decisive defeat.

Four men were killed and another

here when an automobile left the
highway and overturned several

injuries.

Waverly.

rule Tsingtao of reports of imminent

A whole family of owl monkeys
the only known nocturnal species,
arrived at the Zoo today, father
mother and three children.


They huddled into a little ball of
fur, from which five tails dangled
and blinked big, sleepy eyes at cam
eramen and the keepers providing
food after their journey from New
York.


The owl monkey is gentle and
friendly, but timid and hard to keep
in captivity. He is seldom seen in
ZOOS. In his native South American
jungles he forages at night and
sleeps during the day.


In the same shipment were three
saki monkeys, another rare inhab-
liant of South America. The only
others believed in the United States
are owned by Col. Theodore Roose-
welt, who keeps them at his Oyster
Bay estate.


The sakis have long hair and
names and long. bushy tails. They
also are delicate and don't seem to
live long in captivity.


The monkeys are from the collec-
ton of New York woman who had
been observing them and taking
notes on their behavior. She died
some time ago and her estate dis
posed of them.

er. It is wise to cut out great mats

a flrm-knit national unit. The gov
ernmental difficulties which led King
Leopold to dissolve Parliament a
month ago and order the extraordi-
nary general election have apparent
ly been erased.


The voting was a triumph for mod
Grafton. Both the Rexists, the ex-
tremist Fascists and the Socialists
suffered losses as the Catholics and
the Liberals were strengthened. For
that reason, the Liberals probably
will accept representation in the new
cabinet. Thus the financial program
is assured success. The fiscal problem
was factor in the breakdown of the
government. Liberal support for the
program was necessary and 1t was
not forthcoming. Dr. Martens resig-
nation from the academy destroys
the issue on which the Flemings and
Walloons were split. There was a
certain boldness in King Leopold's
dissolution of Parliament, but his
courage has been rewarded.

Silence Prevails.


While there was rejoicing through
out the country over the rescue of 80
men, grim, silent atmosphere pre-
vailed in this city as preparations
to remove the bodies got under way.


But for that sad job and the rails
ing of the disabled vessel, the Navy
had completed, with the first Use of
the new 9-ton escape bell. one of the
most dramatic underwater rescues
Ill tile alllldlS OF CNe sea.


Four times the huge, grotesque-
appearing apparatus was lowered
over the side of the submarine rescue
ship Falcon. Three times it came
up smoothly and promptly, carrying
men from the gloom in which they
had spent more than 80 hours.


Then, on the fourth trip, some
thing went wrong A cable fouled
and held the last eight survivors
suspended midway between the
muddy bottom and the surface.


Divers labored frantically. Finally
four hours later, the giant apparatus
was freed and the last men stepped
to the deck of the Falcon.


AS that trip was completed, Short
ly after midnight (E. D. TD, rescue
operations were suspended until day.
light. Admiral Cole issued the fol-
lowing communique:


This completes rescue of all
known survivors. Investigation of
flooded compartments will proceed
as expeditiously as possible Suspend
ing operations for the night due to
damage to rescue chamber, which
must be repaired before further
use"


AS the rescued men-seven the
first trip, nine the second and third
| trips and eight the last time-left
the big bell, they stepped into
decomposition chamber. The rescue
was history making since the sue
cessful use of the massive chamber
was its first actual test under these
desperate conditions.


Then, as they recovered from cold
and pressure changes, they were
brought ashore.


Trapped Men Took 1t Easy.


Disabled shortly after $40 am
Tuesday morning, when an air ir-
duction valve failed to close and
poured tons of water into the af1e:
compartments, the Squalus lay on
an even keel at the bottom and tie
men in the forward compartments
took it easy" throughout the long
hours to conserve the oxygen.


After telephone communication
with the surface was broken the
men settled down to a long wait.
Then, for hours, the Navy massed its
strength for rescue efforts. Finally
at about noon yesterday the rescue
bell dropped over the Falcons side
and touched the escape chamber of
the Squalus.


The connection was made and
blankets and hot SOUP handed into
the sub to ease the biting cold.
Seven men stepped inside with the
man who came down from the sur

With their arrival on the deck of
the Falcon came first definite news
of the casualties trapped in the
flooded sections of the submarine.
Swiftly word was flashed ashore and
the heart-rending task of advising
relatives was begun.


Wife Seized With Hysteria.


One wife was seized with hysteria
when told that her husband was
dead. Other women refused to give
up hope, clinging to the belief that
in some way, somehow. their men
might be alive in the blocked-of .
water-filled compartments.
Thank God, oh, thank God"
cried the mothers and wives of the
men who came through til ordeal
safely.

the bitter cold in the entcmbing yes

Il don't think I'll ever get warm

First man to breathe free air and
see the sun after the long confine-
ment was 1t. j. c. Nichols. It was
a dramatic scene. The sun broke
through the clouds just as the bell
broke through the oceans surface.
The air was tense with excitement,
dread, hope-airplanes circled over
head A dozen ships, including the

cons deck. The hatch in the roof
opened and 1t. Nichols stepped out
into the sunshine


Cheers broke out from the men on
the deck and answering cheers and
shouts echoed from the other YES
sells.

Because Ray Flaherty and Steve
Owen are recognized as two of the
cagiest coaches in professional foot
ball and because their respective
teams margin of victory over the
Philadelphia Eagles were similar,
the logical question on every fans
lips today was:


who held back the most, the
Redskins or the Giants?"


1t is doubtful If even the most
naive fan believes either team re-
vealed its full strength against
Davey O'Brien & Co. Where, for
instance, when the Redskins played
at Philadelphia. were Dick Todd and
Jimmy Johnston-the rookie ball
carriers for whom Flaherty has pre-
dicted brilliant futures? On the
bench. except for four minutes
played by Todd


Where, last Sunday. were such old
Giant reliables as Johnny Bulb
Karcis, Hank Soar, Ed Danowski
and Dale Burnett? They played,
but Tuffy Leemans and a rookie
named Eddie Miller grabbed the
headlines. We wonder who Owen
thought he was fooling when he
kept that veteran quartet in the
background?

didn't use more than a dozen plays
against the Eagles, and the Giants
probably didn't use any more. Ac-
cording to Bert Bell, the Eagles
owner, the Giants last Sunday were
the best football team I've seen
seen -. far better than they were
last year" Of that's the case,
watch out Redskins. Remember
36-0?)

two New York teams, which Owens
inserts as units, and which he de-
clares are nearly equal, scored only
13 points against the Eagles. who are
acknowledged to have II good foot
ball players, and no more.

a revelation, come Sunday, when
the East's hottest professional grid
rivals meet at Griffith Stadium for
the first time this fall in the local
curtain raiser. Few would be so
foolish as to predict that this years
Eastern championship depends on
this game, but the victor will gain
a big edge.

George Preston Marshall, himself
had set the stage for Washington's
first National Football League game

edented and that Business Manager

LONDON, Jan. 9.-Prime Min
lister Neville Chamberlain leaves for
Rome tomorrow for what many be-
lieved today would be his final effort
to push through his policy Of ap-
peasing the relationships.


The outlook was anything but
bright as the 69-year-old Premier
conferred with his key ministers
today.


The civil war in Spain, now 21a
years old, was the great obstacle
between the dictator, Benito Musso-
lini, and the business man." Cham
berlain.


Although under the Anglo-1talian
agreement signed last April and
accepted by Parliament November
2, Italy agreed to withdraw her
troops from Spain, her newspapers
openly admit Italians are fighting
there now for Insurgent Generals
simo Franco.


1t will be the first time in history
that British Prime Minister has
gone to Rome on a diplomatic mis-
sion. Many in Europe believe the
trip may mark the most decisive
week since Munich, with both die
tatorships and democracies anxious
for peace, but each at its own price.


Will See Daladier in Paris.


Chamberlain's flights to Germany
to seek appeasement of Chancellor
Hitler resulted in the Munich agree
ment and dismemberment of Czecho-
Slovakia.


The premier will pass through
Paris and halt there long enough
for meeting with Premier Daladier
to give a symbolic demonstration of
his sympathy with France against
strident Italian agitation for French
''Tunis, Corsica and Nice"


Over this agitation the talks in
Rome may come cropper. Italy,
backed by her axis partner, Nazi
Germany, has raised a clamor for
concessions.


But France has told Britain she
does not want Chamberlain to "arbi-
trate" and he is expected to respect
this wish to keep firm the alliance
with France, Europe's last remain
ing one between great democracies.


Skepticism over possible results of
the trip was apparent even within
circles of Chamberlain's own con-
servative party in England.


Belligerent Rights Sought.


II Duce was expected to demand
belligerent rights on behalf of the
insurgent Franco But observers
here believed Chamberlain is pre-
pared to refuse this unless Italy re-
moves all her troops from Spain.


Since the Munich agreement there
have been increasing signs that
Chamberlain was taking a stronger
attitude in his dealings with the
dictators. President Roosevelt's S
speech to Congress last week on
defense and the preservation of
democracy undoubtedly encouraged
stronger sand. political commen-
tators said.


The principal hope of achievement
IN Chamberlain's visit is that he
might persuade Mussolini to make
friends with France again. French
Italian relations have been uncer-
tain since the Ethiopian war; they
have come near to the breaking
point since the recent Italian agita-
tlon for French colonies.

The middle-aged man was never

He was never rubber stamp who

No, indeed. Every middle-aged

enced by his companions.


And the middle-aged woman has
the same idealistic picture of her.
self as a girl. She was always
mothers little helper who dotted on
drying the dishes and taking the
baby out in his pram. She always
felt that mother knew best and was
satisfied with the practical clothes
mother bought for her, instead Of

Last nights closing performances
Of the Presidents Birthday Horse
Show at Fort Myer left the Army
riders a bit up on the nearby civil
ians as far as blae ribbon awards
were concerned, but it was only after
the bitterest sort Of a fight were they
able to capture the majority of first
prizes.


Stanch rivals for the past several
years the experts from the Army
post and the daring amateurs from
around Washington went into the
closing nights events tied with two
victories apiece. Wednesday eve
ming the open hunters and the
handy jumpers classes had been
won by exhibitors from the Virginia
Army post, but the civilians had
come with a rush in the last two
numbers, the road hacks and the
open jumpers, to even the score and
thus set up a perfect stage for a
fight to the finish.


The first class of the evening, the
important fault-and-o out, finally
went to the service equestrians, but
only after stirring struggle that
carried one member from each side
into double jump-off.


Half of the eight jumps had been
moved up to 5 feet to settle the SUI
premacy between the Army's Clipped
Wings and Fritz Kleeman's King
Rock. The rest of the contestants,
some % of the finest show ring per-
formers stabbed around town, had
found the catchy course too much
and had dropped out with startling
rapidity.


Hits Final Hurdle.


King Rock, with young Jimmy
Marsh in the saddle, was the first
Of the remaining couple to attempt
the triumph, and for a spell it
seemed he had it in the bag. At
the very last fence, however, a triple
bar affair, the big bay son of Seal
Rock knocked over the top pole but
it still meant that Clipped Wings
would have to go clean if his side
was to gain the main prize-and
the lead over the civilians.


Capt. John Collier, who only a
few days ago received the mount on
the rangy brown mare-one of the
most reliable jumpers in this Sec
tion-apparently realized the great
Importance of the event. Taking a
forward seat and a short rein on
his horse. he carefully nursed her
over each one of the fences and
gave the Army fans plenty to shout

If you drop into the Office of the
Junior League any afternoon
around 4 o'clock you're likely to
find the young women chatting over
the teacups.


You'd think it was just another
tea party unless you listened to
their talk Instead of clothes and
men and baby's formula these
Junior Leaguers are talking about
quotas, about bookkeeping, about
the best approach to a prospect.


For eight hours they have
tramped the streets, rung doorbells,
ventured into all kinds of homes
Now they have reports to make to
their team captains.


That's the daily routine of 79
members of the Junior League dur
ing the Community Chest campaign
Headed by Mrs. Laurence H. Green
chairman, and Mrs. B. Lowndes
Jackson, vice chairman, they have
set up their own Chest headquar-
tiers at their clubhouse, 200l Mas
sachusetts avenue NV.


Six Captains on An-Day Duty.


Six experienced team captains re-
main at their desks all day long
through the campaign so their
workers may reach them at any
time for advice or help. Before the
workers start out in the morning
they report to their team captains
for instructions and materials.


The team captains, all campaign
veterans, are Mrs. G. Rowland
Chase, Mrs. j. Francis Foy, Miss
Anne Carter Greene, Miss Eliza
beth Houghton, Miss Marion Shouse
and Mrs. Harry B. Slocum.


Starting with a single team the
league has expanded its Community
Chest work until now it's six teams
cover the entire Dupont-S Sheridan
Circle area of the Metropolitan
Unit.


When the house, house can
vass was adopted by the Chest the
league teams began the develop
ment and use of their black books. >
which are now used extensively
among other divisions of volunteers
Before the campaign opened each
team captain in the league checked
her territory personally, noting in
her BLACK book" all the building
her workers were to cover. Team
members were given similar books
containing the addresses of build
ings for which they were respon-
! sible


All Must Be Accounted For.


BY the end of the drive all ad-
dresses in the master books must be
accounted for, either with a pledge
or notation for future reference
This method, according to the
league, insures complete coverage
for the area and makes certain that
no more than one worker ap-
proaches any one prospect.


Last year the Junior League
division collected 1896 per cent OF
its quota, which amounted to sl8,-
258.35. This year their quota is s19.-

FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla, Dec.
2-August, the hippo, just stands
and munches on sweet tropical
flowers while his handlers rave.


August, weighing in at tons. is
the center of an expensive, scram-
bled state of affairs at Clyde Beatty's
wild animal farm here-he is where
the sea lions should be and vice
versa.


This usually -docile hippo won't
come out of lake set aside for the
sea lions, who are squeezed into
August's heavy barred cage. The
water horses stubbornness is run
ming into money because he's ac-
quired an appetite for sweet smelling
tropical growth along the lake shore.


It'll cost pretty penny to replace
what he's eaten.


August took to the water more
than a week ago while his handlers
were putting him into his cage.
Beatty lured him with such tidbits
as carrots and cabbage, but nothing
doing.


Then Beatty tried to starve the
hippo into obedience. His food
supply cut off, August countered by
going in for hibiscus, ferns, shrub
berries. He likes them.


Meanwhile, the sea lions are pining
for the lake, but they can't go there
while August monopolizes the water.

BASEL. Switzerland Correspond
ence of the Associated Press) The
military strategists on the western
front have not forgotten the old
theory that the walls of Jericho fell
because trumpeters held their at
tention while the enemy attacked
from the rear.


But in this modern war, there are
whistles instead of trumpets, as both
sides resort to their ingenuity to
fool the other fellows.


Long after the French had aban-
doned the Waarndt Forest last Oc-
tober, French scouts armed with
officers whistles kept the Germans
guessing.


Flat Cars Roll Along.


Later the same month, observers
in Luxembourg noted long lines of
trucks, presumably full of troops,
moving away from the Moselle zone
just the night before the Germans
launched an attack that drove the
French out of their hard-won posi-
tions between the Moselle and the
Saar Rivers.


Wherever a neutral country lies

In our battle for justice we must
realize that there are thousands of
traitors within our own ranks-men
and women who, having mortgaged
their own craven souls to our en-
emies, are willing and anxious to
sell out our group for mess of pot
tage. In myraids of instances they
have already done so. Many of these
beings are like moles which burrow
beneath the surface, and they have
by their per1icious activities placed
the entire structure of our rights in
peril. The vilest, cruelest, most bru-
tai, craftiest, most venomous, and
most cold-blooded outspoken enemy
is far less dangerous than the vile,
crafty, Sinking, snake-like burrow-
ing foe within!


-LLEWELLYN LEWIS.

HONG KONG, June 21.-Jap-
anese forces occupied the Kwang-
tung Province port of Swatow to-
day in quick landing after months
of comparative quiet in the South
China war area.


Dispatches from SWatoW said
japanese units reached the city
proper in midmorning and, en-
countering little resistance, con-
tinued inland. After the arrival
of the troops, which had been
landed nearby, japanese transports
and warships entered the inner har-
Dor and began unloading reinforce
ments and supplies.


SWatow, a city of $4,000, is 220
miles east of Canton, which was
captured by japanese last october
81 after an overland drive which
started on the coast midway be-
tween the two cities.


British Ships Stopped.


British advices said japanese YES
sells had stopped three British ships
attempting to enter Swatow-the
Suiyang, the Yisang and the Marie
Moller. The vessels were forced to
anchor off the coast. where British
naval authorities advised them to
remain temporarily.


The American destroyer Pillsbury
and the British destroyer Thanet are
in Swallows inner harbor, safe
guarding interests of the 40 Amer
leans and 80 Britons there


British naval reports said the
Japanese landing was accomplished
with 800 men divided into two groups
advancing inland from points north
and south of the city. A japanese
announcement had said the landing
force encountered unexpectedly
stiff resistance.


Despite long preparations, Chinese
detachments at Swatow failed to
carry out customary 'scorched
earth" destruction in the city to
leave the invaders nothing but ruins
to conquer. Anticipating the land
ing, some so per cent of the Chinese
civilian population had been evac-
uated.


Missionary establishments at
Svatow include American Baptist
and English Presbyterian missions.


Swatow Americans Safe.


Whitney Young of New York,
United States consul at Swatow, re-
ported that all American there were
= safe.


Other foreign sources at Swatow
reported that at dawn air raids
heralded the japanese attack and
that by mid-morning japanese war
ships had silenced batteries on is
lands commanding the entrance to
the port.


At noon, it was said, three japanese
destroyers with armed traWlers
steamed into the inner harbor and
began shelling the shore. while Japa-
nese planes continuously bombed ap-
proaches to the city.


A Japanese communique said that
the main japanese land force was
pressing inland north and south of
Swatow The Japanese consulate
here issued statements that since the
capture of Canton the Chinese had
been using SWatow increasingly for
the importation of war materials.


All British shippers, acting on ad-
vice from British officials, Cancelled
all calls at Swatow.

Greg, star and Don McNeill of

ASSOCIATED Press Foreisn Correspondent.


VERECzKE. Hungary (at the
Polish frontier), Sept. 22.-The final
internment of thousands of Polish
soldiers and officers, routed by the
German and Soviet Russian inva-
sions, was started today here on
Hungarian soil.


Meanwhile, German units consoli-
dated their occupation of frontier
points. AS fleeing Poles moved
down one side of the Carpathians
the conquerors of Poland climbed
the other toward the strategic bor-
der passes.


Reports on how the Germans and
Russians would divide the Polish
Carpathians were still confused.
Generally Hungarians believed the
division would be about equal, with
the Russians taking the two large
passes which link Northeastern
Hungary to Poland.


| Long professions of Polish in
fantrymen and cavalrymen, with
their guns and supply carts, moved
through darkened frontier villages
before dawn, en- route to internment
camps.


Silently the tired men and their
weary animals slogged through the
mud. Occasionally dim light from
a nearby window fell upon drawn
faces, but most of the time the
marchers were muffled in darkness
ghostly procession of the defeated.


Refugees coming through the Car
pathian passes brought tales Of wild
rule over small section of Poland
by rowing bands of Ukrainians
whose signal for action apparently
was the start last Sunday of the
Russian occupation.


There were stories of day-lonp
battles between Ukrainians and
Polish police, of Poles and Jews
alike killed in a wave of looting
and destruction which completed
the havoc started by German bomb
ing planes. Entire villages were
said to have been burned.


Polish officers arriving on Hun
garian soil told of escaping from
between the Closing jaws of the
German-Russian wise only to come
upon small villages which "dripped
with blood from the activities of
the terrorist bands.


How the terrorists obtained their
arms and ammunition was a mys.
terry.

SHANGHAI, March 27.-The Han
kow headquarters of the Japanese
Army reported today the capture
of Nanchang, once an important
Chinese air base in Kiangsi Prov
ince.


Chinese earlier had reported that
brilliant counter-thrust" north
west of Nanchang had pushed back
advancing Japanese troops in fight
ing that took the lives of 1000 Jap
anese and 500 Chinese.


Siege Began Yesterday.


Japanese yesterday began a siege
of the city, ITO miles southeast
OF Hankow, against strong Chinese
resistance.


The Japanese announcement said
attacking forces intensified their
onslaught, crossed the Kan River
and entered the former capital of
Kiangsi Province simultaneously
through four gates. The japanese
rising sun banner. it said, quickly
was hoisted along the entire length
of the citys walls.


japanese did not disclose whether
the Chinese were carrying on street
fighting within Nanchang or had
withdrawn once the invaders reach
ed the outskirts.


According to dispatches from
Domei Japanese News Agency,
correspondents with the Japanese
Army, the Chinese resorted to
''scorched earth" tactics as they
evacuated Nanchang.


Fires Visible in City.


Domei said fires were visible in
various parts of the city as the
japanese vanguards entered.


japanese officials declared that
occupation of Nanchang had severed
the Chekiang- -Kiangsi Railroad, thus
cutting off important Chlnese-con-
trolled areas from transportation
of munitions, especially war ma
teriel imported from abroad.


The japanese reported that their
artillery laid down thunderous
protective barrage into the one
time capital of Kiangsi from across
the Kan River While their engineers
sought to establish a foothold on a
great railway bridge leading into
the heart of the city.


Chinese machine-gunners swept
the bridge with bullets while the in
vading engineers sought to repair
the dynamited span.

poration counsel, said the colored
janitor of the building had confessed
starting the fire in revenge for
fancied wrong at the hands of the
building owner. The janitor, Will
liam Warren, 81, was placed under
arrest.

NEW YORK, April 22.-Visitors to
the Worlds Fair will be intrigued by
the many new ways Of using color
which experts have devised, espe-
cially on painted surfaces. From the
largest exhibition buildings-some
Of which cover q city block-to the
many attractive model homes, clev-
erly chosen colots not only enhance
the displays but suggest ideas for
backgrounds for better living which
can be applied to your own house,
hold.


In the exhibition buildings the
colors are chosen primarily to show
the products displayed to the best
advantage. The textile building,
with its fascinating hall Of fashion,
has walls Of pastel blue, rose and
yellow, delicately flattering the fab
RIGS. In the marine building, with
its boats Of all kinds and sizes, the
walls are . gay sunset yellow. Those
IN the electrical products building
are rose and jade green, accented
with vermillion, to keep pace with
the increasing smartness Of the elec-
trical gadgets and home appliances.
There are walls here, too, which are

Other boys back home in their

In the times when Ken came

ests to a boy who was acquiring

She hadn't been afraid. Ken'S

sometimes whiStled in the dark

Every mile of the journey, as

They were smooth, sophisticated,

She quailed little under their

Arabs were slain and five wounded,
authorities said, by unidentified Jews
in six incidents today in the neigh
borhood of the Jewish city Tel Aviv

killed and two injured near Rishon
Lezion. One was killed and one
wounded near Petah Tikvah. Two
were killed in the immediate out
skirts of Tel Aviv, where one Jew
also was wounded by stray bullet.


Two Arabs were slain and one
wounded near RaSel Ain, east of
Petah Tikvan. Fou. were killed and
one hurt near Rehovoth.


AS a consequence of the shoot
ings, all traffic to and from Tel Aviv,
Rehovoth and Petah Tikvah was
prohibited from Thursday noon un-
til 4 pm. Friday.


Numerous arrests were made
among Jewish revisionist advocates
in the smaller communities. All the
attacks occurred in the early morn
ing hours. In most cases shots were
fired at Arab passers-by from NOV
ing automobiles.


Meanwhile, 750 Jews were held
as illegal immigrants travelling in
Greek traWler which was stop
ped in territorial waters off Haifa.

pending action by authorities.

sail from Cherbourg aboard the
Queen Mary today, having been
summoned home for consultation
with the State Department.


The Embassy declined to comment
on the nature of the consultation,
but other diplomats believed it
would be in connection with possible
United States recognition of the
Spanish Nationalist Government.
Walter c. Thurston, counselor, has
become Charge d'Affaires in the Am
bassador's absence.


Since Britain and France recog-
nized the Nationalist Government
last Monday, the United States and
Soviet Russia are the only great
powers which withhold recognition.

Small-bore rifle shooting has been
added to the sports in which the
teams of the Naval and Military
Academies will compete, bringing the
annual list to 13.


During the last two years. with
Capt. Ernest w. Mckee as head of
the department of physical training
at the Naval Academy, soccer, SWIM
ming and golf, as we'll as small-bore
rifle, have been added to the inter-
service sports, while tennis has been
resumed.


Swimming and gymnastics. in
which the academy teams had met
lrregularly, were also placed upon
a permanent basis.
The sports in which the teams
already had met were football, bas-
ket ball, fencing, lacrosse, baseball
and track


The service schools now meet in
all sports common to the two schools
except boxing and wrestling.

Realizing a definite demand for
an event to help every one share in
the ribbon awards, Donald Brad
ley and Gardner Hallman, guiding
lights of the Chevy Chase Horse
Show, which will hold its annual
spring meet Sunday on the East
West highway opposite the Meadow
brook Saddle Club, decided to supply
that demand themselves.


Knowing that the young follow
ers Of today are the veteran lead
ers Of tomorrow, they set out to
stimulate interest for those who
could not hope to compete with the
champions and regular winners.
With this thought in mind, they de-
signed a show whereby young and
old alike could have a chance of
carrying of honors. That was about
year ago. Today the show has
quickly grown into one of the most
successful around Washington.


Novices Given Chance.


The show will have 10 classes,
and four of these are for youngsters
and their ponies and four restricted
to novice riders and their inexperi-
enced horses. The latter group also
will have chance to beat the top
Fighters in the handicap jumpers
class, which allows 3-year-old horses
and non-blue ribbon winners to
jump a mere 3l2 feet.


These classes will afford some
enthusiastic but unsuccessful riders
chance to break into the win COL
umn and thus spur them on to great
er efforts in the future. Too many
shows are designed for the champs
only, leaving the rest to remain in
the shadoWed background.


The show will be the first of the
local 1899 outdoor season and prom
ises to attract many leading stables

The outcome of battle between
a British airplane and a German
submarine that sunk British
steamer remained unknown today
as the toll of ships lost in sea
combat rose to 80.


The unusual fight between the
rival oversee and undersea raiders
was described by Capt. H. A. Peder-
son of the United States Lines
American Farmer last night in
radio message reporting his rescue
of 90 crew members of the torpedoed
British steamer Kaflrstan.


The rescue took place 400 miles
off the Irish coast. Six men were
reported missing.


U-Boat Aided in Rescue.


Capt. Peterson said the U-boat
which sank the 5,9l3-ton Kafirstan
used its rockets and blinkers to
help the American Farmer locate
the lifeboats carrying survivors.


In the midst of rescue operations,
however, British airplane ap-
peared and bombed the submarine.
The submarine replied with machine
gun fire, Capt. Peterson said, then
disappeared, leaving very white
smoke on the surface"


The master of the American rescue
ship said the British survivors had
cheered the U-boat commander
and praised him for very humane"
treatment. particularly his offer to
tow them toward Ireland if they
were not picked up quickly.


Praised for Treatment.


Sinking of the Kafirstan raised
Great Britain's known merchant
ship casualties at the start of the
third week of the war to % besides
the aircraft carrier Courageous,
sunk by a submarine. Nine German,
one French and six neutral vessels
also have been lost.


The aggregate gross tonnage de-
stroyed is 176150. At least 2O6
persons have been killed or drowned,


Latest neutral victim was the
5,3l6-to Norwegian motor ship
Ronda, which sank September l3
off the Netherlands coast after
striking mine.


Seventeen aboard, including two
Americans, were lost. Four other
American passengers and Is seamen
were rescued by the Italian freighter
Provvidenza and put ashore at
Flushing, the Netherlands.

DETROIT, Sept. 18.-For one rea-

Not often since Gen. Charles D.

and donated a cup for team golf
competition among the public high

group of high school linksmen had
such a strangle hold on the tourney
as the Rough Riders of Roosevelt
have had for the past three years.


The Roosevelt lads, captained by
Cliff Gruver, are on the threshold
of their third consecutive public
high school team links champion
ship, and face only one more OBJ
stacle before they can toss the big
mug back in the trophy case on
Thirteenth street for another year.


Team Is Well Balanced.


Roosevelt teams led by Andy Oil
veri, the present public links cham
pion, won the Dawes Cup in 1887
and 1888, succeeding the long reign
of outfits at Western High, cap
tanned by Billy Shea, in the role of
champions. And now Roosevelt,

player and boy who consistently
scores well down in the 70s, is about
ready to grab another champion
ship.

ern tomorrow at Indian Spring in a
match which will either decide the
championship outright or will toss
the thing into tie Tech High links
men, before the tournament opened
an unknown golf quantity, are push

slate. Gruver and his lads have
won victories over Wilson, Tech and
Central and come up to the Western
match without loss, knowing that

put his best lineup forth to lick
the leaders.


Need Individual Tourney.


The real tragedy Of high school
golf series this year is that the
schoolboys haven't yet sold" the
idea of an individual champion
snip, ana no group seems willing
to go to bat to put it over Buddy
Sharkey, who won last year, is at
Georgetown this year, but there are
few good golfers among the school
boys. Vass is good, and so are Ralph
Bogart and Earl Skinker of Wilson.
But the latter pair have been in
eligible for schoolboy competition
this year.


Rockville High School lads, with
Scotty Ross topping their team, are
tied with Bethesda Chevy Chase for
the lead among the schoolboys out
side of Washington.


The Roosevelt lineup includes
Gruver, Waggaman, Patterson, Pow
ers, Coleman and Anderson.

Is this the same wind blowing east,
Upon the stiffened bones of steel?
This wind once combed the hair of corn,
But now factory ticks her heel.
This wind once laid her cool hands on
The golden urge of rye and wheat.
Now her sad litany is heard
In the rude squalor of a street.
Vulgarity of city steel,


And smoke stacks of blasphemy,
Reach for her riveted thighs, and feel
Freedom in her impotency.
This wind once combed the hair of corn,
And quenched the thirst of western hills.
Now silent lies her harvest song
In the thunderous, grinding mills.
Her amber thighs and starburnt hands
Embrace the thieving pouch of DEATH
Which hold this secret contraband:
Bones and blood and riveters' breath.


MARY AHLQUIST.

text:
BY Paul Walsh.


Maj. Pierre Charles LEnfant,
dead for more than a century, saved
the District of Columbia some two
million dollars in 1888.


The visionary French engineer,
who followed La Fayette to America,
remained here to design the worlds
most beautiful Capital City, and
then died in broken hearted and
penniless obscurity, had one obses-
sion-beauty. That mania, reviled
and ridiculed when Pennsylvania
avenue was still swampy and Capt.
tol Hill little more than acreage, is
paying dividends in dollars and
cents today.


Commissioned by President WASH
ington to plan the new Federal City.
L'Enfant envisioned Capital of a
grandeur and majesty far beyond
the capacity of normal imagina-
tions to appreciate, Capital so am
bilious and pretentious as to seem,
in the 1790s, ludicrously inconsis.
tent with the poverty and impotence
of the infant Republic. He drew a
Capital for the distant future, when
the 13 States would have grown and
prospered into the worlds richest
and most powerful Nation.


LEnfant marked out on his city
plan vast areas for parks, much
more than ample space for public
buildings, decorative circles and
plazas, and wide boulevards. They
weren't just streets, mere thorough
fares, which the French engineer.
artist planned; they were long, broad
vistas. designed for beauty's sake
and with an eye to the future as
we'll as for ordinary vehicular and
pedestrian usages. Avenues as wide
as 400 feet he mapped out: others,
many of them $50 feet and wider.
That in a day of horseback and
buggy, of meandering lanes which
passed for streets in Philadelphia
(from which city the Federal Gov
ernment was moving! The land
owners went wild. And LEnfant
was fired.


Those landowners, of course, had
a personal interest in the LEnfant
plan. BY the agreement entered
into with President Washington
they stood to make some money.
That agreement included the pur-
chase by the Government of such
ground as was required for public
buildings and the like for s67 an
acre. The landowners agreed to do
nate land for public thoroughfares
The balance was divided into build
ing lots, the alternate lots to be sold
for the benefit of the owner and the
Federal Government. The Govern
ment's share of the income from the
lots would be used to pay for its own
acreage purchases.


When the LEnfant plan, with its
wide streets and seeming waste
spaces. was produced, the landown-
ers saw red. Three e-hundred-foot
streets when 35-foot width would
do for the horse and buggy! Hun
dreds of acres of valuable subdivi-
sion land snatched from the real
estate men just for a dream city!
Poor LEnfant didn't last long as a
city planner after such and similar
complaints.


But his plan, for the most part.
did The deal went through with
wide streets, not 400-foot streets by
any means, but with ample 200-foot
widths. But they still were much
too wide for those and subsequent
days in the Capitals development.
And Sc, encroachment and abutment
by private property owners onto
rights of way resulted. Property
owners built right up to the property
lines, usurping District (street-way)
property for front yards. The prac-
tice was allowed by District officials
through the years, because even
with such encroaching there still
remained plenty of room for streets
and sidewalks and tree space be-
tween.


The District of Columbia discov-
cred, as have large cities throughout
the country, that wider streets were
necessary to handle the modern
traffic. That problem elsewhere
gives city fathers headaches. It
means that the city must buy the
necessary depth of street frontage
from the adjoining property own
ers, undertake condemnation pro-
ceedings, worrisome litigation, and
generally pursue tedious, expen-
sive program for acquisition of the
land necessary for the street widen
ing. In these other cities the
ground between the property line
and the building line is private
municipal regulations or
restrict building some dis
tance back from the property line
except in high-value downtown sec
tions.


In shington-thanks to L'En.-
fant-there are no such headaches
for the District legal and fiscal
staffs, there is no litigation and no
worry about the financing of the
purchase of necessary ground for
street widening. Because the Dis
trict already owns many feet on
both sides of the downtown streets.
Street widening, then, becomes
merely an engineering and trafac
problem.

ish concerns and to some Britons

meetings.

driving like a juggernaut along the
road to the Rose Bowl, routed STAN
ford today in the biggest demon
stration of scoring since the ancient
rivals began their grid relations back
in 1905. The final score was South
ern California 80, Stanford 0.


The game was played-and thor
oughly decided-in the first half.
The warriors of Troy, performing
before $4,000 fans in this Pacific
Coast Conference encounter, scored
one touchdown in the first quarter,
added three more in the second with
powerful display of strength on the
ground and in the air, and quit the
field at half time with 27-0 lead.


Long before the score reached this
all-time high. however, Coach How
ard Jones had reached far back on
his list of reserves, playing fourth,
fifth and six string subs.


Star of the game, if one outstand-
ing man could be singled out of the
Trojan machine. was Grenville
Lansdell, with big Harry Smith, rum
ming guard, seeking when the sock
ing was needed.


Lansdell engineered the first drive,
72-yard affair, and counted the
initial touchdown.

Plebeian dishes that are favorites
with the younger crowd are hearty
macaroni and cheese, macaroni and
tomato sauce with meat balls and
goulash. One of the most informal
Of all main dishes is a combination
Of piping hot frankfurters served
with hot buns so that the guests
can make their own sandwiches.


When the meat dish consists of
cold cuts such as cold roast beef,
pork, turkey, chicken, baked ham,
cheese-the hot dish may be a
vegetable. Scalloped potatoes and
candied sweet potatoes are substan-
tial ones that keep hot easily. Corn
pudding, made with canned sweet
corn, milk and eggs is always popu-
lar. Scalloped apples are colorful
and keep hot.


For light meal the beverage and
bread may be the only two hot
items on menu. Spoon bread is
easy to serve. For buffet break
fast there's nothing better than
waffleS. But for these the hostess
will need one or two helpers to make
them fast enough for crowd. Other
possibilities at any meal are cram
berry mullins, hot biscuits, small
sandwiches of bread and butter and
lettuce or other crisp greens, brown
bread spread with cream cheese.
Or, if time is limited, serve ready
made rolls warmed in the oven and
buttered in the kitchen.


To simplify the meal, offer a choice
only of the foods that can be pre-
pared ahead of time.


Suitable desserts are plain cake
with hot chocolate sauce, ginger
bread, baked in shallow pan, cut
into serving portions and garnished
with whipped cream or orange mar
malade; ice cold ambrosia different
kinds of fruit cut up together and
perhaps with sprinkling of COCO
nut on top; individual cakes or
pies. Some others are ice box cake
jelly roll, vanilla ice cream, with
a choice of sauces and toppings of
chopped nuts or fruit for sundaes,
arranged on the sideboard.


Following is suggested menu for
holiday buffet supper Have plat
tiers OF cold sliced turkey and baked
ham, two jellied fruit rings Zone
might be red cranberry relish in
gelatin-the other green lime gela-
tin with fresh grapefruit in it,, tiny
hot pimiento biscuits, parsley or but.
ter sandwiches, relish dish with
olives, radishes, carrot sticks, celery
picked peaches.


And for dessert, bring in individ-
ual plum puddings each with q
small lighted red candle in it.

girl who tossed in the small, slant

screen test. The long streetcar

Then the test. Stiller saying alb
ruptly, "Lie down on that couch

So morning came again and

attempting to cross the Yellow River
on ice into Shensi Province. The
Chinese said the invaders suffered
heavy casualties and lost two tanks
in the attack.

hitting with his usual accuracy, Jackie
Wilson, colored aspirant for Henry
Armstrong; lightweight crown, even
ed up an old score last Tuesday night
when he stopped Richie Fontaine,
white, in six rounds at the Olympic

a surprise as, in previous encounter,

only one of his professional career.

ing as he foored the rugged French
man twice in the fifth session. The last
time Fontaine hit the deck, the bell
rang saving him. Fontaine was out
cold. Fontaine's handlers worked furi-
ously over him, and sent the reeling,
shaky battler out the next round to
meet the sturdy sepia scrapper, who
continued his fistic bombardment of
leather. After one minute, Is seconds
of battling, Referee Charley Randolph
with Fontaine reeling helplessly about
the ring, waved Wilson to his corner,
awarding the latter a technical knock

BY the Associated Press.


SARATOGA SPRINGS, N. Y, July
25.-They're grooming Saratoga's old
million dollar racing plant more
thoroughly than usual this year for
18th birthday anniversary and 30
day diamond jubilee meeting.


The oldest face course In the
United States, Saratoga will begin
its formal celebration July 81.


The track was built in 1864 by
John Morrisey, a former bare
knuckle prize-fighting champion;
William r. Travers and other rae
ing enthusiasts who came here to
enjoy mineral springs known to In
dians before Colonial times.


Saratoga is the last of the famous
old race courses that once dotted the
Empire State.


Saratoga lacks the grandeur of
Belmont-it has an assessed valua-
ton of only slightly more than a
million dollars, as compared with
Belmont's four million-but it pos
sesses charm peculiar to itself.


Old Traditions Linger.


Saratoga Springs streets are lined
with stately elms and high-ceilinged
brick and frame mansions of an
other era. During the 80 days of
racing each year the turf crowd
literally takes over the town of 10000
population, Figures, of international
society mingle with stage and screen
celebrities, wealthy turf fans and the
common man.


Tradition born in the gay
nineties." when cubes bounded in
the famous Garfield Casino, still
persists. The race crowd specializes
in long tall drinks, strange tasting,
health-giving mineral waters and
talk about horses under the elms.


In the early days the spa failed to
attract the racing set. 1t remained
for the opening of Jerome Park, near
Fordham, in 1866, to boom Saratoga
into career that led William Wood
ward, chairman of the Jockey Club,
to remark:


Modern racing owes its life to
Saratoga"


Travers Is Oldest Stake.


When Travers, Leonard w. Jerome
August Belmont and others organ
lied the American Jockey Club and
opened Jerome Park, they feared its
effect on the upstate track After
their first meeting they rejoiced
Horsemen raced at Jerome, shipped
to Saratoga, took society with them
and installed this little village almost
overnight as the prime favorite of
the American turf.


First in Saratoga tradition is the
Travers, oldest stake race in the
United States, which was first run in
1864. Then comes the Hopeful for
2-year-olds, the Saratoga Gold Cup,
the Saratoga Special-only sweep
stakes event nj America-the Ala
bama for mares and a series of
steeplechase stakes


Americas famous horses all have
raced at Saratoga; many have won
or lost regulations on the beautiful
track. Man o. War lost his only race
in 81 starts in Saratoga's Sanford
Stakes for 2-year- -olds-to a horse
called, appropriately, Upset.


Develops 2-Year- Olds.


Saratoga is noted especially for its
development of 2-year -olds. It's rich
est stake, the $4,000 Hopeful, which
has been worth as much as $4,000,
is juvenile race.

BY the Associated Press.


LONDON, April 14.-The popu-
larity of Tommy Farr, former Brit
ish heavyweight champion. who
failed to win in five fights on United
States soil, was undisturbed here
today following his easy 12-round
decision victory over Red Burman of
Baltimore at Harringay Stadium
last night.


The big Welshman, returning here
after two years, reversed previous
loss to Burman, staggering the
stocky red-head in the third, fourth
and fifth rounds, but never was
able to deal a knockdown blow.


A crowd of 11,600, including jim
my Roosevelt and Henry Armstrong,
cheered wildly as Farr compiled an
early lead and shook off several
authoritative Burman belts in the
late rounds. Burman jolted Farr on
several occasions, but failed to close
Tommy's early margin.


The Associated Press score sheet
gave Farr seven rounds, Burman
three and two even.


Armstrong, who will defend his
world welterweight championship
against Ernie Roderick here next
month, was introduced from the
ring and received an ovation.

CHUNGKING, Aug. R.-The
French and German consulates were
damaged early today as Japanese
warplanes raided the city.


Demolition bombs exploded in the
compounds of the two consulates,
shattering windows and splattering
ceilings with fragments.


Ten Chinese were killed in the
foreign area. They had left the
strictly Chinese quarted of the city
for supposed safety under the swas-
tika and tricolor.


The United States Embassy was
not harmed, but the residence of F.
Tillman Durdin of Fort Worth, Tex,
a correspondent of the New York
Times, was ruined by bomb concus-
sion.


Other residential buildings in the
area were destroyed by fires started
by the bombs. The flames were
brought under control after day
break.


Casualties throughout the city
were not heavy, probably under 80,
as the raiders concentrated their at
tention upon the suburbs. One
Japanese bomber was shot down.

By the Associated Press.


NEW YORK, Sept. 2-Shipping
men speculated today on the where
abouts of the North German Lloyd
liner Bremen which sailed from here
Wednesday night without passen-
gers.


Agents of the line in Copenhagen
said the ship was expected to reach
Bremerhaven tomorrow or Monday.


Another German liner, the Co
lumbus, with all lights out, was
somewhere at sea after discharging
more than 500 West Indies cruise
passengers at Havana on orders from
the German government to proceed
home at once. The passengers were
to be brought to New York from
Miami.


Two other German ships the St
Louis and the New York. both of
which went out of New York harbor
without passengers, were believed
TO be nearing home waters.


The French liner Normandie still
lay at her pier here with sailing
Indefinitely postponed. The Italian
liner Roma was also docked here.
the only sizeable Italian ship in
the Western Hemisphere.


The Cunard White Star liner
Queen Mary was due Monday with
1882 passengers, about $50 above
her normal capacity. Other trans
Atlantic ships also due Monday are
the Cunarder Samaria from Liver
pool; the United States liner Amer
ican Banker from London, and the
Gydnia America POLISH liner Ba-
tory from Gydnia and Copenhagen
All are carrying Americans fleeing
from war-frightened Europe.


Eight ships were scheduled to sail
from New York today for European
ports-the Cunard White Star liners
Fran>onia and Carinthia, the Hol-
land-America liners Zaandam and
Pennland. the United States liner
Washington, whose schedule was
advanced four days to speed up the
removal of refugees; the American
export liner Exeter; the Norwegian
American liner Stavangerfjord; and
the American Scantic liner Scan
penn.

Manor County Club has aban-
doned its usual spring invitation
tournament this year. a little cir
cumstance which is going to deprive
a good many golfers Of chance to
see one of the incest little remod-
cling jobs you ever could imagine
on any golf course. For quite few
years that woods" nine at Manor,
if you could take those enshrouding
trees with poise and equanamity,
wasn't too tough a test of golf 1t

side. The smart boys played their
tee shots with a spoon or even a
big iron, preferring to pole 'em down
the groove fairly short distance
rather than play rat-a-tat-tat on
some of Ralph Gibson's best hard
wood trees. 1t was that kind of
nine. You could play the short and
narrow without losing too much of
the advantage big tee shot gives
you-if you can hit big tee shot.


But that's all changed now. Ralph
Gibson and his brave lads on the
Club Greens Committee. not salts
fled with a workmanlike job of
cleaning out the woods, are stretch

sized distance, and when the new
tees open up next Sunday for the
first time this year. flock of gents
who have played pat ball down in
those woods. letting the pars come
when they may, are going to have
to pull the driver out and take a
chance on the woods


Three New Holes.


Last year they put into use three
completely new holes, using part of
two of the old fairways and aban-
doning the second-a single e-shotter.
The fifth became the fourth of the
new layout, par stretching far
out beyond the old fifth green. The
new fifth is one-shotter and the
sixth, played up part of the old fair
way. has become man-sized par 4,
around 40 yards in length. You
can hit two big smacks on this baby,
and barely get there. But new tees
have been built back of the present
tees at the second and seventh holes,
two holes which have been on the
short side. And when Gibson puts
them In use next Sunday that used
to-be-short woods nine no longer is
going to be a pushover for the boys
who hit 'em only a little way from

GAINESVILLE, Ohio, july a.
Forty divorce DEGREES, granted over
period of two years, were voided
yesterday because court costs on
each award had not been paid.


Common Pleas Judge L. H. Tan
nehill issued the order multiplying
the decress, saying ample notice"
had been given each person affected.


Judge Tannehill explained that a
divorce decree did not become final
under Ohio law until entered in the
court journal, and that entry could
not be made until costs were paid.
Costs of a divorce here, court at
taches estimated, averaged between
$50 and $50.


Judge Tannehill pointed out that
persons wishing to obtain final de-
crees must refile their petitions and
submit again to regular court hear
ings


Court attaches were not able to
say if any persons affected by the
ruling had remarked.

New York's baseball fans haven't
started chanting subway series"
yet, but it's fact their Giants are
the hottest thing in baseball right
now, and in the inflammable Ma
tional League anything can happen.


Bill Terry's Terribles completed
their Western swing by sweeping an
entire three-game series with the
pace-setting Cincinnati Reds-an
unheard-of conquest this season.


The 80 victory ground out by
the Giants yesterday was their 18th
in Is games since June 7. At the
start of this streak New York was
in sixth place, 10 games behind the
Reds. Now the club has climbed to
third place, just half a game be-
hind the st. Louis Cardinals and
four and one-half behind the Reds.


Zeke Ace Clutch Hitter.


The Giants haven't made less than
seven hits in the 15-game stretch
nor less than nine in their last
nine games. Until yesterday no
pitcher had gone the route against
them during the squirt.


Zeke Bonura, taking over the
league leadership in runs batted
in, has lifted his percentage hitting
20 points to .370 and clouted four
home runs in less than three weeks.
He tripled in the second inning
yesterday to start a tWo-run punch
and then singled the winning run
across in the third inning.


Perhaps most significant of all.
the Giants have won in spite of
handicaps other than the usual
rigors of a road trip. Walter Brown,
their best relief pitcher, sprained
an ankle and didn't finish the swing.
Burgess Whitehead has been out of
the lineup, and Joe Moore and Billy
Jurges, among others, have been i'll
or injured at some stage of the
jaunt.


Cubs Hold Swift Pace.


Pressing close behind the Giants
and Presaging more trouble for the
Reds and Cardinals, the Chicago
Cubs have lost only one of their last
nine games, although tied once. The
defeat came Saturday, 10, when
Joe Marty hit home run to win a
2-hit game for Hugh Mulcahy of the
Phillies. The trade which sent
Marty from Chicago to the Phillies
was redeemed yesterday. however,
as Claude Passeau outpitched Kirby
Higbe to win, 4-3, for the Cubs.


The Boston Bees gave the Giants
and Cubs challenge boost by
sWamping st. Louis in Sunday
doubleheader. With Max West
getting a homer in each game the
Bees took the opener, 8-5, and the
second one, 20. on the steady Shit
hurting of Bill Posedel.


The Brooklyn Dodgers eased the
embarrassment of their Western
woes by nosing out the Pittsburgh
Pirates, 6-5. Although Dolph Ca
mill and Babe Phelps homered earl
ier it remained for Harry Lavagetto
to decide the game with a 2-run
double in the ninth after an error
by Pep Young on play which would
have retired the side.


Browns at Last Beat Yanks.


st. Louis lowly Browns finally
smote the mighty Yankees to split
doubleheader. After eight losses to
the champions the tailenders batter
around for five runs in the ninth
inning of yesterdays first game to
win, 7-3. Bill Dickey accounted for
all the Yankee runs with two homers.
In the second session Oral Hide
brand handcuffed his former mates
on five hits and New York slugged
out familiar 11-2 triumph.


The Cleveland Indians and Phila-
delphia Athletics also divided bar
gain bill. Ben Chapman, Hal Trosky
and jeff Heath hit consecutive
homers the seventh inning to tie an
old record and clinch the first game
for the Tribe, 8-4, while George Cast
er's 7-hit pitching shared the night
cap. 1912.

White Sox again were rained out.

BOSTON, Dec. 23.-New England's S
flying Santa Claus tuned up the
reindeer under the hood of his air.
plane today, readying Bitten. and
Vixen and the others for renewal
of his annual Christmas visit to the
lonely lighthouse keepers along the
bleak Northern coast.


Santa, who in real life is Capt
William Wincapaw, will take off at
dawn tomorrow to begin his 126
yuletide calls on the isolated posts
which watch and wait for him
eagerly. At each lighthouse he will
drop a package containing candy
cigars, newspapers and magazines.


Santa Wincapaw, busy ferrying
gold and mining machinery over
steaming South American jungles
was unable to make the Christmas
tour last year for the first time in
nine years, but this year his en-
ployers made special arrangements
to rush him back by plane for his
chore, begun by Capt. Wincapaw
because of the favors the lighthouse
keepers did for him when he flew
along the coast years ago.

ect to enable shut-in children to

Dealings were exceptionally list

Speculative forces inclined to step

Business news, while far from de-

Of their recent highs Corporate

Obvious signs of war preparations
in England and France this summer
were contrasted with the picture last
year before the Munich crisis in an
interview with Miss Jean Ross How
ard, recently returned from Euro
pean tour.


So far as war atmosphere was con-
cerned, her tour abroad last summer
was tame" compared with her trip
this year, she declared. Few emer-
gency preparations were apparent 10
the tourist last summer, she said.


Miss Howard. who was graduated
from George Washington Univer-
sity last February and is a member
of Chi Omega Sorority and the
American Association of University
Women, personally conducted the
tour, her party consisting of four
other women.


Landing at Havre, Miss Howard
took her party to Paris, where she
remained until after July IA,
Frances Bastille Day There were
few Americans in Paris, observed
Miss Howard, in comparison to last
year, when she also spent the sum-
mer in Europe.


Two of the young women in Miss
Howard's party were commercial art
students and interested in dress de-
sign. so the party's itinerary in
cluded visits to some of the famous
dress designers.


Though outbreak of war has closed
most of the French fashion houses
and styles are turning toward
strictly tailored effects, according to
latest dispatches from Paris, Miss
Howard found midsummer fashions
tending toward the bizarre.


"One of the well-known stylists
was showing the strangest fashions, .
she said. Small hats with huge,
soft perforated brims dropping over
the face; also, small high hats in
which music boxes were placed,
playing the Lambeth Walk Skirts, "
she continued, were shown ex-
tremely short. with variety of odd
hip combinations-in most instances



From France the travellers went to
Switzerland, where, she said, the
Swiss, in face of impending war, still
rejoiced in the impregnability of the
Alps. "A guide pointed out numer-
GUS Notifications to us" Miss How
ard said, land remarked that,
though they looked pathetically in
adequate, the mountains were las
formidable as they had ever been,
when they had successfully resisted
the invasion of armies"


Hotels in Switzerland had few
tourists. she added, two of the larg-
est hotels in Interlaken, famous
Swiss lake resort, being closed.


From Switzerland Miss Howard
and her party went to Belgium,
where, in Brussels, they were guests
of Mrs. Orme Wilson, wife of the
American Charge d'Affaires.


Mrs. Wilson took us for tour of
Brussels" said Miss Howard, land
pointed out the newest houses,
which are compelled by law to be
built with bombproof cellars.


"The Belgians fully expected war"
she continued, Saying, we can ex-
pect it when the haying is over"


From Belgium the Americans went
to Holland, where Miss Howard
states preparations for defense were
pathetic,

BASEL, Switzerland, Oct. 13 tPl.-
French troops have closed the Rhine
River Dam gates at Kembs, 10 miles
north of here, pushing flood waters
high over the shoals opposite Ger
many's rhine Gibraltar at Istein.


The French acted shortly after
reports reached here that German
forces were working in the shoals
under cover of darkness, leading to
the belief they might be preparing
to cross the Rhine at this tip of the
Maginot Line.


Closing of the gates also conceded
with reports of German attacks
against the walled French town of
Lauterbourg, 100 miles north along
the river.


The series of dams on the Rhine
below the great Istein Rock, which
is now one of the strongest forts OF
the Siegfried chain, serve two pur-
poses-feeding the Alsace Canal on
the French side, which takes trafflc
around the rapids, and as power
for supplying electricity to the
region on both sides of the French
German frontier


The main power dam is operated
by a Swiss concern from the French
side of the river, but before the war
started French Army engineers took
over the plant and control OF the
gates.


German guns at Istein could easily
smash open the dam, military ad-
visers pointed out, but until they so
into action French engineers can
regulate the water flow above the
fort.


The flood tide not only made a
German attack extremely difficult,
military advices said, but would aid
the French troops in surprise ad-
vance.


The combination of heavy rain
fall and closing of the dam brought
the Rhine level up 712 feet within
the last week, but had not endan-
gered the French or German fortifi-
cations along the bank.


Frances Maginot forts have been
adjusted to meet the highest levels
the stream has ever attained, while
German engineers made changes last
May in their Notifications when the
Rhine rose more than II feet.


German troops made little prog
ress in their Lauterbourg attack, re-
ports reaching here said, in the face
of heavy French counterattack
from the Wissembourg Lauterbourg
Railroad line along . ridge parallel
ing the river.

Officially, of course, there is no
ivy League" It's just a name
coined to fit a loosely allied group
of old-line colleges, most of which
belong to the Eastern baseball and
basket ball leagues and stick pretty
we'll together otherwise.


They're the colleges that started
intercollegiate football in the first
place and led it up to its present
status. They're so solidly founded
in tradition now they don't have to
worry much about high pressure
football or fancy schedules. Count
ing Army, Navy and Brown into the
group, the league has 10 members,
and six steadfastly have refused to
depart from the traditional first
Saturday of October opening date
for football.

ern rivals last week, and Saturday

College golf is largely a spring
affair. The boys play their golf in
the fall, but they don't have any
regularly organized series of team
matches.


Just now the college boys around
town have revived a subject they
talked about last spring-a round
robin golf affair among several of
the local colleges. With Maryland
and George Washington coming into
the links picture, even though they
are not ready yet to challenge
Georgetown's supremacy on the
links, it's time they started action
looking toward formation of a COL
lege loop next spring.


Georgetown in Saddle.


The Hoyas have turned out ex-
ceptional golf teams for more than
a dozen years, dating away back to
those good outfits which included
Maurice Mccarthy and Dick Wilson.
The teams of the last two years, with
Billy Shea, Billy Dettweiler and
John Burke, have been good ones,
although they haven't quite won
the Eastern college crown. But the
Hoyas have been the top college
team around town.


Maryland. with Julian Murphy,
Jim Brownell and George De Witt,
is ready now to move into good col
lege golf competition, and may do
so next spring George Washington,
with a team headed by Lafayette
Franklin, jr., doesn't seem as strong
as the other two, but still may do
all right.


It's time the rah-rah boys organ
lied their own golf loop and if they
did Georgetown wouldn't have the
romp they might expect.


Would Include Virginia Schools.


Duke, with what probably is the
best college golf team in the East,
isn't interested in coming North for
intensive competition among the
bigger colleges. But Duke, cham
pion of the Southeast, was good
enough to whip Georgetown by a
heavy margin. And Georgetown
was good enough to place second in
the Eastern college loop. That makes
Duke loom as one of the strong ones
and an outfit that would go strong
against any college team.


How about, for example, a college
loop consisting of Georgetown,
George Washington, Maryland, Vir-
ginia and William and Mary? All
these teams play spring golf
matches. but they haven't any rec
ognized circuit.


College golf is big stuff and it
should be bigger. For out of the
colleges come many national am
ateur champions.

News of the death of Grace Abbott.
professor of public welfare admins
tration at the University of Chicago,
has been received in Washington
with profound sorrow. The Nations
Capital was her home during the
thirteen years through which she
presided over the Children's Bureau.
and she will be remembered with
gratitude here. But it was to no
single neighborhood that she devoted
her genius. The truth is that she
served the whole world. Her quail
tiles OF sympathy, earnestness, sim
cerity and efficiency were pledged
to humanity at large. In that
notable respect, she was an ideal
American.


Yet there is no easy explanation
Tor the vast success of Miss Abbott's
career. She was not a reformer in
the ordinary meaning of the word.
Rather, she was builder. Her mind
and heart had no negative aspects.
With materials readily available,
she constructed new social val
ues in people. To hear her speak
was to catch vision, to labor with
her toward any useful goal was to
share in a dream being made real.
She quickened hundreds, perhaps
thousands, by the fire of her own
spirit. But her enthusiasms were
governed and controlled by her scien-
tlflc attitude toward every problem.
She was gracious and kindly per-
son because she willed so to be. Her
achievements were practically helpful
because of her determination that
they must have direct application.
None OF her contemporaries excelled
her in knowledge of human char
acter.


Miss Abbott focused her principal
effort upon the neglected portion of
the population. She befriended the
mothers of the United States be-
cause she realized as few other
soclologists did that they hold the
fate of the republic in their hands.
With similar comprehension she
strove for every conceivable advan-
tage for children, appreciating the
fact that democracy can survive only
with the support of a loyal younger
generation. Her fame, then, was not
temporary. She created immortality
Tor herself. But those who knew her
best, always understood that she
cared nothing for honors. The re-
membrance she wanted was imper-
sonal. ALI that she asked was that
the task should be finished, the
obligation met, the duty done. She
Will have her wish. Her inspiration
is living force now and forever

phia and Pittsburgh and those teams

l78 points to the opposition in nine

| neither has been able to make a

dinals carrying little more than two

A SlX-day alrplane night separated
Shanghai from Warsaw, but within a
week of my arrival in the Polish capital
the same scenes were repeated-with
German planes overhead and Poles run
ming and ducking on the ground


In the beginning the German planes
bombed only military objectives on the
outskirts or suburbs of Warsaw proper,
so that residents of the Polish capital
for few days-saw and heard bomb
ing with comparatively little danger.


Then the German planes swooped
closer and lower. Every dawn, midmorn-
ing, noon, midafternoon and dusk the
Nazi air raiders methodically bombed
In a narrowing circle while Warsaws
civilian population began q mass evac-
uation.


One afternoon while pecking away at
my typewriter in our flce-apartment
block from the Vistula River more than
so German planes buzzed overhead.
Bombs began to rain down. Some landed
along the nearby river bank (narrowly
missing a vital BRIDGE, shattering the
windows. billowing the floor and making
the typewriter dance OF course was
scared for minute, but what could you
do about it?


A window from the stairway provided
a grandstand seat for the spectacle over
the river and I sat on the stairs fas-
cinated by the plane diving with scream
ing wings, the thunderous explosions.
the sudden spurts of dust and debris
from where bombs scored hits, and
water-spouts from where they missed.


kept the telephone wire to the AS
sociated Press bureau in Budapest 40
minutes. describing the picture over the
river, the wheeling and diving planes,
pulling the phone to the end Of the
cord SO the other Office could hear the
whines and screeches. archie guns and
earth-shaking explosions When the skies
were empty again and all quiet once
more, told Robert Parker, at the other
end of the wire, the bombers had gone
and I'd go check on the damage. "Okay,"
said Parker. I'll call you again soon.
They may come back"


Flight to Naleczow.


They came back several times, but the
telephone never rang again. And the
next day, with the Polish government
and the embassies gone, communication
with the outside cut off, the population
fleeing and the German artillery pound
ing the only remaining exit, we decided
to pull out-destination the village Of
Naleczow, two hours away, where the
Polish government had established the
temporary capital.


I never caught up with the Polish
government or general staf1. On the
run and unable to get settled beyond
range Of the German planes, they moved
from place to place, welcome nowhere
because they were magnets for the
bombers.


To the far Russian border, then south
ward to the Rumanian border, and
finally one sad day, when they knew
all was lost, they crossed the Dniester
River and were interned


President Ignace Moscicki, old and ill,
became guest" in one of King Carols
hunting lodges. Marshal Smigly-Rydz,
virtual dictator of the country and COM
mander in chief of the army is interned
at Craiova Stunned by his own officers.
Foreign Minister Beck lies i'll and heart
broken at Braslov.


A Weeks Nightmare.


Thousands of their countrymen and
countrywomen also fled across Poland
:. trudging through the dust carrying
children on sardine-packed trains
until they were bombed or the tracks
blasted :. in shining new and ancient
secondhand motor cars until they ran
| out of gasoline (and hundreds of cars
| were abandoned along the way :. driv-
| ing their horses with loaded carts
| mercilessly ahead of me, behind
me, and on all sides.


| What was normally days drive be-
came a weeks nightmare Lublin,
Tomasczow, Lwow, wherever we went
German bombers were overhead. terror
izing cities, bombing railways, strafing
highways.


A nations population was in flight.
| Food was unobtainable. Cigarettes dis
appeared. No matches. Swift German
motorized columns cut in and out scat
tering the fleeing refugees in all direc-
tions. No one knew directions. Every
way one turned he met new obstacles,
more bombers overhead, saw more shat
tered cars, more dead sprawled like bum
dies of old clothes.


You couldn't find place to sleep
until you dropped. exhausted, alongside
the road oblivious to the planes, the
swiftly moving German troops, the un-
ending confusion Of HUMANS fleeing to
safety.


Then Russian tanks, coming from no
where, began rolling across Southern
Poland and the hungry, sleepless and
footsore thousands were given the
strength of fresh fear to struggle the
last few miles and across the Dniester
River to peace and safety.


They still wondered what it was all
about.


The sudden calm, the letdown in
nerves, the peace Of Indian summer skies
