Mr.. Lehrbds, Associated Press for
eign correspondent, has just returned
from assignments during which he
spent tUo years couering 1DarS-the
Sino-JapaneSe conflict and Germdny's
tDhirl1Dind conquest of Poland. In the
tolloying story he tells some of the
tragic scenes he witnessed and also
makes some comparisons between
Asiatic and European 1Oartare.
War, whether in an Asia lightly We
neered by western civilization or in the
heart of continental Europe's age-old
culture, tastes, smells, sounds and looks
much the same.


The romantic trappings and heroic
sacrifices of men fighting for conquest
or to defend their good earth give you
the same goose flesh thrills.


The mud vermin, blood and suffering
have nunbing and futile sameness


And pagoda and Polish palace are
both just piles of broken brick and debris
when they crumble beneath bombs.


It is difficult to tell dead Chinese
awkwardly sprawled in rice paddy
from the dead japanese clutching at the
sky on the other side of the sprouting
green rice field.


Dead and mangled Poles wear diff
ferent colored uniform from dead and
mangled Germans.


You get so you don't look any more.
The fighting, still surging over China
after two years and five months. has
killed and wounded more men, women
and children, caused greater and more
widespread destruction and suffering
and brought more tears and terror to
millions than were left in the wake OF
four years of the World War.


Instruments Of Death.


In II days and nights of laundering
guns and lightning attacks in Poland
saw guns, planes and tanks spread more
death and destruction than were Bel
eiurn's black heritage from the World
War.


1t simply takes longer to kill and MAIN
and make homeless wanderers out OF
44000O,OOO Chinese spread over the vast
map of China than it did to kill, capture
or make 100000 Poles men without
country and rub their 1000-year-old
history as nation of the record.


Japanese and German planes swooped
like destroying hawks over Chinese and
Polish cities and towns and human
specks running around desperately to
avoid death were as helpless as barn
yard chickens.


There were not enough bomb shelters
anywhere and Polish clerks and Chinese
peasants dug shallow trenches or ran
into open fields.


You expect soldiers to die, but when
you see plain everyday people dead IN
the ruins of their homes dead in shallow
trenches and dead in harvest fields you
cannot help but feel that you are IN an
age of insanity.


The Chinese and Polish armies fought
back calamity here and there, but were
unable to stand up against the mass and
power of the invaders attacks with their
overwhelming superiority in planes,
tanks, artillery and other fast and death
spraying mechanical and motorized
equipment.


It was human clay throwing itself
against sharp pointed steel.


Eyes Watch From Aloft.


Japanese and German superiority in
the skies enabled them to watch and
know every move of their prey, bomb
and demoralize the population far be-
hind the swaying battle lines and
maneuver motorized columns to smash
every attempt the defenders made to
concentrate their strength, dig IN or
counterattack.


The Chinese and Poles, without aerial
eyes, could only fight back blindly until
they were killed, overwhelmed or sur
rounded and marched into captivity.


And the civilians-men, women and
children-in both China and Poland died
In greater numbers and suffered IN
greater degree than their armies.


There were differences in the wars IN
China and Poland, but they were most
frequently differences merely in point Of
view.


One night I stood behind sandbags
with four United States marines on one
side Of Soochow Greek when Japanese
launched their last attack against the
Chinese "lost battalion" holding out IN
q warehouse after their comrades had
retreated from Chapel.


A few figures scuttled from the ware
-, house across q street and were grabbed
by waiting British outposts on the SET
tlement side and we knew the 'lost bat
talon" had given up the fight and were
beginning to escape, preferring intern
ment to death.


BY daylight nearly 400 had scurried
across that street in threes and fours
From our sandbags we plainly saw the
running Chinese in the foreground and
two angry japanese machine guns
block away commanding the street-and
could see and hear why it was possible
for the Chinese to escape from what ap-
peared to be a suicidal run.


The Japanese machine guns fired
simultaneously instead Of alternately
While the guns were being reloaded the
Chinese ran. Most got across safely

in the assembly hall at the camp
as a climax to the program, which
included peanut races, dart con-
tests and badminton games In
which substantial prizes were award
ed to the winners.


The picnic took the place of the
clubs usual weekly luncheon at
the Willard Hotel.


Mrs. Jean Bennett, club president,
is superintendent of Central Union
Mission to which Camp Bennett
belongs. The camp provides sum-
mer recreation farm for about 600
Washington children.


Although the June picnic is not
always held at the camp, one of
the buildings there is named for
the club because of its financial aid
in its erection.

chairman of the committee making
the arrangements for the picnic

Zirkin, Miss Mary Bourke, Miss
Mary Turner, Mrs. Cynthia Warner
Miss Ruth Baker, Mrs. Emily Shah
and Miss Rena Pond. The assem-
bly, hall is equipped for moving pic
ture sound effects. Mrs. Good had
with her colored moving pictures
she made last winter at Key West
Fla, showing views of the new high
way there.

Faithful circus fans of this vicin-
ity got their annual spring thrill
yesterday afternoon when AZ gaudy
carloads Of "the big show" slid to
a halt in Potomac Yards and began
to discharge thirsty animals and
hungry troupers.


Elephants, camels, horses and big
cats were fed and watered, along
with countless menagerie stars. All
the stock which could be led was
hustled out to break the long trek
from Sarasota, Fla, to New York
by stretching their legs on the rail-
roads cinder track.


The fans learned that Ringing
Bros. & Barnum and Bailey is COM
ing back bigger and better than
ever" after last seasons disastrous
labor troubles. It was the biggest
spring train the show ever pulled
through Washington.


Fans Are on Hand.


Among the fans waiting impa-
tiently to greet their old friends
was Attorney Melvin D. Hildreth,
president of the Circus Fans Asso-
ciation; Zoo Director William M.
Mann, president of the local top"
and Director Fred Orsinger of the
Department of Commerce Aquarium.


The train carried only animals
and equipment for the indoor OPEN
ing at Madison Square Garden next
Wednesday.


Another trainload of canvas,
seats, dray horses, etc, will be
brought up when the show takes
the open road, arriving in Wash
ington May Is.


Gorilla Has Car to Himself.


Occupying a fiat car all to him
self yesterday, in his air-conditioned
cage, was Gargantua, the huge
gorilla, which added to his weight
and stature in winter quarters, his
trainer said.


Looking to the needs of their so
lions, tigers and leopards which
they will work this season, were
Capt. Terrell Jacobs and his wife
Dolly.


"Good-by," shouted Washing
tons faithful fans as the engineer
took up the slack in the long train,
and the rearmost coach began to
move, We'll see you in Madison
Square Garden!"

prices-the offer of three pairs Of
mems 35-cent socks for a dol

a quarter-are tickling consumers
thrifty instincts and stepping up
sales of inexpensive articles.


Retailers have found these offers
so effective in looseningsup the Gus
toners purse strings that they are
seeking ways and means to apply
a similar idea to wider variety of
merchandise The National Retail
Dry Goods Association in a recent
survey noted decided trend toward
greater use of the multiple price
system.


Special multiple prices" the sur
vey states. ''are best adapted to
staple, quick consumption items that
the customer would normally need
in quantity, although they have
been in use with success for such
items as bedding and basement
dresses


The greatest response from the
spending public has been noticed III
inexpensive articles where only
a small additional payment is neces-

by this pricing system.


Far from merely bringing future
purchases into the present, multi
pie prices actually increase con-
sumption OF small, quickly used items,
retailers say. When there is a new
toothbrush in the closet. the old
stubble is thrown away much more
quickly than when it's necessary to
make a special trip to the corner
drug store to buy new one.


Among other articles for which null
tlple prices have boosted sales are
hosiery, underwear, mems furnish
lngs, toilet goods, childrens wear,
stationery and groceries.

Puerto Rico, facing within the next
two months the greatest unemployment
in It's history and sharp drop in its
dollar income, has been deluging Wash
ington with sharp protests against re-
strictions which have been placed on its
industries by the Federal Government,
together with requests that the United
States announce its future policy with
respect to the islands political and eco
nomic status. Insular spokesmen charge
that Congress and the administration
have throttled Puerto Rican industries
through quotas, reciprocal trade agree
ments and various other legislation, and
they are demanding the removal of these
handicaps.


In addition, political and industrial
leaders point out that the island has re-
ceived far less than its per capita share
OF Federal relief appropriations, although
the people of Puerto Rico are American
citizens and presumably entitled to share
in Federal funds on the same basis as
territories


BY cable, airmail radio and personal
visits these protests have been reaching
Washington in an increasing number
during recent years. There have been
as many as 80 Puerto Rican government
officials and businessmen in the Capital
at one time on certain occasions, SEEK
ing to have the island included in some
bills and excluded from others, persuad-
ing Federal agencies to- allocate funds
to the territory and trying to get various
restrictions removed.


Sugar Curb Starts Protest.


The first serious protests came in 1884,
when the sugar quota system originally
was established and Puerto Rico, alone
among the domestic sugar producing
areas, was forced to reduce it's production
substantially. Inasmuch as sugar had
come to account for two-thirds Of the
Islands total income by that time, the
whole island felt the reduction in one
way or another. Until the sugar legisla-
ton was passed Puerto Rico had felt
kindly toward the Federal Government
for aid extended following the hurricanes
in 1923 and 1882 and the promise OF
extensive relief funds for general eco
nomic rehabilitation.


The next major blow was the Cuban
reciprocal trade agreement, which also
went into effect in 1884. This agreement
halved the duty on Cuban fresh pine
apple and reduced sales of the Puerto
Rican fruit. But little was said about
a. Gle
the pineapple industry was in relatively
few hands.


Then, in 1887, Congress passed a new
sugar quota bill which reduced Puerto
Rico's quota still further, while granting
an increase to Cuba, and resulted also
in depressing the price Of sugar. The
insular government and businessmen
again protested vigorously and sent sew
eral delegations to Washington.


Even up to this point, the objections
from the island were relatively mild, be-
cause the dollar income from all Puerto
Rican industries had been increasing
steadily and business conditions were
gradually improving.


Labor Act Increases Indignation.


1nsular indignation reached a new
peak last June, however, when Puerto
Rico at the last minute was icluded
under the Fair Labor Standards Act,
fixing a minimum wage of 25 cents an
hour for all industries not exempted.


The bill clearly meant the end of the
islands s21 100000 needlework industry
which is believed to have offered full or
part time employment to about 10000
workers, most of whom had no other
means of support. Wages in that indus
try had been considerably lower than
the 25-cent minimum, in some cases less
than 10 cents an hour, but that was the
only reason the industry ever had sprung
up. Competition for the most part was
not with similar concerns in the United
States mainland but with foreign coun-
tries where wages were greatly lower.


Other smaller industries were SINH
larly affected by the wage and hour
legislation and Puerto Ricans soon en-
visioned another 100000 workers joining
the ranks Of the unemployed, which
already numbered about 10000 indi-
viduals. A half dozen delegations visited
Washington, called on Administrator
Andrews and attended hearings. Gables
and radio messages came faster than
ever, until 1t became clear that only an
amendment to the act could save the
needlework industry.


Just as the wage and hour law went
into effect the State Department an
nounced hearing on amendments to
the Cuban trade agreement Lower
tariffs on sugar, tobacco and rum were to
be considered, and Cubas Col. Batista
was reported to have announced that the
lower sugar tariff already had been
agreed to. Once again the Puerto Rican
delegations arrived, fortified with briefs,
and testified against the proposed reduc-
tions.


Another Outlet damned.


1t then was discovered that the re-
ciprocal trade treaty with Great Britain
had reduced the duty on coconuts to the
point where the Puerto Rican product
could not be sold profitably on the main
land market, thus crippling another
small but essential industry.


Meanwhile, the United States Depart
ment of Agriculture which administers
the sugar quotas announced that Puerto
Rico would have to reduce its 1899 and
1910 sugar production by about IS per
cent in order to reduce the existing sur
plus of sugar in warehouses. Though

From time to time, great masses
OF soldiers from Asia have pushed
their way westward toward Europe.
These soldiers most often have been
Mongols. One of their famous
leaders In the Middle Ages was
Genghis Khan. The huge "em-
pires" Of the Mongols did not last
long, but their conquests were inn
portant in one way or another.


Seven centuries ago, the so-called
Ottoman Turks were driven from
their homeland in Central Asia.
Fleeing before the Mongols, they en-
tered Asia Minor and settled there.


The Ottoman Turks we're named
n honor of one of their early lead
ers, man known as Osman or
Qthman. He might be called "the
Father of Turkey" but several other
leaders also helped build up Turkish
power.


The Ottoman Turks were relatives
Of the Seljuk Turks, who had moved
westward in the earlier days. and
had won Persia, Palestine and parts
Of Asia Minor. After the Ottomans
came, they took away the power of
the Seljuks, and became the rulers
Of the Turkish empire.


The empire kept growing and
growing, The Ottoman Turks con-
quered Syria and Egypt. They also
obtained sections of Northwestern
Africa. For time their warships
were the strongest on the Mediter-
ransan Sea.

men aboard the City of Flint told
the Associated Press today they
feared the vessel now is "a marked
ship" on the seas and expressed
doubt concerning her next move.


Although newspaper reporters were
not at first permitted to board the
ship, a woman representative of the
Associated Press managed to 60
aboard and talk with members of

Advised by the sailors that they
were under orders to say nothing,
she suggested:


1T would be nice If your families
in America got word quickly that
you men are all right"


Tell them we're all right"
spokesman for the crew answered.


Sailors, dangling over the side to
repaint the Stars and Stripes on
the hull, greeted the reporter with
broad grins. To the query "How
are you feeling now?" one replied:


"It's fine now, but I was scared
stiff while the Germans were
aboard

treated we'll by the Germans, who,
they said, were aware their task was
unpleasant for the Americans. The
chief breaks in the worrisome.
fatiguing routine aboard the ship
were enumerated briefly by the
sailors.

the German pocket battleship
Deutschland on October halted
and inspected the City of Flint, then
put aboard the crew of the sunken
British steamer Stonegate and de-
cided to claim the Flint as a prize
of war.


The next break came with the first
stop at Tromso, Norway; then fol-
lowed the dash to Murmansk, Soviet
Arctic port, through bitter cold and
dangerous seas.

STOCKHOLM, Dec. 5.-Sweden,
in increasing alarm at the extent
of the Soviet Russian incursion into
Finland, called more troops to the
colors today and for the first time
acknowledged partial mobiliza-
tion."


About 10000 men, including ar
tillerymen, engineers and commits
sary detachments, were ordered into
service, bringing to about 10000
the number under arms-as against
a normal standing force of 10000.


The troops are for wartime serv-
ice," published notices said. Pre-
vious military orders referred only
to preparedness"


Refugees Increasing.
Sweden continued to direct her
efforts toward neutrality. one official
informant remarking, I'VE may be
wealthy, but our forces are too
small to send to the aid Of another
country"


Finnish refugees reaching Hapa-
randa, on the Swedish side Of the
frontier, related today they were
machine-gunned by Russian planes
which they rushed out to greet near
Petsamo in the mistaken belief they
we're Red Cross craft.
Newspapers and citizens organi-
cations in Stockholm are gathering
clothes and raising funds for the
refugees, whose numbers are in
creasing rapidly.


Erkko In Stockholm.


Among about $50 Firms and
Swedes arriving from Helsinki and
Abo yesterday was Elias Erkko, for
mer Finnish foreign minister, who
is to be charge daffaires in Stock
holm.


Erkko and the Swedish foreign
minister, Richard Sander, con-
ferred until after midnight.
Indicative of public feeling here
was last nights meeting of the
Stockholm Town Council. Its three
Communist members were refused
permission to ask any questions.


A rumor here, which could not be
verified, said new map of Scan
dinavia" was being circulated in
Russia, showing Finland and the
northern half of Sweden as Russian
possessions and the southern half Of
Sweden as German soil, with Nor
way and Denmark unchanged.

Every one knows that helium has
aided man to soar safely to great
heights; few know that this valuable
gas is enabling man to venture safe
ly to great depths under the sea. A
report by medical officers attending
the divers who salvaged the ill-fated
submarine Squalus reveals how
helium fortified the courageous div
ing crew against their deadliest
enemy, the bends-long a scourge Of
the men who 60 down to the sea In
metal helmets and rubber suits.


The Squalus tragedy afforded the
men of the Navy's experimental div
ing unit at the Navy Yard here their
first opportunity to test under condi-
tions of an actual emergency the he
lium equipment with which they had
been experimenting for many months
in their laboratory and in test dives in
the lower Potomac River and Chesa-
peake Bay. Those researches had
convinced the Navy that helium
could perform miracles for deep-sea
divers. BY mixing the light, inert,
colorless gas with the oxygen pumped
to the divers, it was found that the
men safely could stand pressures
that otherwise might prove disas-
trous. Moreover, the process of de-
compression, whereby divers are
subjected to gradually decreasing
pressures as precaution against the
bends, was greatly accelerated by use
OF the helium mixture.


The experiments with helium were
far from complete, however, when
the diving unit last May was ordered
to proceed at once with their equip
ment to the scene Of the Squalus
tragedy. The stricken submarine
was 240 feet below the surface of the
ocean-a dangerous depth for ordi-
nary diving operations. The first
group of divers to reach the Squalus
ignored danger and dared the depths
without benefit Of helium. They be-
came dizzy and nearly helpless. Then
the helium apparatus was installed
and a marked difference was noted.
The divers were able to work in COM
parative comfort for long periods.
And when they were hauled aboard
ship and placed in the decomposition
chamber they had no horror Of the
bends, serious and sometimes fatal
disorder, caused by formation Of gas
bubbles in the bloodstream. During
all the months of the difficult salvage
operations on the sunken Squalus
there was not one case of bends, the
medical report points out. All Of
which is additional proof that the
United States Navy, which gave the
world the lung" and the rescue
chamber, continues to lead the world
in submarine rescue and salvage

CHICAGO, Aug. 26.-The Chicago
Herald and Examiner carried an
announcement tonight that, effective
Monday, 1t would be merged with
the Evening American under the
title of the Chicago Herald -Ameri-
can, an afternoon and Sunday news
paper.


The Herald and Examiner, one of
Chicago's two morning newspapers,
and the American are members of
the William Randolph Hearst news
paper chain. AS result of the mer-
ger, the Chicago Tribune will be the
city's only morning daily.


A strike against the Herald and
Examiner and the American was
called last December by the Hearst
units of the Chicago Newspaper
Guild and has not been settled.


H. Richard Seller, international
representative of the American
Newspaper Guild, said tonight:
"The strike against Hearst will con-
tinue no matter how they switch
names or editions. until a fair settle
ment is reached"


The Herald and Examiner has
been published as tabloid during
week days since September 4, 1898.
The old Herald, founded in 1881, was
purchased by Mr.. Herast and merged
with the Examiner May 2, 1918.


Mr.. Hearst started the American
in 1900 and two years later started
the Chicago Examiner, a morning
newspaper.


In March. 1898, Mr.. Hearst said
he was relinquishing active business
management of his vast publishing
and financial holdings. Last July
%, the Syracuse (N.Y) Journal and
Sunday American, Hearst news
papers, announced suspension of
publication and sale of the name,
good will and syndicated features
to the rival Syracuse Herald.


Other contractions have included:


Merger of the New York American
with the New York Evening journal
and tabloid Mirror, sale of the
Omaha Bee News to the Omaha
World Herald, consolidation of the
Milwaukee News with the Milwaukee
Sentinel transfer of the Washington
Herald and Times to Mrs. Eleanor M.
Patterson and consolidation of the
Hearst wire services, International
News and Universal Service.


Today's merger, announced in
two-column. front page statement
in the Sunday edition of the Herald
and Examiner, sounded the death
knell for what was once one of the
most picturesque newspapers in the
country. Before the Herald and Ex-
aminer merger in 1918, the Old
Herald had absorbed three papers
the Times, the Record and the Inter-
Ocean.

The battered German tanks and

red lion shields taken from post
offices or other public buildings. The
Nazis left behind small outpost of
men to await the Russians.


Wooden Bridges Left Behind.


The troops went to border railway

The German high commands

One of the most bitter of small

carried on under more agreeable

German officers were swarming

struments, taking last minute

From the River Dnestr, which
forms the boundary between Rus
and Rumania, to the Adriatic, Ger
man minorities which form innu-
merable population islands in Hun
gary, Rumania and Yugoslavia are
stirring with apprehension at the
prospect of being forced to return to
Germany.


In this region, which Germany
hopes to make her "Lebensraum,"
nearly two million Germans reside,
the big majority of them the de-
scendants of families which have
populated this area for centuries,
mingled with, but not absorbed by,
the Croats, Slovenes, Serbs, Mag
vars, Rumanians and Ukrainians, in
whose midst they have been i'm
bedded.


Rumania contains some 100000
Germans, residents of old Saxon and
Alsatian towns on the slopes of the
Carpathian Alps and in the Banat,
which were established as early as
the twelfth century, when the Hun
garians persuaded the Crusaders to
settle in the passes of the Carpath-
ians and thus prevent the inroads of
barbarians into Europe. They are
purely German people, preserving
their national character along with
their religion. In their Rumanian
homes they have gained consider
able wealth through agriculture and
industry.


In Yugoslavia, Germans, total
ing 100000, constitute the largest
minority group, inhabiting mainly
the Voyvodina, highly fertile valleys
Of the Sava and Drava Rivers,
Croatia-Slavonia and Slovenia. They
are for the most part wealthy farm
ers and tradesmen. Like the Ger
mans in Rumania, these groups COM
pose historic enclaves in a sea of
Slavic peoples.


In Hungary, adjoining Austria, the
presence of 100000 Germans, espe-
cially in Budapest and west of the
Danube, has been particular prob
lem for the Magyars, although radi-
cal Magyars, rather than the Ger
mans. have been the backbone of
Hungary's Nazi movement.


Outside the Reich these peoples,
who have used their Germanic char
acter to claim special treatment and
minority rights, have watched the
economic enslavement of Germans
within the Reich, secure in their own
prosperity and possession of lands
and businesses. But Chancellor Hit
ler's plans for repatriation of foreign
Germans first in the case of
the Tyrolese and currently in the
case of the Baltic Germans-has
reused acute fears that similar dis
possession will be used to take
home" the Balkan Germans.


Particularly in Hungary and Yugo-
slavia has reaction to this fear been
marked by a mass shedding of the
Germanic cloak these people have
worn for centuries. Names are being
Magyarized and Slavicized. Orthodox
priests in Yugoslavia are registering
conversions of German Protestants
to the Serbian church, and the past
emphasis on German nationality has
suddenly been replaced by marked
hush around minority claims.


The German repatriation move

Bucharest, for whether by dislodging
the Germans from their homes or

means greater domestic peace and

living obscurely in Bohemia for some

who commanded Czechs resist

Hundreds of young men have been

whisper, to join the legion of Czech
patriots being formed by Gen.

here. 1t was known, however. that

friends.

any underground announcement
from Czechs in the United States.
Ex-President Benes is now in
America.


Only after verifying to their sat-
isfaction reports that Volta Benes
had gone to Poland did his friends
admit he had been living quietly in
Bohemia.

-degree-below-zero temperature,

many, Italy and Japan in their

citizens.

Nazi party symbol-crossed arrows
was disappearing.


Police were scraping the emblem
from walls and billboards, and mer-
chants sympathetic to the Nazis
were taking posters from the win
dows.

Human tackling dummies made

Never Swears by 1t.

ica who last year coached at Iowa

Glen Stralka. the guard from

Auburn tackle, received bloody noses.
while Andy Farkas had the wind

his head into defenders tummy.

ing. they were those two native
guards, Steve SlivinSki and Dick
Farman. who continuously led the
interference and bowled over such
stalwarts as Wee Willie Wilkin. Turk

last three veterans. incidentally.
were the first three wearers of the
dummies and when they were

When Walter Wanger's newest
United Artist picture enters pro-
ductlon late in June it will have as
its permanent title "Eternally
Yours!' and its co-stars, Loretta
Young and David Niven, will have
one of the strongest supporting casts

will be Hugh Herbert, who will head
the supporting cast, playing the
patient and devoted valet to "the

thony" with his trick rabbits and

wear and full-length sable coat.

Yours!" from an original screenplay
by Gene Towne and Graham Baker.
Merritt Gerstad, who photographed
Wanger's recently completed Win
ter Carnival" will act as cinemato-

has for its backgrounds scenes in
New York, London, Rio de Janeiro,

CSpeciaD.-Theft of several gold
certificates, old large-size bank bills,
gold coins and jewelry, all valued

Viola Custer, 81, has been revealed.


Miss Custer, second cousin of
Gen. George Custer of Last Stand"
fame, discovered the robbery on
returning on December 26 from
Brunswick, Md. She said the money,
representing her life savings, was
hidden about her house because she
was "a bit mistrustful" of banks.


Miss Custer said she and her
brother, Garland, S. earned their
living and the savings with bee
culture and other activities on the
10-acre plot near here, where they
were born.


State police are investigating.

CHICAGO, April 25.-Taking ad-
vantage of rising temperatures and
abating rainfall, farmers through
out the grain belt today hastened
SOIL preparation and planting-work
which has been delayed by cold, wet
weather.


Crop experts received reports of
rotting of oats and serious delay in
seeding in important producing
regions where the crop should have
been in the ground by mid-April.
Many fields have failed to sprout
and may have to be reseeded or
planted to other grains.


Farmers in the Northwest hoped
10 complete spring wheat planting
this week or next, but operations
were 10 days to two weeks later than
year ago. Throughout the country
ploWs were furroWing the earth,
preparatory to seeding of corn, but
there were many localities where
wet soil or standing water kept
farmers off the fields.

which are bringing high prices in
comparison with the value of grains
used for feed. Most grains were
priced lower than year ago.

POUGHKEEPSIE, N. Y, June 10.
-Poughkeepsie has been the heart
of American rowing since a torrid
day in 1865, when 10000 rabid fans
lined the Hudson River banks to
watch a local amateur four-oared
crew defeat the Brooklyn Biglins
with a disputed decision that re-
manned unsettled until two men were
violently killed.


That lusty regatta and it's two
days of ribald revelry was the FORE
runner to the 44-year- intercol-
legiate eight-oared rowing cham
pionship that will be renewed June
II.


Around $4,000 spectators will crowd
into this river town on regatta day,
more than usual this year because
the race will be run on a Saturday
and because the East. which broke
the Far Vests domination a year
ago, has strong contenders again.


Start Near Roosevelt Home.


Some watchers will line the broad
4-mile course along the Hudson
from Krum Elbow. starting point
adjacent to President Roosevelt S
summer White House at Hyde Park
to the colorful flotilla of fag-be-
decked Government and private
craft which form a funnel at the
finish line near the city.


Other spectators will pay S. and
ride the observation train that
shuttles back and forth, following
the races. Some persons will be in
vited aboard Government or private
ships. A few individuals will pilot
their own little skiffs.


The city will be gayly decorated.
There'll be block dance regatta
night. Due to the Saturday date.
many persons are expected to make
a week end of the crew classic, with
railroad and boat excursions de-
signed to attract Worlds Fair visi-
tors.


The citvs business increases %
per cent on regatta day with hotels,
taxis and restaurants enjoying most
of it. The uptown merchants prac-
tically close shop during the regatta
afternoon. Roadhouses. bars and
similar celebrative spots figure on
regatta night even more than New
Years. Prices, they say, are not
hiked up.


City Goes Collegiate.


Poughkeepsle is turned over to
visiting alumni. students and sports
fans. The citys attire is gay and
collegiate, with streets and stores
plastered with pennant colors of the
competing crews. If the day is wet,
as during the last few weeks,
sou 'westers appear and rubber hats
are worn. Hotel lobbies are thronged
with crowds. Bars do a rushing
business. Scotch and soda is the
perennial regatta favorite alumni
drink. Students generally go for
the more economical beer.


BY early afternoon the city proper
Is deserted as the thousands stream
TO the water front. a 15-minute
walk. Many persons park cars on
craggv bluffs and listen to radio
broadcasts of the race until the
crews can be sighted with field
glasses.


High above the race. on a railroad
bridge. swings Mike Bogo. huge
bartender. who is the official regatta
bomb-shooter When the race is
done. Mike shoots the number of
bombs to correspond with the win
ming lane number and lowers
string OF college flags, hung in the
order of the finish.


Dance Till Dawn.


Regatta night is night of revelrv.
Bars are four-deep. Roadhouse res
ervatlons are sold out. Every hotel
room is party room. Dancing lasts
until dawn. Collegiate pranks are
numerous. The police are lenient.


Some of the crews come to Pough-
keepsie three weeks before the big
race and their time trials twice a
day interest the toWnsfolks almost
as much as the regatta itself. The
oarSmen are Quartered away from
the city. Seven sets of oarsmen,
coXsWains, coaches. managers, train
ers, riggers. shells and even some
private chefs are here this year, rep
resenting Washington, California.
Cornell, Navy, Columbia, Wisconsin
and Syracuse.


The varsity race is the big attrac-
ton, but there are junior varsity
and freshman races, too.

By the Associated Press.


CLEVELAND, Aug. 3l.-The
Cleveland Rams, junior member OF
the National Football League. likely
will be in the dark horse role this
season.


At nearby Baldwin Col
lege. Coach Earl (Dutch) Clark is
working with an impressive squad
that has nine ends, dozen tackles
seven guards, three centers, a halt
dozen signal callers, a quintet OF
wingbacks and tailbacks and three
fullbacks. In addition to II hold
overs from last season, five new
corners have National League expe-
rience.


One of Clark's tackle candidates
is Art Lewis, his assistant coach
who handled the Rams part of last
year.


Clark apparently is we'll pleased
with his flock. He's confident the
Rams are going places this year
but hesitates to say just where.


Teams Always Are Scrappy.


His comment has been limited to:
We'll have good, scrappy team
this year" That's hardly original
for all of Clarks teams have been
noted for their scrappiness.


Dutch Clark rightfully has been
called the greatest player profess
sional football ever developed. He
was chosen all-league quarterback
six times. This marks his eighth year
with the pros, but his first as q
bench manager. Last season he
coached the Detroit Lions.


The Rams are placing high store

especially Warren Drummer, touted

ors since Don Zimmerman; Bronko
Smilanick from the University of

the backfield are Corby Davis,
Johnnie Drake, all-league second
team fullback last season; Julius
Alfonso and Victor Spadaccini. Vet
eran linemen include Art Lewis, Ted
Livingston, 225-pound tackle; Chuck
Cherundolo, Phil Ragazzo, guard
from the Green Bay Packers, and
Tom Hupke, who played four years
at guard for Detroit before joining
the Rams last year.


On the flanks are Dale Prather,
who may be shifted to tackle, and
James dittle Footsie) Benton, from
Arkansas, second-year man with
Cleveland.


No elevn ever is much stronger
than its forward wall, and Cleve-
lands chief problem is to develop a
line formidable enough to blast the
way for Clark's fast-breaking backs.


The Rams will open their cham
pionship campaign against the Bears
at Chicago September Is.

BY the Associated Press.


WEST PALM BEACH, Fla, Aug
16.-Charles Jefferson, "a, who posed
as a theatrical promoter to lure two
Miami schoolgirls from home, plead
ed innocent today to indictments
charging him with kidnapping, rape
and murder in the death of 17-year-
old Frances Dunn.


Judge C. E. ChillingWorth, before
whom Jefferson was arraigned folt
lowing his indictment yesterday by
the Palm Beach County grand jury,
set trial for September 25 on the
murder charge.


The court appointed Jack w. Sal
isbury, former States attorney here,
to defend Jefferson.


The indictment was returned fol-
lowing testimony by Jean Bolton
young Miami night club singer, who
has said she and her school chum
Miss Dunn, were lured by Jefferson's
pose as movie talent scout. Miss
Bolton was held captive by the man
for three days last week.

ST. PETERSBURG. Fla. March
28.-Manager Joe Mccarthy cited
the record books today to prove his
contention a combination of team
work and pitching was the success
secret of the New York Yankees.


"All this talk about the Yankees
blasting their way to the champion
ship on sheer power does not COIN
eide with the records" said Nc
Carthy, getting ready to close the
spring training camp here and head
northward with his team.


What power are they talking
about? The Yankees only had
three hitters in the 800 class last
year. Look it up for yourself"


A quick check of the averages for
1888 upheld the stocky manager.


Team Play Great Help.


Washington, Chicago and Boston
all had seven sluggers who hit for
300 or better last year. Cleveland
had four, and the rest of the clubs.
including New York. had three each.


Look at the team batting aver
ages and see where We finished"
Mccarthy prompted.


The Yankees finished sixth at
.274, nosing out only Philadelphia
and Detroit.


If you want to know how the
Yankees win championships. it is
because they play championship
ball." Mccarthy continued. We
have the best team play. Our club
has been playing together for years.
The boys work together. They
know each others weaknesses and
fine points. They back up plays.
They talk baseball and discuss win.
ming plays. They are out there
helping each other all the time.


Yanks' Pitching Superb.


But the chief thing that is over
looked when people start talking
about Yankee power is our pitching.
We had the best pitching in the
league last year, if you'll recall the
records"


Again cCarthy was right.
Yankee pitchers led the league in
yielding the least number of runs,
the least number of earned runs and
had the lowest earned run average
per game, 3.31.


You can't win without pitching
and the Yankees have been getting
it." Mccarthy said, almost wistfully
as if he had his fingers crossed for
his pitching in 1889.

MOSCOW, Aug. 23.-German For
eign Minister Joachim Won Ribben-
trop and Premier Foreign Minister
Vyacheslaff Molotoff began formal
negotiation of a German-Russian
aggression treaty this after
noon.


The talks started at pm. at the
Kremlin, just two hours after Won
Ribbentrop's plane alighted here
from Germany.


1t was noted that the Japanese
Ambassador, Shigenori Togo, did not
go to the airport to greet the repre-
sentative of Japans anti-comintern
partner.


japanese circles were reported un-
officially to be deeply disturbed by
the Russian German collaboration
which has upset the calculations of
European diplomats.


Won Ribbentrop and Molotoff, with
Schulenburg also attending, still
were in conference at pm, three
hours after they assembled at the
Kremlin.


F0rmalities Are Waived.


Diplomatic formalties were dis
pensed with, and Won Ribbentrop
paused only for luncheon with the
German Ambassador, Friedrich Wer-
ner Schulenburg. Even the Gus
tomary official courtesy calls were
waived before the Won Ribbentrop-
Molotoff meeting.


A small group of Soviet officials
was on hand at Moscow's civil air.
port to greet the emiSsary of Russia's
traditional political enemy.


When Won Ribbentrop stepped
from his Fuehrer's plane, the entire
staff of the German Embassy gave
the Nazi salute.


Won Ribbentrop shook hands with
Soviet officials. Ambassador Angus
to Rosso, representing Germany's
axis partner, Italy, also was at the
field.


Ivan Potemkin, vice commissar of
foreign affairs, was the ranking
Soviet official to meet the plane.


Won Ribbentrop was driven i'm
mediately in an American car to
his quarters in the one-t time Aus
trian Legation.


Pact Expected Soon.


That the Soviet-German pact
would be concluded, possibly within
a few days, was accepted by diplo-
matte quarters as virtual cer-
tainty.


Won Ribbentrop's coming-by way
of Koenigsberg, East Prussia-Was
unheralded in the Soviet press.


Both British and French military
missions awaited instructions from
home. Reports on the situation here
were cabled last night by the British
and French Ambassadors, both of
whom saw Molotoff individually in
long conferences yesterday.


The fact no newspapers COM
mented on the coming Of the Ger
man delegation was indicative of
the extremely cautious way in which
Russian was handling the delicate
diplomatic situation.


The newspapers also failed to
carry the news the British Parlia-
ment had been recalled This an
nouncement was picked up by radio
and spread like wildfire among the
alarmed foreign colony, however.


Step to Peace Seen.


Soviet quarters continued to in
sist the way was open for both
non-aggression pact with Germany
and defensive alliance with Bri-
tain and France. They contended a
Soviet-German treaty would go
long way toward insuring European
peace


In sharp contrast to the alarm
felt by the foreign colony was the
almost unnatural calm of the av-
erage Russian, who unconcernedly
pursued his daily task.


For one thing. the Soviet press
was printing only sketchy reports
from abroad The forthcoming in
ternational cotton conference In the
United States was given a much
bigger display than the European
situation


The average Russian apparently
feels that if war does break out
Russian will be neutral and in
strong and safe position. They also
are quick to point out non-a -aggres-
sion pact with Germany is not an
alliance.

In 1888 Lombardi had finished his
season voted the most valuable in
his league. He was the standout
guy-the top man.


A year later he finishes the sea-
son lying on his back in the dirt of
home plate-a blazing sun beating
down upon him-runner knocking
him down and running around-the
crowd booing and jeering-dazed
and bewildered-a heartbroken ex-
hero who happened to run into one
OF those breaks of sport.


If Frey and Myers only had han
died that double play correctly-the
surest and easiest double play of the
series-a high school double play
all those terrible things would never
have fallen upon the harassed soul
Of big Ernie.


But they caught him in the big,
white spotlight. The glare was on
him at that moment and the hero
of 1888 was suddenly the goat of
1899, when Dame Fortune-"the
cockeyed wench" suddenly turned
against him.

Selection of Davey O'Brien, a
johnny Lately in his first pro-
fessional football campaign, in place
Of Ace Parker, one of the greatest
all-around backs In the game, pro-
vided the biggest surprise of the
official 1899 all-National Football
League team picked by the 10
coaches and released today.


Secondary only to the O'Brien- for
Parker choice was the failure Of
the new world champions Green
Bay Packers to place more than one
man on the two. teams chosen, End
Don Hutson being their lone repre-
sentative.


The New York Giants, Eastern
champions routed by the Packers in
the playoff, received the biggest
play from the coaches with six NOM
inees, four on the first team and two
on the second. The remaining
members of the first II were pro-
vided by only three other teams
the Chicago Bears. who placed three:
the Redskins, who placed two, and
the Philadelphia Eagles, represented
by OBrien.


Pittsburgh is the only team I'M
represented by a single player on
either the first or second team, with
Brooklyn and Cleveland each plac-
ing three men on the second eleven
and the Detroit Lions and Chicago
Cardinals one apiece.


O'Brien Finishes Strongly.


Apparently, the coaches were will
ing to overlook OBrien's early-sea-
son shortcomings when the opinion
was widespread that lii Davey was,
as many had anticipated, too small
for the big league. But his feats
in the last three games when he es-
tablished two all-time passing rec
ords evidently impressed the ment-
ors, who gave him 26 votes, II more
than Parker and as many as any
other back in the league with the
exception of Bill Osmanski, the Chi
cago Bears rookie all-league full
back.


Andy Farkas and Jim Barber
were the two Redskins selected, thus
justifying local belief that they were
as good as any halfback or tackle in
the league. Farkas' establishment
of new all-time mark for touch
downs in single season and Bar
bers consistently outstanding work
both on offense and defense merited
their selection.


But the complete omission of Red
skin Guard Jim Karcher, who made
the second team in 1888 and who
played even better this season, and
the failure to recognize End Wayne
Millner, who had his greatest year,
were distinct surprises.


Amid a plethora of backs, fans
could argue all year as to the best
possible backfield combination and
there is little to choose between
the first-named quartet of Tuffy
Leemans, Farkas, OBrien and
Osmanski and the second of Parker,
Parker Hall, Lloyd Cardwell and
Johnny Drake. Osmanski and
Farkas were one-two in leading the
league in ground-gaining this year,
while Leemans was no worse than
seventh best in that respect. Os-
manski averaged ST. yards per rush,
Farkas 39 and Leemans 33.


Sets Record for Rockies.


Selection of OBrien and Osman-
ski. incidentally, marks the first
time in the leagues history that
more than one rookie has been
named to the first team. How out
standing these backs must have
been is seen by their being favored
over such recognized stars as Clarke
Hinkle, Cece Isbell. Bill Shepherd,
Frank Filchock and Fred Vanzo.
Two rockies also made the second
team, Parker Hall of Cleveland and
Ki Aldrich of the Cardinals.


Only four of the first team are
hold-overs from 1938-Mel Helm of
the Giants, Danny Fortmann and
Joe Stydahar of the Bears and
Hutson of the Packers. It is the
seventh consecutive year that the
31-year -old Helm has been picked
as all-league center.


Ed Widseth of the Giants, Lloyd
Cardwell of the Lions and Parker
all first-team choices last year
were dropped to the second, while
three other '38 selections-Ed
Danowski of the Giants and Russ
Letlow and Clarke Hinkle of the
Packers-were omitted.

Next time you want something
new. girls, try crayon embroidery.
Flower designs are always lovely,
so let's make poppy cushion first.


You can buy pattern and stamp
1t on your material or trace off a
flower picture and transfer it with
carbon paper. Both dark and light
materials make effective back
grounds.


Decide whether you want Oriental
poppies or the golden California
ones, and get wax crayons the color
you decide on, with greens for the
leaves and brown for stems. Now
paint your design with the crayons,
shading your petals and leaves as
realistically as you can. If you can
find picture to follow, it will help
you. Be sure to keep within the
edges of your design.


Make the petals darker near the
center, using yellow over the red to
tighten the edges. Use yellow to
shade the leaves, too. Or you can
use several shades of red and green
If you have them, but the yellow
will give very satisfactory results.


When your design is painted, take
matching silk and outline the whole
thing. Make yellow and black
French knots for the centers. A
complete outline of black also gives
wonderful effect with some designs.
You'll soon learn which is more
effective.


Now place your design face down
on several thicknesses of blotting
paper and press it thoroughly with
a fairly hot iron. This sets the
colors so the article can be carefully
laundered.

SHANGHAI. May 8 (P.-Japanese
war planes caused great loss of life
and property today in repeated at
tacks along the South China coast
to stop goods of military and COM
mercial value from entering the
country.


Authorities closed business places
and ordered the people to move in
land to escape the raids. which Chi
nese officials said were reckless" at
tempts to break Chinese morale"


An increase of activity of Jap
anese armed forces was noted near
Annoy, where warships were con-
stantly coming and going and air.
craft were passing, apparently
headed toward inland raids.


Capital Move Denied.


Official Chinese quarters vigor-
ously denied reports Generalissimo
Chang Kai-shek planned to move
his government-for the third time
in % months of warfare-from
Chungking to Chengtu, Sczechwan
province capital ITS miles to the
northwest.


Domei. Japanese news agency, re-
ported that Chang Kai-shek flew
to Chengtu to consult his military
leaders about shifting his capital
there. Nothing definite. however,
was known here about the general
issimo's whereabouts.


Chungking. bombed yesterday and
Thursday with heavy damage and
casualty toll estimated at 1000 to
5000, was besieged today by refugees
who fled last week but were forced
by hunger to return.


Authorities gave great quantities
of thin soup to the populace, which
had dwindled from an estimated
100000 week ago to about 800, ,000
after the raids.

NEW YORK, Sept. 22.-United

porary headquarters would be estab-

prepared to leave Spain.

BY the Associated Press.


PARIS, Oct. 27.-The Germans
have moved tanks and rapid fire
artillery into attacking positions on
the Siegfried line, French military
observers reported today.


French patrol reports indicated
that the Germans facing the Magi-
not Notifications were in 'jumpoff"
spots all along the northern flank,
but an intense cold snap proved an
ally of the French, who said they
were all set for a German offensive.


The Council of Ministers, meet
ing with President Albert Lebrun
in Elysee Palace, approved ratifica-
ton of the French-British- Turkish
mutual assistance accord signed
October 10 in Ankara.


Premier Daladier gave the min
listers a long review of the war and
the diplomatic situation


Two DEGREES submitted by Agri-
cultural Minister Henri Queuille
were signed, providing for the pur-
chase and storage by the govern
ment Of agricultural surpluses.


The cold and flooded regions in
some parts of the front caused
French observers to doubt that a
German drive would be immediate,
but they said they expected it as
rift in the weather appeared.


Reconnoitering units skirmished
in snow. sleet and icy rain along
the 10O-mile northern flank last
night, getting some artillery support
as they wallowed in the ice-crusted
mud.


The French morning communique
said that during the night there was
local activity of reconnaissance
units"


Believe Push Is Imminent.


The sudden rigid control of Ger
man communications with Belgium
and the Netherlands also led the
French to suspect that big Ger
man push was imminent.


The French have estimated that
Germany now has 100000 men
either in front line or supporting
positions.


French reports also said huge
numbers of Nazi bombers and fight
ing planes were being brought up
to airdromes just behind the Sieg-
fried line. but the French were de-
pending on the weather to keep
them grounded, at least temporarily.

BY the Associated Press


FREE CITY OF DANZIG, July
20-The killing of a Polish soldier
near the Danzig frontier village OF
Postelau this forenoon suddenly in
creased tension between the Free
City and Poland.


Poles charged that the Polish SOL
dier, Vitold Budziewicz. was shot by
DanZig border official on Polish
SOIL


Free City authorities said the
Danzig customs officer, Max Stein.
fired in elf-defense.


officials told widely differing
stories of the incident which Great
ed great excitement at the office OF
the Polish commissioner in Danzig


Self-Defense Claimed.
The account of authorities of the
Nazifled Danzig government was
that Stein while patrolling near the
Polish -Danzig frontier saw a man
on bicycle riding toward him from
Poland with rifle slung over his
shoulder.


At the border, Danzigers said, the
man dismounted, raised the rife to
his shoulder and released the safety
catch as he aimed at the Danzig
official.


Stein asserted ne shot the Pole
in self defense.


Danzig authorities said they were
not certain the Pole was dead. but
the Polish commissioners Office re-
ported Budziewicz died a few min
utes after he collapsed at the from
tier.


Provocation Charged.


The Polish version was that a
Danzig customs officer and two men
in Danzig Storm Troopers uniforms
approached the border and without
warning shot Budziewicz. who was
several yards within the Polish side


Poles described the incident as
"ineKcusable provocation."


The Polish commissioner, Marian
Chodacki, conferred with Danzig
Senate oficials while both sides still
were receiving reports from the
scene Of the shooting. on the Free
City districts southern frontier.


AS the incident occurred. the Nazi-
controlled Danzig Senate was pre-
pairing for conscription of men and
wealth and taking further measures
to meet emergencies which might
arise from the Nazi campaign to
reunite the Free City with Germany


Decree Under Preparation.


Senators worked on a decree which
would give swe- ping authority for
requiring all citizens to serve the
state and for the use of any private
property in defense of the COM
munity.


The Free City government already
has authority under a decree to
conscript men for its enlarged police
force, which has been increased to
1900 men on active duty.


Defense organizations already
have Communicated some trucks
and automobiles for public duty.

CHICAGO. June 3.-Ten years of
official supervision of the sport of
outboard racing finds that form of
recreational boating still far from
the peak of expansion and speeds
still are mounting on the regatta
circuits, says James w. Mulroy, sec
retary of the National Outboard
Association.


The observance of National Out
board Motor Week starting on June
l8 will mark, among other things.
the formation 10 years ago of the
National Outboard Racing Commits
sion to foster the growth of what
was then a comparatively new form
of sport.


Outboard races had been held
since 1925, but, starting with the
first national championships at
Peoria. ILL.,. in 1929, outboard popu-
larity began a phenomenal growth.


Racing has been one of the chief
mediums of introducing outboard-
ing throughout the country, the
portable outfits having been trekked
into the most remote sections for
weekend regattas. There has fol-
lowed the widespread use of the out
board motor for creational boat
ing. and unit production for the last
two years has reached an all-time
high.


The modern compact and reliable
outboard motor that is used today
by upward of 100000 American
sportsmen was developed largely
through the medium of the regatta
circuit. Racing records have in
creased by more than 20 miles an
hour since the first nationals were
held 10 years ago and the speeds
still are advancing.

treat inland. moved their capital
successfully from Nanking to Han
kow to Chungking; the japanese,
while pursuing inland, at the same
time spread their power north and
south along the coast from Shang-
hal, eventually closing every normal
means of communication between
the inland Chinese forces and the
outside world.


Since the Chinese were cut off as
we'll from much of their normal do
mestic sources of supply new con-
tact with foreign sources became
necessary. The 1,000-mile Chung
king o-Burma highway was China's
answer to the problem.


French Railway to Running.


China already had an inland route
to Running, in Yunnan, her
southwesternmost province. This
was narrow-gauge railway, French
owned and completed in 1904, from
Hanoi, French Indo-C China.


However, this was a dead-end
route until China built the motor
highway, which has as its most i'm
portant leg the 50O-mile section
south from Chungking through
Kweiyang to Running This gave
Chunkgink direct connection to
the sea through Hanoi.


From Running the motor high
way forks west through Talifu and
Yunchang and then over mountain
ranges, some as high as 10000 feet,
to Lashio, in Burma, terminus of a
British railway running through
Mandalay t. the sea at Rangoon.


Thus since completion of the high
way it has been possible for China
to get supplies from either British
Rangoon or French Hanoi and ship
them into the heart of the country
at Chungking. The lifeline" imme-
diately had moral as well as ma
terial effect.


To cut this line the Japanese
forces would have to drive inland to
Running over 600 miles of difficult
territory. The first part, through
Kwangtung and Kwangsi Provinces,
appears relatively easy.

GILLIAN, Chile (via Buenos
Aires), Jan. u (P).-An endless file
of ox-drawn funeral carts slowly
made its way through the ruined
streets of historic Chillan today.


In somber despair men and women
who had lived through the horror
of earthquake limped and labored
alongside the creaking carts to bury
sons and daughters, mothers, fathers,
lifelong friends.


The weary way led to communal
graves-some of them bitches the
living had been able to dig, some
Of them deep assures with which the
violent earth convulsions. Scared
the countryside Tuesday night.


The military and those who could
work dug into the shambles for more
dead-so many that they cannot be
counted. The living that remain of
the city of 10000 are being counted
instead.


Mayor Silidoro Tapia believed
10000 perished as the city fell on
the trembling earth which similarly
destroyed the old Chillan 100 years
ago. Hundreds and probably thou
sands more were dead in nearby
cities and villages.


Most of the streets of Chillan
now are narrow paths winding
through heaps of homes. stores and
Offices.


Some of the dead were taken from
the ruins of two theaters which
cascaded into formless heaps of
brick and masonry shortly before
performances would have ended
Tuesday night.


The dead of one theater were
patrons of performance for char
ity, the need of which now is enor-
nous.


The central plaza around which
the carefree population once PROM
enaded can be reached only after
dangerous scramble through what
remains of the towns tallest build
ings.


Whole Families Buried.


The low moaning of injured
pleading for water mingles with the
calls of mothers for lost children.
Under the ruins whole families are
known to be buried.


The temblor was so quickly violent
that there was little time to escape
the crashing roofs and walls.


Troops sought to halt the aimless
hunting by relatives and to bring
order to the confused scenes of
misery. An occasional shot sig
nailed an end to an isolated attempt
at looting.

Forest another engagement char
acteristic of this war had just taken
place. A French patrol came in to
report they had met and turned
back German patrol. For evidence
they carried ; blood stained Ger
man helmet, two machine guns and
an assortment of hand grenades and
other trophies of victory.
Bring Back Two Dead.


Behind them came party carry
ing two German dead. Their field
gray uniforms and heavy boots were
still fresh. They were young, blond
infantrymen. Around them, not
with animosity, but with the curri-
osity of youth crowded young French
troops.


The French patrol of IS said they
encountered 80 to 40 Germans in
the forest, dropped into position
and fired as the Germans advanced
Two Germans were killed imme-
diately, one just as his bullet-clip
was moving through a machine
gun. Two others were wounded
gravely and the rest withdrew, leav-
ing their dead, wounded and equip
ment. The French had four wound
ed slightly.


The Warndt Forest, which has
been one of the main theaters Of
action, is one Of deep pine woods,
with wide lanes running through.
For mile and half I drove
through 1t to the German town of
Lauterbach, which one of the first
towns taken by the French.


There French troops now stand
on guard. That part Of the front
Is now quiet, with the Germans
holding the ridge east Of Lauter-
bach.

HSl yOuIH IleTe
GANnF alone was left, she
SstONs thought, bit of the
cr@nN life serene that was
SHON of the days of her


parents, and her
own childhood. The world was 90
ing mad, panic-stricken, she felt.
True, the lilacs by her door strove
to keep their heads erect, and to
urge the new yearly shoots to dig
nifty. But the simpering bridal
wreath bush bowed to every passer-
by, as the wind promiscuously
showered her white petals, as con-
fetti. The soft dirt road had broad
ened, and become black and hard,
with frequent baths of repulsive,
sticky oil.


How soon would the city and mod
ernity invade her sanctuary? she
questioned.


She looked with Mortified eyes at
the roadside stands. Hot dogs! Be-
fore her eyes danced a jumble of
signs, big and little, proclaiming-
why, actually, they had cuts of dogs,
In natural color, holding flaming red
trankfurts in their teeth. Terrible!


She. pushed her expense book
across the table. "Marcella Pratt"
she argued, you've got to do some
thlng-and soon. You can't eat this
house. And you have taxes to pay.
Marcella, at your age, you've got to
wake up!''


Next morning a pathetic little sign
appeared on her lawn. FUDGE!
She was sure of it's quality. They
could walk right into the dining
room and buy from her fathers
desk. Very simple.


But the first thing she knew she
found young men sprawled in her
chairs-mother's wedding present.
Mud on the floor. Actual petting
couples-but she took their money.
Couples full of jokes, modern things
that made her eyes wrinkle at the
corners, and her mouth want to
smile.


She repeated some to the cat,
leaving out the slang.


The invasion of her home was
becoming less sacrilegious. The
fudge business was paying well.


She tried raspberry jam sand
wiches. Just a plate. Thin white
bread, heavy with homemade Jam.
These we're still within her puritan
ical bounds. These brought the
same folks again and again, and the
men (big boys) called her "Auntie."


Then, afternoons, she left off the
percale dress and put on demure
black silk, with fresh white collar.
Above her silver hair was like a
halo. Her eyes and pink tinted
cheeks were made to love.


Miss Marcela was glad, was sad.
These bright, happy souls might
have been her own. The nephew
she loved most for the reason that
he was Stephens boy. Fortunate
Stephen to be loved by two girls.
Miss Marcella had stepped into the
shadows that he might marry her
sister. Children mean a lot.


After a while her fudge expert
ment was like bubbling yeast; bub-
bling over, clamoring for more
room, paying well for her work.
She had money saved and no bills
to pay. She could have the best of
food, if she cared to revel in such.
But these she didn't crave, and yet
she was restless.


Then it was that she read of an
orphan girl. She wrote immediate
ly, giving plenty of references as to
her honesty, character and church
connections. The society willingly
exchanged the girl for these. In
this lottery she drew a prize.


Every night Miss Marcella went
to bed thankful, tired and happy.
Money piled in and she applied for
a boy. He came, another orphan,
made so by some terrible accident.
A poor little mechanical body living
in stupor, caused by the sudden
calamity.


How she did love them. It was as
if they were her own children, who,
being lost, had been found and re-
turned.


But Miss Marcella forgot to reck-
on that two hungry children would
cost a lot of money. The tin box
was getting low, and although the
fudge and sandwich business was
brisk, still her expenses were large
mostly food She meditated long
on the problem.


Then one night, after the children
slept, she donned her outer gar
ments, took the family lantern and
trudged stoically across the field to
the home of John Mason.

fuels, paint materials, fine and

Offset higher prices for potatoes,

BUDAPEST, Oct. 9.-Italy waa
reported today to have offered new
friendship pacts to Hungary and
Yugoslavia.


These reports were confirmed semi
ohicially in Belgrade, while similar
rumors were heard in Bucharest
Italian radio broadcasts heard here
also said negotiations were under
way.


Diplomatic circles said Adolf Hit
ler's Reichstag speech last Friday
declaring Germany and Russia
would settle jointly all Southeastern
Europe's problems had speeded
Italian action to protect her own
Balkan and Danubian interests.


More Than Mere Treaty"


Usually reliable Yugoslav sources
said the italian negotiations were
"only the beginning of something
much bigger than a mere treaty


ASSOCIATED Press dispatches
from Rome contained no official
confirmation of the reported
negotiations. Some quarters, how
ever, advanced belief Italy was
seeking to eliminate differences
which have divided the Balkans
preparatory to forming a bloc
under Italian leadership. This
bloc, it was suggested. might take
the form of a consultative pact
and economic agreement similar
to the Rome protocols which once
bound Austria, Hungary and
ItalyD


With Italian diplomacy thus far
aimed at preserving neutrality, the
small southeastern nations saw their
chances of staying out of the war
enhanced by possibility of some sort
of pact with Italy.

NEW YORK, Nov. 4.-Giant
trucks rumbling along the New York
water front in an endless stream sig
nailed the lids of" on the shipment
Of war materials to Europe today
as President Roosevelt prepared to
sign the new neutrality law.


simultaneously, with pier sheds
already bulging, maritime experts
began to plan against recurrence
of the nightmare of congestion
which choked Americas No. / port
in 1914-1917.


For more than two years, even
before we got into the last war,
New York was swamped with goods
piled high on the wharves and no
ships to move it," said Cornelius H.
Callaghan, head of the New York
Maritime Exchange.


I'VE won't let that happen again,
at least. Railroad and shipping
officials are working out a plan to
forestall dumping cargo unless there
are bottoms to handle it,"


More Freight Than Ships.

edged that they already have "a
good deal more freight than ships"

voy system in the immediate future

trade.

pected to prevent collapse of this

sity Park League. The RambIers

right end; Johnny Thompson, left
tackle; and "Moby" Reddick, were the

Iowa's amazing iron men, the fairy

The indomitable iron men, seven

Minnesota's crushing power had

the ball on the 8-yard line and raced
across the goal line unmolested.
Kinnick calmly drop-kicked the
extra point and the iron men were
only two points behind.

The Gophers, struggling desper-
ately now to hold their lead, fought
of Kinnick's passing thrusts until
the final four minutes.


Again Iowa's aerial lightning
struck. Starting from their 21-yard
line, the Hawkeyes, aided by an in
reference ruling on pass, reached
the Minnesota 28.


Kinnick, although rushed by hard
charging Gophers, sailed the ball
into. the end zone, where bound
ing Bill Green, substitute Iowa full
back, tucked 1t close to his chest.


Hawkeye Fans Near Hysteria.

into near hysteria, for it meant the
first victory over the Gophers since
Iowa won, 8 to 7, in 1929, and the
first Iowa triumph over q team

nick's drop kick TO rthat extra point

gain In motor output, business de-

These factors stood out as the
week came to close:


Steel production slipped for the
seventh consecutive week. Car

NAL upturns were scored In residen-

Leonard Ayres, Cleveland econo-

automobile industry. Businessmen

Buying Power Gains.

the buying power of the dollar is
somewhat larger than at this time
year ago, as calculated by the Ma.

research organization supported
by large industries and corporations.
The second was that farm income
was reported by the Commerce De-
partment at a slightly higher level
than last year.


The week brought the following
entries to the business ledger: Com
mercial, industrial and agricultural
loans gained a little. Engineering

prices for farm products, hides, raw

The renewed fighting followed the
breakdown of peace efforts yester-

surrender


The action drew artillery and war
planes into battle in the snow-cov-

and infantry units, were withdraw
ing into France.


Reports reaching the border said
the battle started with an exchange
of shots between the government
rear guard and insurgent field gun
units which were approaching PUG
cerda.


Planes Join Fight.


Shortly afterwards insurgent
planes joined the fight, strafing the
northbound militiamen, while gov
ernment artillery poured shells into
insurgent positions.


Military observers at the border
said the bombardment was louder
than any heard during previous ar
tillery engagements high in the
mountain passes.


Three insurgent planes machine
gunned the city of Puigcerda itself
this morning for period of eight
minutes. Flying less than 200 feet
from rooftops, their rapid-flre guns
sprayed thousands of slugs into
streets and houses. Spanish sources
said the injured probably would
reach more than 100.


The pilots refrained from bomb
ing the city, from which'a majority
of the civilian population had been
evacuated during the last two days.
Troops and police we're the prin-
cipal inhabitants when the attack
occurred.

still insisted that Spain's freedom
from foreign influence, plebiscite
to determine her future government
and clemency for government sup
porters be conditions for peace.

Moscow Tossing Bouquets.

Jumped into the arena"

anything seen here for months. The
next few days, 1t was believed, might
clarity the situation still further.

The recent speech of the British

Of the French government also con-
stitute step forward for clarif1ca-
ton of problem which agitates all
peaceful people"


"The policy of several states is
evolving in direction correspond

"The U. S. S. r., powerful and
peaceful, always has worked for
consolidation of peace. She always
has pronounced herself for a clear
and precise position on the most
important international problems"


Armed Threats Cited.

East and Southeastern Europe, as
we'll as the Near East, were direct

with characteristic clarity and

BY the Associated Press.


BARBERTON, Ohio, June In
veStigators unearthed a broken gas
main today outside the wrecked
school building where a blast in
jured SO children and four adults.


Fire Chief Claude Witwer said a
complete break was found in the
IA Inch pipe feeding the frame
temporary school, former resi-
dence, with natural gas. The break
he said, was about nine feet outside
the basement and the ground around
the break was permeated with
fumes.


Chief Witwer said investigators
theorized that the pipe might have
been defective before the explosion,
and that fumes perhaps seeped into
the basement from the break. School
officials said the gas meter inside the
structure had been turned off about
two months ago.


Of the ST injured, two small chill
dren and a janitor were given
scarcely fighting chance to sur
vive.


Four Others Seriously Hurt.


Doctors described as serious the
condition of four others, including
teacher. Thirty-one of the 81
injured were confined to hospitals.
The blast occurred at midafter-
noon yesterday, blowing out walls
and buckling the floors of the two
story, elght-roOm structure, a resi-
dence converted last fall into a
temporary school for first to fifth
grade pupils.


Those near death were First
graders Dorothy Young, 6, and
Frances Fisher, 7, both injured about
the head and body, and P S. White,
SO, janitor, critically burned.


Investigation Opened.


Seriously hurt were Ray Clemens,
7, internal injuries; Lucinda Will
liams. 7, colored, burns; Mary Mat
tingly, 7. possible skull fracture, and
Miss Mabelle Miller, 38, 1-B teacher
fractured leg and ribs and possible
internal injuries.


The State Department of Indus
trial Relations opened an investiga-
ton of the tragedy, remindful of
the 1887 New London, Tex, school
blast, in which 297 children and
teachers met death. The United
States Bureau of Mines ordered two
chemical engineers who have spe-
cialized in gas to investigate.


The worst part of this is that
some of the little girls probably will
be disfigured for life said a work.
man who aided in rescue work.


Fire Chief WitWer said earlier that
evidence indicated gas accumulated
in the basement from a lead near the
buildings foundation.


The janitor, who said he had been
burning paper in the basement. NUT
tered before lapsing into uncon-
sciousness: The whole basement
must have been filled with gas


Building Ripped Apart.


AS the blast ripped the building
apart, the sides of the structure
erumpled. Some children literally
were blown to the ground. The lit
tie tenants of the 1-B room. on the
first floor, plunged into the base
ment amid a litter of desks, timbers
and plaster.


Second-story floors slanted as on
hinges, hurting children and equip
ment downward. Many youngsters
were buried under debris.


Miss Miller was injured when
struck by a falling piano She was
rescued by John Ruhlen. carpenter
at work on the nearby grade school
which is being rebuilt. Another
teacher was less seriously hurt.

PHILADELPHIA, April 24.-In-
dividual athletes may steal the show
this week end when the University
of Pennsylvania presents its 45th
annual relay carnival-an event
originally built around the four Imam
running combination.


Relay races, from sectional high
school affairs to American cham
plonship events, dominate as usual
the tWo-day program Friday and
Saturday. But the individual events
have attracted entries of some of the
Nations outstanding stars.


The presence of six defending
champions and the Nations leading
sprinters and hurdlers account for
the potential brilliance of the special
events.


Great Sprint Battle Looms.


Mozel Ellerbe of Tuskegee and
Wilbur Greer of Michigan State will
compete in a picked field for 100
yard dash honors. Greer recently
turned in 95 seconds performance
in winning the Texas relays, while
Ellerbe. national collegiate century
champion, turned the tables at Sat-
urday's Kansas relays in the same
time, winning by inches when Greer
pulled a muscle.


Such Eastern standouts as Herb
Weast, Columbia: John Maher, VIII
lanova, and Frank Oil, Pittsburgh,
are others in the sprint field.


Defending Champion Don Kinzle
of Duke University, Pennsylvania
native, who won Southern Confer
ence honors, faces title holders of
two other conferences in the 120-
yard high hurdles event. Elmer
Gedeon of Michigan, Big Ten cham
pion; Jay Shields of Yale, I. c. "A
indoor champion, and w. E. Whaley
of washington and Lee are rated
as Kinzles chief rivals.


Other Defending Champions.


Other defending individual cham
pions include Francis Ryan, Colum-
bias shotputter, seeking his third
straight relays victory; William
Watson, Michigan broad jumper;
William Faymonville of Notre Dame,
who set carnival record in the
discus last year; Nick Vukmanic,
Penn States national collegiate,
A. A. U. and I. c. 4-A javelin throw
champion, and Richard Ganslen of
Columbia. who tied for first place
in the pole vault last year.


Three collegiate quartets will be
seeking their third straight Ameri-
can championships in the relay
events-Manhattan in the mile,
Indiana in the 4-mile and Pitts
burgh in the sprint medley. Not
since 1908, when Michigan won its
last of six straight titles, has any
college won more than two conse-
cutive 4-mile races. The last team
to win the 2-mile event three years
in a row was Pennsylvania 1912
quartet.


Rideouts Again in Meet.


The Rideout twins, Wayne and
Blaine, will return as members of
North Texas Teachers 4-mile team
that set new world record last
year. They turned in a remark
able job Saturday to help clip more
than II seconds off the Kansas
relays distance medley standard.


The 1-mile relay classic, with
Pittsburgh as defending champion,
has strong field that includes
Fordham's indoor world champion
ship combination.

CRISFIELD, Md, Aug. 5.-A
swirling waterspout defied tradition
during sudden downpour yester-
day, swept inland from the POGO
moke River and caused slight dam
age to several homes in Birdtown,
small river-bordering village miles
from here.


The spout, one of several that
lifted off the river within 80 min
utes, disregarded the custom of
waterspouts, which usually stick to
water, and swerved suddenly toward
shore.


A number of windows were
broken and several homes were
splattered with marshland mud,
carried along by the twisting tunnel
of water.


Allen Parks, a crabber on the
river in 28-foot boat, narrowly

LILLE, France, Aug. 5.-The
mystery of 600 rubber balls
found on a highway leading
from the Belgian frontier was
solved today after police dis
covered they were only tennis
balls without their canvas COW
ers which had rolled off a truck
during routine shipment from
Lille to Paris.


Detectives had announced
after cutting open some of the
balls and finding in them two
pellets filled with yellowand
ivory-colored corrosive liquids
that the chemicals were similar
in some respects to explosives
used by Irish Republican Army
terrorists in England.


A representative of the man
ufacturers, however, explained
that the pellets were designed
to melt with the heat and form
a gas which give the tennis
balls more bounce.

CHICAGO, Oct. 7.-Wheat prices
dropped more than q cent a bushel
today following the official forecast
Of scattered showers for most of the
grain belt, including the hard winter
wheat belt .,ehere serious fall
drought prevails.


The weekly weather forecast also
predicted rains In important grain
belt territory.


The price slump, which wiped out
what was left OF the steep upturn
that followed the Hitler speech yes
terday, carried December and MAY
contracts down to 81M in early deal
1ngs and thereafter prices fluctuated
nervously near that level. Weakness
in securities and uncertainty regard
Ing the European situation en-
couraged some selling. Failure Of
the Winnipeg market to follow the
decline here resulted in steadiness
after the lows had been reached.


The Kansas Weather Bureau re-
ported that September gave that
State a combination of heat.
drought and unfavorable growing
weather that has not been equaled
In any other September on record.
Few localities had as much as "a
inch of rain. Dust storms occurred
with considerable frequency in
southwestern counties.


European export demand for
North American wheat remained
quiet.


Corn prices fell about a cent with
wheat. H. c. Donovan, crop expert,
reported that throughout Northern
Illinois husking is under way. The
quality generally is good, he said,
although some late corn shows
shrinkage due to forced ripeninR.
Yields are heavy.


Oats and rye were fractionally
lower and lard also was down
slightly.

Collegiate fistic supremacy of the
East and South will be settled to-
night at College Park when Mary
lands undefeated Southern Confer
ence champions exchange wallops
with Army's unblemished Eastern
intercollegiate titleholders at 8
o'clock.


Maryland will enter the climaxing
scrap of its season with a deficit,
electing to forfeit the heavyweight
engagement rather than risk injury
to its representative against hard
hitting formidable Harry Stella, 2l0-
pound Army football star


In remaining bouts, however, the
Terps are conceded an excellent
chance and are relying chiefly on
Benny Alperstein, Frank Cronin and
Newton Cox, its Southern Confer
ence champions, although each Of
those lads will face undefeated box
ers at their respective weights.


Benny Battles Backer's Son.


Alperstein, swinging for the last
time after capturing four titles at
Maryland, will stack up against
Harry Rising, a local lad, whose
father, Maj. Harry Rising of the
Ordnance Department., long has
been an admirer of Benny's. Rising
has fought three times this season
and won on each occasion.


Cronin, who has won eight
straight bouts in his only year of
boxing. also will be taking his fare
we'll punches against respected
foe, Dick Negley, Army 155-pounder,
who has remained unbeaten in five
bouts this season. while Cox's op-
ponent in the 165-pound class bout,
Don Hull, also has won five argu-
mentS.


Army boasts 1888 Eastern inter-
collegiate champions in Walter
Lavendusky, 120- FOUNDER. and
Thomas Stanley. 145-pounder who
won the lightweight title last year,
and is favorite to take the team
title in the same event next week.
Lavendusky will trade blows with
red-haired George Dorr, while
Stanley will clash with Nathan
Askin.


Army Has Superior Record.


Maryland, tied three times and
victorious twice in dual matches,
will concede a superior record to
Army, which has walloped Western
Maryland, Syracuse, Cornell. Yale
and Penn State and compiled a
record of winning 26 of % individual
bouts.


Bob Bradley, Marylands unpre-
dictable featherweight, will collide
with Walter Clement, while homas
Ward, Army light-heavyweight, will
face Morton Steinback in engage
ments which will have an important
bearing on the outcome.
